Scientists Just Challenged a 50-Year-Old Theory About How Evolution Works

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In bacteria and yeast, a gene’s importance did not predict its mutation rate, challenging the idea that evolution gives vital DNA preferential treatment.
  • Not all genes are equally important.
  • Sources indicate that for decades, scientists have debated whether essential genes are naturally less likely to mutate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In bacteria and yeast, a gene’s importance did not predict its mutation rate, challenging the idea that evolution gives vital DNA preferential treatment.

Not all genes are equally important. Some are essential for survival, controlling basic functions such as copying DNA and keeping cells alive. Others can be lost with little or no effect. But does that mean evolution has found a way to shield its most vital genes from potentially harmful mutations?

Sources indicate that for decades, scientists have debated whether essential genes are naturally less likely to mutate. Now, researchers at the University of Bath have put that idea to the test, with results that challenge a long-standing evolutionary hypothesis.

According to recent reports, dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D. Hurst, from the university’s Centre for Evolution, examined spontaneous mutations in the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). Their study, published November 12 in PLOS Biology, found no evidence that essential genes receive extra protection and offers a new explanation for why earlier research may have suggested otherwise.

“We’d expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more crucial genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them – what you can think of as ‘ghost mutations’,” Hurst said.

To reduce that problem, the team used data from “mutation accumulation” experiments designed to minimize the effects of natural selection. Three separate tests found no evidence that selection had substantially skewed the results.

“This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date,” Radrizzani stated.

In a recent development, the researchers compared mutation rates with experimental evidence showing what happens when individual genes are removed. Deleting an essential gene kills the cell, while losing other genes has little or no effect. This gave the team a way to test whether genes a cell depends on most were less likely to mutate.

“Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate,” Hurst said.

The team also assessed importance through the amount of a gene’s protein the cell produces and the strength of natural selection acting on the gene over evolutionary time.

In a recent development, “We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don’t have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate,” Radrizzani noted.

It has been revealed that these findings address a debate that began in 1972 and resurfaced as recently as 2023. At stake is the relationship between the two steps in the conventional account of evolution. Mutations first generate genetic variation. Natural selection and other forces then act on that variation, favoring some traits over others.

In a recent development, darwin’s finches, which Charles Darwin encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835, offer a familiar example. Random mutations contribute to differences in beak size, allowing birds to use different food sources. When conditions favor particular foods, birds with beaks better suited to eating them are more likely to survive and reproduce. Their traits consequently become more common over generations.

The disputed proposal suggests that a gene’s importance also influences how often mutations arise in it. Vital genes would receive greater protection, while genes where change could help adaptation would mutate more frequently. Examples of the latter include genes in which mutations give bacteria antibiotic resistance or alter birds’ beak dimensions.

There is a theoretical difficulty with that proposal. Gene mutation rates are already so low that reducing them further for individual genes would offer very little benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

“The claim that mutation is slower for key genes is a triumph of hype over substance,” stated Radrizzani, who co-wrote the paper as part of her PhD. “It’s a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.”.

Genes copied later during DNA replication did tend to mutate more frequently in the team’s analysis, showing that some features of the genome can help explain differences in mutation rates.

Industry observers note that “While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm,” Hurst said.

Reference: “The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate” by Sofia Radrizzani and Laurence D. Hurst, 12 November 2026, PLOS Biology. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3004089.

Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component.
  • People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity.
  • Industry observers note that in a typical optical clock, an electron within an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, and an ultra-stable laser is tuned, or locked, to the frequency of that oscillation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component. It could be used to diagnose shifts in the sun’s velocity or probe processes on its surface.

This is not your mother’s sundial. People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity. But contemporary record-breaking timekeepers, which are called optical clocks, derive their accuracy from quantum mechanical effects and typically have atoms that have been isolated from the external world at their core. Now, Scott Diddams at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and his colleagues have built an optical clock that relies on sunlight instead.

Industry observers note that in a typical optical clock, an electron within an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, and an ultra-stable laser is tuned, or locked, to the frequency of that oscillation. Next, these oscillations – the ups and downs of the light waves that comprise the laser beam – are translated into usable ticks of a clock. To do this, researchers use a device called a frequency comb, which turns visible light into microwaves that can be processed by standard electronics.

First working nuclear clock heralds a newly introduced era in timekeeping.

In the upcoming experiment, the researchers still used a laser and a frequency comb to build their clock, but the role of the atom was played by a process that happens near the sun.

Specifically, instead of locking their laser to an electron’s jumps within an atom, the researchers locked it to a process where sunlight causes similar jumps as it hits iron atoms in our star’s atmosphere. This process leaves a signature in the spectrum of colours that comprise sunlight, so the team collected sunlight into a special fibre and fed it into the rest of the clock. This type of solar optical clock has never been built before.

Industry observers note that while the latest clock doesn’t rival the best atomic optical clocks in accuracy, the researchers highlighted that it could possibly be used as a tool for studying stars. During the partial solar eclipse in 2024, they observed a signature shift in the sunlight’s spectrum due to the moon passing in front of the star. If the clock was fed light from a faraway star in place of sunlight, similar shifts could indicate the presence of orbiting exoplanets, which raises the possibility of the new clock design becoming a tool for astronomical discovery. In this case, however, starlight would have to be collected through large telescopes, sometimes over long periods of time.

Researchers have designed a quantum version of a pendulum clock. It could shed light on timekeeping in the quantum realm.

Piet Schmidt at the National Metrology Institute of Germany claims that the new work is interesting because it demonstrates an optical clock design that leverages light from the stars rather than being based exclusively on objects under tight control in the lab.

But as an astronomical instrument, it doesn’t yet surpass existing methods for studying light from stars, and for very distant stars, the latest clock’s usefulness would be seriously limited by how faint their light is, says Schmidt.

In a recent development, there may, however, be advantages in studying the properties of our sun, he says. For example, the clock could probe eruptive events, sunspots and the effects of solar “wind” made from streams of charged particles in the outer layers of the sun’s atmosphere.

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.28485.

  • In a recent development, scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, science has reached a fresh low. Temperature, that is.

In a recent development, scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

Recent findings suggest that to make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an glitch for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why you should watch for the November Leonid meteors this year.

In a recent development, itâs always worth being vigilant when skywatching in mid- to late November. Every year, a few Leonid meteors punctuate the November morning sky around the 17th. These silent harbingers are only a hint at the showerâs true storm potential, which culminates once every three decades.

The Leonid meteor shower can put on a true spectacle, and while 2026 isnât expected to be a âstorm year,â we could be due for some enhanced activity in the late 2020s going into the early 2030s.

According to recent reports, the source of the Leonid meteor shower is periodic comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. On a 33 year orbit, comet 55P reaches perihelion 0.975 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun just inside Earthâs orbit once again on May 20, 2031.

Hubble captures Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Credit: NASA/HST/STScI.

Industry observers note that in 2026 the Moon phase is favorable at 41% illuminated, reaching 1st quarter phase a day after the showerâs peak night on November 16-17th. This means the Moon sets in the west, right as the radiant rises to the east.

Sources indicate that the peak of the 2026 Leonids is set for November 17th at 3:00 Universal Time (UT), favoring Europe towards dawn, and North America just a few hours later. While 2026 is projected to be a 20 meteors per hour peak year, you just never know what a particular shower might have in store.

In a recent development, the Leonids are also real fast movers, approaching the Earth nearly head-on with a combined velocity of close to 70 kilometers per second. This is very near the theoretical maximum for inner solar system meteors. Most years only see a paltry 20 or so meteors per hour, though when the parent comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle is near perihelion, great storms are possible.

The Leonids hail from the backwards, question mark-shaped âSickle of Leoâ asterism. The radiant tracks from the +3rd magnitude star Epsilon Leonis past the bright double star Algieba in November. If you can trace a meteorâs flight back to this region, itâs a Leonid.

As an added treat in 2026, the planets Mars and Jupiter are very nearby, along with the bright star Regulus and the antihelion point towards which our planet is currently headed.

Recent findings suggest that the rising Leonid radiant in 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Industry observers note that the Leonids top out with great outbursts every 33 years. A loose definition for a âmeteor stormâ is when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) tops out at about a 1,000 per hour, which is a fast-paced rate of one meteor every 3-4 seconds. Keep in mind, the ZHR is an extrapolated, ideal rate, assuming dark skies with the showerâs radiant directly overhead at the zenith. Most observers will always see less in reality, as fainter meteors slip by.

According to recent reports, records of the Leonids go all the way back to Arab annuals dating from 902 AD. 1833 saw an historic storm from the shower, as frightened residents along the U.S. Eastern Seaboard awoke to a sky awash in meteors. This single event was not only responsible in part for several religious movements of the day in the U.S., but also helped to push the modern scientific understanding of meteors from a purely atmospheric phenomenon to one originating from space.

Sources indicate that A depiction of the Great Leonid Storm of 1833, depicted in 1889 by Adolf Vollmy. Credit: Public Domain.

It has been revealed that the morning of November 17, 1966 saw a formidable performance from the shower, with observed rates over the southwestern U.S. topping out at an estimated 160,000 per hour (!).

Sources indicate that I still remember catching the 1998 Leonids from the deserts of Kuwait, a year before the advertised outburst in 1999. The meteors lit up the desert floor just seconds apart towards sunrise with brilliant photo-flash flares. The spectacle continued right up until dawn. To date, it was still one of the best meteor showers Iâve ever witnessed.

Are we in for another great âmeteor stormâ in or around 2033? Well, we passed the mid-point in 2017. We did see a steady uptick in meteor activity through the late 1990s leading up to 1999. A caveat, however is in order with the approach of the Leonids in the early 2030s. Current models suggest we wonât see any great storms on the 2031 and 2064 passes of the comet, with 2099 being the next great âstorm yearâ. We may, however, still see respectable showers in excess of 100 per hour in the early 2030s laid down by older streams, topping the annual Perseid and Geminid meteors.

In a recent development, A Leonid double-shot. Credit: Eliot Herman.

According to recent reports, observing a meteor shower is as simple as laying back and watching the sky, no special equipment needed. All you need is clear, dark skies and patience. Youâll see more in the early morning hours, as Earth hurdles headlong into the oncoming meteor stream. Imaging Leonids is a simple as setting up a tripod-mounted DSLR camera equipped with a wide-field lens to take long exposure shots of the sky, and seeing what turns up. An intervalometer hand control works great to automate this process.

An all-sky capture featuring a Leonid meteor. Credit: Eliot Herman.

Finally, be sure to count and record what you see, and send those observations to the International Meteor Organization.

Weâll see what the coming years has in store for the November Leonid meteors. One thing is for certain: youâll see zero meteors if you donât try. Time will tell if the coming years see the Leonids roar once again.

#7174. Breaking: What Is Science, Really? Even Scientists Can’t Agree

Breaking: What Is Science, Really? Even Scientists Can’t Agree

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.
  • Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both?
  • In a recent development, study leader Marina Dubova, a former Santa Fe Institute postdoctoral researcher, is now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even scientists in the same specialty disagree about science’s purpose, a survey finds, raising concerns that AI could automate one narrow approach at others’ expense.

Is science a search for objective truth, an exercise in creative problem-solving, or both? A study published in Royal Society Open Science found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science more than the general public does.

In a recent development, study leader Marina Dubova, a former Santa Fe Institute postdoctoral researcher, is now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. Working with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu, she surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants evaluated 18 historical descriptions of science, including science as detective work, a search for truth, and a mirror reflecting reality.

It has been revealed that scientists and the public generally agreed that science involves following curiosity and solving mysteries. The public tended to share an idealized picture of science as a reliable way to discover how the world works, placing less emphasis on creativity or uncertainty. That outlook could shape how people judge research and help explain their frustration when scientists cannot give firm answers or revise their conclusions as new evidence emerges.

According to recent reports, the public’s views were closer to those of physicists and biologists than to those of researchers in psychology or the social sciences. One possible explanation, Dubova suggests, is that physics and biology feature more prominently in science education. More research is needed to test that connection.

Some scientists emphasized the search for objective truth, while others gave more weight to the judgment and creativity researchers bring to their work. They also disagreed about whether research follows established methods or requires improvisation. Few of the 18 descriptions received scientists’ full support, and they often had reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

It has been revealed that “What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield,” says Dubova. She suspects that researchers develop their approaches partly through experience, much as chefs develop different instincts about when to follow a recipe and when to improvise. Those differing conceptions of science could influence which discoveries researchers pursue.

It has been revealed that that diversity also raises a question for efforts to automate scientific research. As researchers develop artificial intelligence systems capable of conducting science, whose understanding of the work will those systems embody? Dubova worries that automation could reinforce one narrow conception of science at the expense of other valuable approaches.

Recent findings suggest that for Dubova, the study is an early step toward understanding how these outlooks shape research itself. “Don’t take the common understanding of science for granted,” she says. “Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Everyone knows what science is…until you ask” by Marina Dubova and Qiawen E. Liu, 11 November 2026, Royal Society Open Science. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260933.

Industry observers note that the research was supported by SFI’s Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, established in 2022 to support exploratory research by early-career scientists. Dubova used the funding to compensate study participants, helping make the research possible.

Breaking: Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts.
  • Sources indicate that tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century.
  • It has been revealed that this isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Sources indicate that tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

It has been revealed that this isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

According to recent reports, but this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

Industry observers note that teCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

Sources indicate that this unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole latest operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

According to recent reports, those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel.

According to recent reports, that being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. At the moment, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do initiative to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

Researchers Have Discovered That a 6,000-Year-Old Clue to Ireland’s Farming History Was Completely Wrong

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.
  • For more than 30 years, the “Kerry Cow” helped shape a story about how farming reached Ireland.
  • The fragments were unearthed during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriter’s Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protein tests on ancient bones have removed evidence of farming’s influence in Ireland before 4000 BCE, reopening questions about when the island first encountered agriculture.

For more than 30 years, the “Kerry Cow” helped shape a story about how farming reached Ireland. Bone fragments found on the coast of County Kerry appeared to show that domesticated cattle had arrived while the island’s inhabitants still lived by hunting and gathering. A upcoming analysis has revealed that those supposed cattle were a bear and a wild boar.

The fragments were unearthed during excavations in the 1980s and 1990s at Ferriter’s Cove, a small bay on the Dingle Peninsula. Dated to the end of Ireland’s Mesolithic period, which lasted from 8000 to 4000 BCE, they were considered the earliest evidence of domesticated farm animals in either Ireland or Britain.

Their identification as cattle challenged existing theories about Ireland’s transition to farming, suggesting that its hunter-gatherers had established links with Neolithic farmers arriving from continental Europe before agriculture took hold on the island.

It has been revealed that researchers led by Dr. Martin Moucheron at University College Dublin (UCD) returned to the original archaeological material, now stored at University College Cork (UCC). Working with Drs. Benjamin Gearey, Barra Ó Donnabháin, and Margaret McCarthy at UCC, and Kate Kanne at UCD, the team sent the bones to the CNRS laboratory in Lille, France.

There, the fragments underwent analysis using ZooMS, a technique that identifies animals through proteins preserved in ancient bone collagen, a structural component of bone. The results identified bear and wild boar rather than the domesticated cattle on which the earlier interpretation depended.

Reported in the latest edition of PAST, the newsletter of the Prehistoric Society, the findings remove a major piece of evidence from debates about when and how communities in Ireland and Britain moved from hunting and gathering to farming. There is currently no archaeological evidence supporting the idea that domesticated cattle, and by extension early farming communities, had reached or influenced Ireland before 4000 BCE. Losing that evidence does not establish a upcoming arrival date, but it changes the basis for reconstructing that transition.

“Ferriter’s Cove is an iconic archaeological site, originally excavated by the Late Professor Peter Woodman, Department of Archaeology, UCC; this latest collaboration with colleagues at UCD marks an exciting new phase of research and these remarkable results are set to change our understanding of the earliest evidence for agriculture in Ireland,” remarked Gearey.

According to recent reports, the work is part of a Research Ireland-funded postdoctoral project at UCD’s School of Archaeology, led by Moucheron under the mentorship of Professor Graeme Warren. The project is reexamining vital Mesolithic archaeological sites using modern scientific techniques.

Warren added, “These exciting results show the real value in going back to key sites with fresh analytical techniques – which can change the stories we tell about our past”.

“For at least four millennia hunting and gathering people lived on the island, and there is a common conception that they left little trace and that we know very little about them – unlike the megaliths of Neolithic farmers, who are portrayed in ways that feel very familiar in Ireland,” said Moucheron.

“But there is much we can understand about Mesolithic people just by going back to the sites and material we have, and by looking at them with latest eyes and new techniques – and an open mind.”.

Further analyses are underway to determine whether the bear remains belonged to brown bears or polar bears. The researchers hope this work will provide upcoming insights into Ireland’s prehistoric bear populations before their extinction during the Bronze Age.

Reference: “No sacred cows: ZooMS identification of the Late Mesolithic bone assemblage at Ferriter’s Cove, Co. Kerry, Ireland”.

#7170. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1367 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy.
  • According to recent reports, one of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground.
  • Sources indicate that despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, one of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Sources indicate that despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Industry observers note that since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

It has been revealed that this image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille).

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

According to recent reports, "We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

In a recent development, this is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

Industry observers note that the researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions.".

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

It has been revealed that astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

In a recent development, this is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

According to recent reports, more observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide crucial observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

#7169. Breaking: James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Planet That Was Hiding in Plain Sight

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: James Webb Telescope Reveals a Giant Planet That Was Hiding in Plain Sight

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding planets like Earth may depend on better ways to read telescope images, after a fresh technique uncovered a giant world already captured by JWST.
  • According to recent reports, A giant planet was hiding in observations taken by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), even though astronomers already knew it existed.
  • Sources indicate that this is one of the biggest challenges in photographing planets beyond our solar system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding planets like Earth may depend on better ways to read telescope images, after a fresh technique uncovered a giant world already captured by JWST.

According to recent reports, A giant planet was hiding in observations taken by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), even though astronomers already knew it existed. The telescope had captured its faint light, but the overwhelming glow of its host star made the planet impossible to distinguish using conventional image-processing techniques.

Sources indicate that this is one of the biggest challenges in photographing planets beyond our solar system. Stars are extraordinarily bright compared with the worlds orbiting them, and even JWST, which can observe galaxies billions of years in the past, struggles to separate a planet’s faint signal from its star’s glare.

Researchers led by Northwestern University developed a latest computational technique that helped overcome this problem. By accounting for tiny imperfections in the telescope, they improved its sensitivity to faint planets by 2 to 15 times and recovered a giant planet that had remained hidden in two-year-old observations. Their findings were published in the journal Nature.

Industry observers note that “Planets are a million times fainter than their stars,” said Northwestern’s Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, who led the study. “So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare. That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears. Slight shifts or tilts — even on the scale of just a few nanometers — can change the pattern of light. Our method models how light travels through the telescope and accounts for those tiny changes, allowing us to remove the glare much more precisely.”.

In a recent development, ferrer-Chavez is a Ph.D. student in astronomy at Northwestern’s Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and a member of Jason Wang’s research group. Wang, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Weinberg, co-authored the study. Both researchers belong to Northwestern’s Center for Interdisciplinary Exploration and Research in Astrophysics (CIERA).

Astronomers have long relied on specialized instruments called coronagraphs to block starlight when searching for planets. Even relatively bright young giant planets can be 100,000 times fainter than their stars, making this step essential. However, some light still escapes around the coronagraph, creating patterns of glare that can conceal nearby objects.

“For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference,” Wang mentioned. “Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden.”.

The difficulty is that a telescope never remains perfectly still. Minute changes in its mirrors and other components can alter how starlight spreads across an image. Even a slight mismatch between the reference photograph and the original observation can leave enough residual glare to hide a planet.

Recent findings suggest that “We try to make telescopes extremely stable, but there are extreme engineering challenges that we haven’t quite solved yet,” Wang noted. “There are known causes of instability and unknown causes. Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer. Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. So, there are problems like those but also issues that we still don’t understand as we learn how to build these complex telescopes.”.

To address these limitations, the Northwestern researchers developed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP). Instead of relying entirely on reference photographs, the technique creates a digital twin of the telescope, a computer model that recreates how starlight travels through its mirrors and reaches its detectors.

The team used powerful computational tools to adjust millions of parameters in the model, accounting for subtle movements, optical distortions, and other imperfections. By repeatedly refining the simulation until it closely matched the real observations, FLIP could reproduce the unwanted starlight more accurately and subtract it from the image.

Recent findings suggest that this visualization demonstrates the image processing method, called FLIP, as it subtracts starlight from a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observation of star 51 Eridani A (51 Eri) in the F430M filter. Starlight subtraction proceeds with the iteration number shown in the lower left, eventually revealing the faint planet 51 Eri b at its expected location. Credit: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez.

Although the approach used optimization techniques commonly associated with machine learning, it relied on the known physics of the telescope rather than artificial intelligence to recognize planets.

Sources indicate that “We used the same computational tools that researchers use to train AI models, but we did not actually use AI,” Wang mentioned. “Because we already know the physics, we don’t need AI to understand what’s happening.”.

Industry observers note that the researchers tested FLIP using existing JWST observations of three stars. Two, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, had known planets, while the third, TYC 5899, had no known planetary companions. The technique consistently outperformed conventional image processing, particularly when examining light from extremely faint objects.

It has been revealed that one of the clearest demonstrations involved 51 Eridani b, a giant planet previously discovered using ground-based telescopes. Although astronomers knew the planet existed, it had remained hidden in JWST observations at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 microns.

That wavelength is especially valuable because carbon dioxide strongly absorbs infrared light there, potentially allowing astronomers to investigate a planet’s atmospheric composition. However, carbon dioxide absorption in 51 Eridani b’s atmosphere made its already faint signal even harder to detect.

When Ferrer-Chavez applied FLIP to the same observations, the planet emerged from the glare.

It has been revealed that “We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see,” Wang stated. “This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way.”.

Sources indicate that the result suggested that valuable information about distant planets could already be present in existing telescope observations, waiting for better processing methods to reveal it. More precise removal of starlight could also help astronomers study planets at different wavelengths, potentially uncovering new details about their atmospheres.

It has been revealed that the approach could have implications for future space missions as well. NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars. Detecting such small, faint worlds may require optical stability at the picometer scale, equivalent to trillionths of a meter. That would mean keeping the telescope roughly 100 to 1,000 times more stable than JWST.

Rather than relying entirely on engineering to achieve that precision, methods like FLIP could potentially compensate for some of the tiny imperfections that interfere with observations. For now, the researchers hoped their technique would help astronomers recover previously hidden planets and expand the range of worlds they could study.

Industry observers note that “We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system,” Ferrer-Chavez said. “It’s not that they don’t exist. It’s that we cannot see them. Every time we improve our techniques, we discover fresh types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is.”.

Reference: “Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit” by Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Jason J. Wang, Katherine L. Bouman, William T. Freeman, Laurent Pueyo, Brandon Y. Feng and Marshall D. Perrin, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z.

Supported by the Space Telescope Science Institute (award number JWST-AR-07942), the Sloan Foundation (award number FG-2025-24976) and the National Science Foundation (award number PHY-2525568).

How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Octopuses have made many a great escape.
  • Industry observers note that the cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from Fresh Zealand’s national aquarium?

Industry observers note that the cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

It has been revealed that octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”.

Recent findings suggest that sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

According to recent reports, kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Sources indicate that octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Organization of Biologists.

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

According to recent reports, when the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Manufacturer of Biologists.

In a recent development, mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba notes. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

Recent findings suggest that the team hopes these escape artists will inspire newly introduced soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, notes Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”.

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Presently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.
  • The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.
  • Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.

The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

The El Niño climate phase, which has already warmed surface waters in the tropical Pacific to record temperatures and continues to heat up, tends to keep the vortex strong in autumn and early winter. Then, in late winter, it often weakens the vortex, allowing that cold air to spill southwards into Europe and sometimes North America.

In a recent development, but on 10 November, the polar vortex weakened to the point that it broke down, with the winds reversing direction to blow weakly from the east. While these collapses happen every few years, they almost never occur in November. This is the earliest it has happened since weather balloon records began in the 1950s, beating the old record by 18 days.

Sources indicate that this may have been due to random fluctuations in the atmosphere. It is also possible, however, that the extremely strong El Niño could have sped up the weakening of the polar vortex that typically happens later in the winter, though that isn’t proven, according to Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s weather service.

It has been revealed that “There probably is some kind of El Niño influence on it,” he indicates. “That would be my suspicion, but we don’t know that for sure.”.

Recent findings suggest that as east-to-west trade winds weaken during El Niño and the warm water they built up in the western Pacific washes back eastwards, a low-pressure centre of warm, rising air moves eastwards with it. This causes extra waviness in the jet stream, another band of strong westerly winds that circles the globe, except further south and lower in the atmosphere than the polar vortex. The jet stream meanders further southwards around Alaska, deepening a low-pressure system there called the Aleutian low.

Recent findings suggest that but the El Niño-linked wave doesn’t just propagate side to side in the jet stream. It can also propagate upwards into the stratosphere, where the polar vortex is. As the air gets thinner, the wave’s amplitude gets bigger until it crashes into the polar vortex like a wave crashing onto a beach, states Scaife. And while the polar vortex is westerly, these waves carry easterly momentum.

“When they dump that momentum, they push the polar vortex against its flow, and they weaken it,” he indicates.

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world.

In a recent development, but another reason for the polar vortex breakdown could be a high-pressure “blocking” system that developed over Scandinavia in recent weeks, which blocked the jet stream and caused large meanders in it. This waviness could also have weakened the polar vortex through the same wave-breaking process, regardless of El Niño.

“I would be wary of saying it was caused by El Niño,” states Andrew Charlton-Perez at the University of Reading, UK. “I would say the blocking high is probably more important.”.

The reversal of the polar vortex isn’t related to the current cold weather in the UK. But it could bring even more cold, snowy weather in the coming weeks.

A polar vortex breakdown is also known as a sudden stratospheric warming event. As the winds weaken, high-level air rushes in over the north pole, increasing atmospheric pressure and raising temperatures, just as pumping up a bike tyre warms it up.

Meanwhile, over the following weeks, cold surface-level air can descend from the Arctic into northern Europe. A polar vortex breakdown preceded the “Beast from the East” cold snap in 2018, when blizzards covered much of the UK in snow and killed 10 people.

While the polar vortex is expected to strengthen towards the end of November, bringing warmer weather, it could break down again this winter, Scaife warns.

“The risk of cold easterlies this winter is increasing,” he says.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that raise an atomic clock by just a few millimeters, and it ticks slightly faster because gravity is weaker at the higher position.
  • Scientists have now developed a theoretical method to detect the quantum effects of these different flows of time using advanced atomic clocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have developed a theoretical framework that could allow atomic clocks to reveal a strange quantum effect in which different flows of time exist simultaneously.

Sources indicate that raise an atomic clock by just a few millimeters, and it ticks slightly faster because gravity is weaker at the higher position. Today’s most precise clocks can detect this tiny difference, confirming a prediction of Einstein’s theory of relativity. But quantum physics introduces a stranger possibility: A single clock could exist in a superposition of different motions, potentially experiencing multiple rates of time simultaneously.

Scientists have now developed a theoretical method to detect the quantum effects of these different flows of time using advanced atomic clocks. Published in Physical Review Letters, the research demonstrates how trapped-ion clocks could reveal a previously unobserved connection between quantum mechanics and relativity. The proposed approach uses existing experimental technology and could bring researchers closer to testing how time behaves in the quantum world.

According to Einstein’s theory of relativity, time passes at different rates depending on an object’s speed and the strength of gravity. Atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect these differences across height changes of just a few millimeters. They measure time using precise atomic frequencies and are essential to technologies such as GPS.

According to recent reports, quantum mechanics introduces another possibility. An atomic clock’s motion can exist in a superposition of different states, potentially exposing it to multiple rates of time simultaneously. Under these conditions, the clock’s motion becomes entangled with its internal energy, producing changes in its quantum properties that researchers believe can be measured.

“It’s the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock’s motion becomes “entangled” with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques,” explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University’s Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the study’s lead authors.

It has been revealed that the international research team, led by scientists at Kyushu University and working with collaborators in the United States, Canada, and Sweden, also developed a theoretical approach for precisely controlling the motion of trapped ions. This could substantially increase the detectability of the quantum effect.

“We introduced a fresh technique for controlling the atomic clock’s motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.”.

The next challenge is to translate the theoretical framework into an experiment that can reliably detect the predicted quantum signature while accounting for disturbances and uncertainties in real laboratory conditions. If successful, the approach could establish atomic clocks as tools for investigating the quantum behavior of time and potentially improve future clock technology.

Sources indicate that “Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the big next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model,” concludes Foo. “We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Quantum Signatures of Proper Time in Optical Ion Clocks” by Gabriel Sorci, Joshua Foo, Dietrich Leibfried, Christian Sanner and Igor Pikovski, 20 April 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/qhj9-pc2b.

LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe.
  • For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources.
  • According to recent reports, this latest view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

According to recent reports, this latest view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON.

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This fresh view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

According to recent reports, the other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON.

Sources indicate that according to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A computer search has identified thousands of crystals worth testing as sources of ultrathin materials, potentially widening the options for future electronics.
  • Peel a crystal down to a sheet just a few atoms thick, and you may change what the material can do.
  • These ultrathin sheets are known as two-dimensional, or 2D, materials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A computer search has identified thousands of crystals worth testing as sources of ultrathin materials, potentially widening the options for future electronics.

Peel a crystal down to a sheet just a few atoms thick, and you may change what the material can do. Its electrical, magnetic, or chemical behavior can shift, opening possibilities for electronics, energy storage, and faster chemical reactions.

These ultrathin sheets are known as two-dimensional, or 2D, materials. They have attracted scientific and technological interest since graphene was produced in 2004.

It has been revealed that the challenge is finding crystals that will yield a sheet that holds together. Researchers have mostly started with crystals built like books, whose layers peel apart relatively easily because weak forces hold them together. Crystals with strong bonds running in every direction are much harder to separate.

Industry observers note that A team at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) and TU Dresden has now developed the first efficient computational method for predicting separable atomic layers in any type of crystal. The findings, published in Nature Communications, give researchers a much wider selection of materials to investigate.

In a recent development, the team screened more than 24,000 known, non-layered crystal structures from one of the largest experimental materials databases and selected 2,531 particularly promising candidates for detailed calculations. These candidates would retain their chemical composition when a layer separated, and their calculated bonding ratios strongly favored a two-dimensional structure.

Recent findings suggest that the predicted sheets differed markedly from existing database entries. Some could become metallic even though their original crystals are semiconductors, a fundamental change in how they carry electricity. Others could develop a direct band gap, an electronic feature potentially useful for devices that absorb or emit light. Magnetic candidates could also support spintronics, which uses electron spin to process and store data.

For most candidates, calculations indicated that separating a layer would require comparatively little energy. Many also appeared stable against small atomic disturbances and energetically favorable, basic requirements for technological use. Experiments must establish whether these materials can actually be made and under what conditions.

Recent findings suggest that “Given that this class of materials is still so young, selecting suitable materials for experiments was often based on experience and intuition,” explains Dr. Rico Friedrich of HZDR’s Institute of Ion Beam Physics and Materials Research and TU Dresden. “Using our universal method, we can now determine the points at which a crystal in any material can best be split and whether a potentially stable two-dimensional structure can form in the process.”.

The method starts by calculating how strongly individual atoms are bonded. Its core model, called the eXfoliation and Cleavage Potential, or XCP, makes these precise calculations using the elements involved and the distances between atoms.

It has been revealed that two additional algorithms then look for ways to separate a sheet. One searches for easily separable planes within the crystal. The other gradually removes the weakest bonds from the model until two-dimensional structures remain. The approach also detects separation surfaces that are uneven at the atomic scale.

“Calculating the electronic structure for every conceivable surface would be incredibly time-consuming,” states lead author Tom Barnowsky. “Our efficient model, on the other hand, can search major materials databases with minimal computational effort. Detailed calculations are only required for particularly promising hits.”.

Sources indicate that tests across a wide range of two-dimensional materials already produced experimentally revealed that XCP reliably identified the preferred planes for separating layers. The method is freely available as a web tool.

“Our results vastly expand the horizon for two-dimensional materials,” states Friedrich. “The method doesn’t guarantee that every candidate can be produced in the lab. But it does show which crystals are actually worth the experimental effort.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “High-Throughput Prediction of Exfoliable Non-van der Waals Materials from a Universal Potential” by Tom Barnowsky, Carsten Timm and Rico Friedrich, 25 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76806-8.

SpaceX sent its Starship on a flight that was meant to feature a first-ever retrieval of both rocket stages, but a launch-pad catch of the first-stage booster had to be canceled due to safety concerns.

It has been revealed that instead, the Super Heavy booster was diverted during its descent to make an offshore splashdown. Observers at SpaceX's Starbase on the South Texas coast could hear the sonic boom and see the fiery plunge that took place minutes after launch at 4:47 p.m. CT (2247 GMT) today. "Wow, you could feel the rumble of that splashdown there," launch commentator Jessie Anderson stated.

This 15th flight test still has a chance to make history: The mission initiative calls for the Starship second stage to spend as much as 22 hours in orbit â ending with a return to the pad for a midair capture by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms. SpaceX has caught Starship's booster during three previous test flights, but this would be a first for a second stage.

Hours after launch, SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice remarked the booster's control system triggered an abort of the launch-tower catch because the boostback engine burn ended early, apparently due to a low fuel mass alarm. SpaceX's team was still troubleshooting the root cause of the alarm, she said.

In a recent development, anderson mentioned the offshore splashdown averted the risk of damage or injuries at the launch site. "Safety is always our No. 1 priority," she said. If any further safety concerns arise, SpaceX's mission team has the option of ending the flight early and sending the second stage â known as Ship 42 â down to a controlled ocean splashdown.

After reaching orbit, Ship 42 deployed 26 satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. Three of the satellites were equipped with a suite of cameras to inspect Ship's heatshield after deployment.

Starship ranks as the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, standing 407 feet (124 meters) tall and providing 17 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The rocket is designed to deploy dozens of Starlink V3 satellites at a time â and eventually send thousands of explorers and settlers to Mars.

NASA is counting on SpaceX to provide a Starship-based system for landing astronauts on the moon by as early as 2028. As a preparatory step, NASA is planning to test Starship as well as Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system in low Earth orbit next year. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman referred to that test mission, known as Artemis III, in a post to X that took note of the video sent down from orbit via the Starlink network.

It has been revealed that "Congratulations to the SpaceX team on another spectacular launch," Isaacman wrote. "Very much appreciate how you bring the world along in high resolution. We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III.".
