📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, states Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani claims. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” claims Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

It has been revealed that scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani states.

Recent findings suggest that the same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these problems. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

It has been revealed that G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

Industry observers note that there may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough Reveals What Happens When the Brain’s Cleaning System Fails

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study suggests that a little-understood genetic risk factor may influence Alzheimer’s progression by weakening the brain’s natural defenses against toxic plaques.
  • In a recent development, A gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease may play a crucial role in protecting the brain from toxic protein buildup.
  • The findings suggest that CASS4 influences Alzheimer’s primarily through the brain’s immune system rather than by acting directly in nerve cells, as some scientists previously suspected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study suggests that a little-understood genetic risk factor may influence Alzheimer’s progression by weakening the brain’s natural defenses against toxic plaques.

In a recent development, A gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease may play a crucial role in protecting the brain from toxic protein buildup. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that CASS4 helps immune cells contain harmful plaques, and experiments in mice show that disrupting the gene can accelerate plaque accumulation, damage neurons, and contribute to cognitive decline.

The findings suggest that CASS4 influences Alzheimer’s primarily through the brain’s immune system rather than by acting directly in nerve cells, as some scientists previously suspected. Researchers now believe that restoring or strengthening its activity could offer a upcoming approach to treating the disease.

Industry observers note that alzheimer’s disease, which affects more than 6 million Americans, is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and abnormal tangles of tau proteins in the brain. These changes are associated with progressive damage to neurons and worsening memory and cognitive function.

Recent findings suggest that specialized immune cells called microglia help defend the brain against these threats. When functioning properly, they gather around amyloid-beta plaques, form protective barriers, and compress the deposits into smaller, more compact structures that can limit their harmful effects.

Researchers led by John Lukens, PhD, found that CASS4 plays an vital role in this protective process. In laboratory mice lacking normal CASS4 function, microglia became less effective at surrounding and compacting plaques. Amyloid deposits accumulated more aggressively, neuronal damage increased, and the animals experienced cognitive decline.

Industry observers note that although previous genetic studies had repeatedly associated CASS4 with Alzheimer’s risk, scientists had little understanding of its biological function. The UVA team investigated how the gene influences microglial activity and what happens when that activity is disrupted.

“Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper,” noted Addie Walsh, a UVA physiology graduate student and the study’s first author. “These are key findings because they give us fresh insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.”.

Disrupting CASS4 also triggered widespread changes in gene activity. The researchers suspect that some of these alterations could be relevant to other neurodegenerative disorders, although the gene’s involvement in those conditions remains under investigation.

The results raise the possibility that CASS4 could eventually help researchers identify Alzheimer’s related changes earlier or develop therapies that improve the brain’s ability to manage amyloid plaques. However, the findings come from preclinical research, and further studies are needed to determine whether targeting the gene would benefit patients.

“These findings break fresh ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer’s disease,” mentioned Lukens, director of UVA’s Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer’s and Neurodegenerative Diseases. “Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer’s and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.”.

Sources indicate that the study also supports growing research into how immune dysfunction contributes to neurodegeneration. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate around them, scientists are increasingly investigating whether modifying microglial responses could help protect brain tissue.

“We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it,” said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. “Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer’s. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.”.

Walsh prepares to continue investigating the role of microglia in neurodegenerative diseases as she moves into pharmaceutical research.

“I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical firm Novartis,” she said. “I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration.”.

Lukens, 27 October 2026, Journal of Experimental Medicine. DOI: 10.1084/jem.20260104.

Latest Update: Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.
  • Industry observers note that there are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles.
  • All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.

Industry observers note that there are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.

All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).

The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.

This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180.

Fresh research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.

âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.

This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.

âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how crucial the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.

âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.

Recent findings suggest that SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Major Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.

âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.

Industry observers note that this image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA.

In a recent development, previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?

To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.

"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.

"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.

Sources indicate that this artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser.

The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.

"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.

In a recent development, SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," noted Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â.

According to recent reports, so the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.

But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that as we age, staying warm can become more difficult, but the reason may go beyond changes in circulation or muscle mass.
  • According to recent reports, now, researchers at City of Hope have uncovered a biological mechanism that helps explain why this natural heating system slows with age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The body’s inner heater weakens with age, but experiments in older mice suggest it can be turned back up.

Sources indicate that as we age, staying warm can become more difficult, but the reason may go beyond changes in circulation or muscle mass. Deep inside the body, a specialized type of fat acts like a built-in heater, burning calories to produce warmth when temperatures drop. Over time, however, this system becomes less responsive, potentially affecting not only how the body handles cold but also how it uses energy.

According to recent reports, now, researchers at City of Hope have uncovered a biological mechanism that helps explain why this natural heating system slows with age. Their study, published in Nature, reveals how communication between nerves, immune cells, and heat-producing fat changes over time.

“Learning how the body controls this process may offer insights into obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic disorders,” stated Qiong “Annabel” Wang, Ph.D., the study’s corresponding author and an associate professor at City of Hope’s Arthur Riggs Diabetes & Metabolism Research Institute.

Recent findings suggest that the body’s heat-producing fat contains cells with different levels of activity. Previous City of Hope research found that some have abundant UCP1, a protein that generates heat, while others contain less and produce less warmth. The latest study identified a similar mixture in human thermogenic fat samples, although most experiments were conducted in mice.

That mixture appears to give the body a reserve of heating capacity. When temperatures fall, nerve and immune signals encourage less active cells to increase their heat output. When the demand for warmth eases, the system can reduce that activity again.

In a recent development, in older mice, this adjustment became sluggish. Their thermogenic fat retained the ability to produce more heat but took longer to respond, making it harder for the animals to maintain their body temperature during cold exposure.

Industry observers note that the researchers then tested whether they could interrupt the pathway behind that delayed response. Using the drug mifepristone to block one part of the pathway restored some heat production in older mice. The animals generated more warmth and burned more energy. The finding suggests that at least some of the decline in thermogenic fat function may be reversible.

In a recent development, “That possibility matters for more than staying warm,” Wang said. “Thermogenic fat also burns glucose and fat, and its activity tends to decline with age. If scientists can find a safe, precise way to restore that activity, this foundational research could eventually deepen our understanding of age-related metabolic problems, including obesity and type 2 diabetes.”.

In a recent development, reference: “Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis” by Anying Song, Yifan Wang, Guan Wang, Marie Bae, Zhichao Wang, Guoming Gao, Zhuyin Wu, Geming Lu, Jieyi Meng, Jiayu Yu, Soojin Park, Adolfo Garcia-Ocaña, Patrick T. Fueger, Loredana Rao, Andrea Frontini, Yong Liu, Lei Jiang, Yi Zhu and Qiong A. Wang, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7.

This study was funded by NIH/National Institutes of Health, the Caltech-City of Hope Biomedical Research Initiative Grant, the City of Hope startup, and salary-saving funds.

  • According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories.
  • Industry observers note that the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

Industry observers note that the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:.

Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

Industry observers note that GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

According to recent reports, one matter addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser demonstrates how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:.

According to recent reports, we are not claiming to have discovered a latest gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

Immune cells may help pancreatic tumors hide from the body’s defenses, with differences between patient groups offering clues that could eventually guide more personalized treatment.

Recent findings suggest that understanding what makes one pancreatic tumor different from another could help doctors tailor treatment to each patient. Researchers at the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center have found fresh clues in both cancer cells and the immune cells around them.

The study, recently published in Cancer Research, was led by Nina Steele, PhD, an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine and a Cancer Center member, in collaboration with Howard Crawford, PhD, scientific director of the Henry Ford + Michigan State University Pancreatic Cancer Center.

Industry observers note that steele began the project at Henry Ford Health. Working with colleagues there and at UC, she mapped genomic information from a representative sample of Americans diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. The team used a multiomic approach, examining multiple layers of biological information.

Recent findings suggest that “We didn’t have an accurate reflection of all of the patients impacted by the disease reflected in the data,” Steele said. “There had never been a large-scale multiomic effort looking at tens of thousands of biological markers across a diverse cohort of pancreatic cancer patients.”.

According to recent reports, pancreatic cancer incidence and survival vary across American populations, with Black African Americans 20% more likely to develop the disease. Comparing their tumor samples with those from non-African American patients, the researchers found differences in B cells, a type of immune cell. In Black patients’ samples, these cells were more abundant and more immunosuppressive, dampening the body’s natural immune response against cancer.

“This may mean the B cells are helping the cancer cells hide in this patient population,” Steele noted. “This could help explain why this population is more likely to get the cancer, and why it’s worse when they get it, but more work is needed on pancreas tissues from individuals that do not have cancer.”.

The cancer cells themselves also highlighted distinct molecular signatures between the two groups.

According to recent reports, “The cancer cells make unique RNAs and proteins, so that could be relevant to how individual patients from different groups could respond to targeted therapies like RAS inhibitors,” Steele mentioned. “The markers upregulated in Black patients likely represent a type of cells typically associated with drug resistance, so this biological difference could play a role in outcomes.”.

In a recent development, RAS inhibitors target proteins involved in cell growth. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms behind the observed differences and their effects on outcomes. The findings could eventually help researchers identify fresh pancreatic cancer subtypes, as has happened in breast and prostate cancer, and develop more personalized treatment approaches.

Recent findings suggest that “The Cancer Center is here to serve everybody, and to find the answers that help all patients,” Steele mentioned. “The hope is to know more about the characteristics of the cancer cells earlier on, so that we have a plan of attack for what therapies come after current standards of care in a very rational way. We’re headed toward forecasting, the ability to better predict what will happen to every patient in their journey before it happens.”.

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

It has been revealed that the bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team claims. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Sources indicate that blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

It has been revealed that those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

According to recent reports, grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”.

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, notes she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

Sources indicate that the heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she indicates.

According to recent reports, schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

In a recent development, “I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer claims. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”.

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we at the moment think.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.
  • The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier.
  • "Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.

"Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot mentioned.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.

Years of development â including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023 â led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX noted the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

SpaceX looks to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

This 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the boosterâs offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceXâs Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the organization mentioned.

At the end of the trip, the second stage fired a single engine for roughly 10 seconds to start its descent through the atmosphere. As the temperatures rose, a brlght glow surrounded Ship 42âs leading edges. The craft executed a bellyflop maneuver to maximize its deceleration. Then it righted itself, and fired its engines a final time to sink into Mechazillaâs arms.

SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered, while âBaby, Come Backâ played on the soundtrack for the webcast. âBaby, sheâs back,â Huot joked.

According to recent reports, bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.

Sources indicate that in a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman said the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

SpaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric re-entry. The tech giant is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.

Sources indicate that in the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already declared his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.

It has been revealed that "I donât think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. Fresh era.".

#7151. Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)

Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you listen closely to an underwater seagrass meadow, you can hear the actual sound of photosynthesis.
  • Industry observers note that “As long as the meadows are more than 2 metres beneath the ocean surface, when the bubbles break they generate a vibration that is in the same sound frequency as bells,” he notes.
  • It has been revealed that but most of the time, this remarkable acoustic phenomenon is drowned out by human-caused noise pollution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you listen closely to an underwater seagrass meadow, you can hear the actual sound of photosynthesis. During the day, tiny bubbles of oxygen float from the blades of the seagrass to the ocean’s surface. The popping sound these bubbles make when they burst is like “tinkling bells”, according to Carlos Duarte, a keen scuba diver and expert on ocean noise at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia.

Industry observers note that “As long as the meadows are more than 2 metres beneath the ocean surface, when the bubbles break they generate a vibration that is in the same sound frequency as bells,” he notes. “If you have a hydrophone and you quantify this, then you could even calculate photosynthetic rates.”.

It has been revealed that but most of the time, this remarkable acoustic phenomenon is drowned out by human-caused noise pollution. There is barely a habitat on Earth that isn’t subjected to anthropogenic noise pollution from boats, cars, aeroplanes or any number of other noisy human activities. In the oceans, ambient noise levels are about 10 times higher than they were in 1950. “To understand the impact of noise on the marine environment, we need to imagine ourselves living in a great party, 24/7, throughout our entire lifespan. It is really a persistent and chronic impact,” indicates Duarte.

Human noise pollution drives monkeys to rely on communication by scent.

Sources indicate that now, scientists are learning more about how serious and widespread the impact of noise pollution is on wildlife subjected to it – and the results are disturbing. A meta-analysis published in the journal Science earlier this month looked at 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species, spanning six continents. It concluded that noise pollution altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in 80 per cent of the species studied, with the effects occurring in every habitat. In short, noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of a huge range of animals across land and sea.

In a recent development, “Every ecosystem, or every major habitat, is affected by noise,” says Hansjoerg Kunc at Queen’s University Belfast in the UK, who conducted the analysis with his colleague Rouven Schmidt. “We looked at a lot of different physiological responses [in wildlife] and basically nearly all of them found an effect for noise.”.

Recent findings suggest that in general, noise forces predators to work 2.5 times harder to catch 25 per cent less prey overall, reported Kunc and Schmidt. Creatures like bats expend more energy and are less successful at hunting when subjected to ambient noise, while noise from ship engines disrupts communication and disorientates marine life such as whales and dolphins.

Animals also learn to avoid noisy habitats, which shrinks their available area and therefore limits their population size. Dolphins, for example, actively avoid noisy coastlines, while bats have been shown to avoid roads that were noisy during a motorcycle rally long after the vehicles had left the area.

In noise-polluted areas, mortality among animals studied jumped by 138 per cent, on average. Sometimes, the death is instantaneous: underwater explosions from oil and gas exploration, for example, can cause a fish’s bladder to explode. Other times, it is slower and more painful, such as gradual starvation from reduced hunting success.

In a recent development, not every animal suffers a negative impact from noise pollution, Kunc notes. Some predators might benefit from noise – enjoying increased hunting success when human noise flushes their prey out of its hiding place, for example.

But even though some animals might benefit in the short term, the overall effect is negative on the ecosystem, he says, because its natural dynamics are being warped by external stress. “If you think about an ecosystem, all species in this ecosystem have adapted to the way it should be,” he says. “So, from my point of view, it doesn’t really matter who is more affected or less affected. It is changing, and that is what we want to avoid, because we want to protect a functioning ecosystem.”.

Powerful newly introduced book explores how noise has taken over the world.

Recent findings suggest that kunc wants more thought to be given to protecting the soundscape of the natural world, alongside the conservation of physical habitats. “We know that the acoustic environment is a strong evolutionary force, and we have shown that it really changes the physiology, development and behaviour [of wildlife],” he claims.

In a recent development, some efforts are already under way. In the US, national parks such as Yellowstone have designated quiet zones, which reduce the amount of noise made by visitors by 3 to 5 decibels according to Rachel Buxton, formerly of the US National Parks Service and now at Carleton University in Canada.

She thinks more can be done to reduce noise pollution, especially in protected areas, such as by closing roads to traffic during certain periods or re-routing aircraft to shadow busy road networks and avoid wilderness areas.

Industry observers note that “Think of the Grand Canyon. We wouldn’t dream of building a giant building in the middle of the Grand Canyon, and yet there are overflight tours that pass over the airspace all the time, polluting the whole space with noise,” she points out.

Recent findings suggest that pitcairn Island, one of the remotest places on Earth, was once home to mutineers. Today it’s a trailblazer in biodiversity protection with lessons for us all.

It has been revealed that we also need to tackle noise pollution at sea, notes Duarte. He argues for enforcing acoustic limits in marine protected areas, which could include setting noise limits for ships and other marine activities.

New technologies also give hope for a quieter future. Emerging evidence suggests that electric vehicles are quieter and therefore less disturbing to most wildlife. Similarly, electric motorboats and ferries could lead to quieter shorelines for marine life, says Duarte. “Moving to electric mobility, which we’ve done largely on land, to the ocean will immediately reduce noise around the shorelines,” he says, pointing out that countries such as Sweden are leading the way in creating a market for electric boats.

The covid-19 pandemic offers an insight into what happens in the natural world when the noise stops. Noise pollution across oceans dropped by 20 per cent during the crisis, notes Duarte, and led to extraordinary sightings of marine life returning to busy waterways and city shorelines, and the sound of birdsong filling cities.

Unlike pollutants that linger in the atmosphere, shutting off the noise immediately removes the problem, Duarte points out. “As soon as the noise stops, then animals claim back their ancestral territory and home,” he says.

#7150. A 120-Year-Old Gap in Einstein’s Physics May Hold the Key to the Universe’s Earliest Matter

A 120-Year-Old Gap in Einstein’s Physics May Hold the Key to the Universe’s Earliest Matter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A missing piece in Einstein’s century-old theory could help scientists understand how matter behaved in the universe’s earliest moments, revealing more about a time we can barely recreate.
  • Industry observers note that in particle accelerators, scientists smashed ions together at nearly the speed of light to recreate the fluid that existed just after the Big Bang.
  • That fluid, called quark-gluon plasma, offered a glimpse of the universe’s earliest matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A missing piece in Einstein’s century-old theory could help scientists understand how matter behaved in the universe’s earliest moments, revealing more about a time we can barely recreate.

Industry observers note that in particle accelerators, scientists smashed ions together at nearly the speed of light to recreate the fluid that existed just after the Big Bang. The resulting droplets were roughly the size of an atomic nucleus and survived for only tens of septillionths of a second. One way to investigate their interior was to track heavy quarks, particles that traveled through the droplets without being part of the surrounding fluid.

That fluid, called quark-gluon plasma, offered a glimpse of the universe’s earliest matter. In the first fraction of a second after the Substantial Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree mixture of quarks and gluons, subatomic particles moving at close to the speed of light. This state lasted just a few microseconds before the particles came together to form more stable protons and neutrons.

According to recent reports, reading the clues carried by heavy quarks required an accurate description of how the fluid pushed and pulled them. Albert Einstein established a relationship between a particle’s motion and a fluid’s microscopic structure in 1905. At speeds approaching that of light, however, the familiar description missed some of the interactions that shaped a particle’s journey.

It has been revealed that jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute, and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) developed a theory to address that gap. It predicted how a particle moving at relativistic speeds, meaning close to the speed of light, was likely to be pushed and pulled as it passed through a fluid. They reported their findings in Physical Review Letters.

Sources indicate that the researchers began with a relativistic heavy quark traveling through a gas of weakly interacting quarks and gluons. Those weak interactions made the calculations manageable. They calculated the forces acting on the heavy quark through the strong nuclear force, the fundamental force that held quarks and gluons together, to determine how its momentum was likely to change.

Their calculation produced a probability distribution, a curve showing how likely different changes in momentum were. It also described the likelihood of kicks of different strengths, since stronger kicks produced larger changes in momentum.

Industry observers note that “Our result reveals a latest source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion,” Du Plessis said. “How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.”.

According to recent reports, the idea of learning about a fluid by watching particles move through it had roots in a much more familiar setting. In 1827, botanist Robert Brown observed grains of pollen jiggling and swirling in seemingly still water. That erratic movement became known as Brownian motion and later inspired Einstein’s work.

Recent findings suggest that einstein’s 1905 theory explained how invisible activity within a fluid could keep a larger particle moving. Atoms and molecules in the fluid exerted random forces that combined to kick and jostle the particle, while drag from the fluid slowed it down. The relationship between these random kicks and drag determined how the particle eventually reached the same temperature as its surroundings.

According to recent reports, scientists subsequently used Einstein’s explanation to study many fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They assumed that a particle passing through the plasma would experience a balance of microscopic kicks similar to that experienced by pollen in water. In this familiar picture, the kicks followed a bell-shaped probability distribution. Typical kicks clustered around the peak, while extreme kicks occupied the tails and were equally unlikely in opposite directions.

According to recent reports, “Einstein highlighted that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings,” Du Plessis explained. “For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we’ve known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.”.

The new calculation resembled Einstein’s bell-shaped curve only for small kicks.

“The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare,” Du Plessis stated. “For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.”.

According to recent reports, when the researchers repeated their calculations for plasmas made up of different particles, they found the same tilted pattern, with uneven tails at either end of the distribution. They also recognized the same structure in an earlier calculation for a strongly coupled plasma, where particles interacted strongly, despite the differences in the underlying microscopic physics.

“This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized,” Du Plessis noted. “This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.”.

The researchers envisioned applying the theory to predict how heavy quarks moved through quark-gluon plasma, then comparing those predictions with experiments. That comparison could help characterize the plasma’s microscopic structure and establish what kind of fluid existed in the universe’s first moments.

Du Plessis mentioned the primordial plasma was likely “more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It’s more like a liquid and less like a gas.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm” by Jean F. Du Plessis and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld, 5 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/7fd5-1kq5.

This research has benefited from the Mitchel Postdoctoral Scholar Career Development Fund at KITP.

The First Foreign Astronaut Will Visit China's Tiangong Space Station in Two Weeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket.
  • The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission).
  • According to recent reports, the process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket. It will be the country's 18th crewed spaceflight and will see three taikonauts rendezvous with the Tianhe core module. Similar to previous Chinese crewed missions, the names of the crew are not expected to be confirmed until the day before the flight - except for one. On this particular flight, a Pakistani astronaut will accompany the pilot and commander, becoming the first foreigner to travel to Tiangong.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission). One of these astronauts will accompany the two Chinese taikonauts as a payload specialist, marking the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's space program. After spending a week aboard the station, the Ali or Daud will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

According to recent reports, the process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong. The two candidates were chosen after a rigorous selection process consisting of preliminary screenings, secondary evaluations, and final selection, which concluded in April 2026. Once Ali and Daud complete training in China, one will be selected for the mission while the other will serve as the backup astronaut.

Recent findings suggest that this agreement represents an historic expansion of China's ambition in space and a major shift in the strategic partnership between the two nations. Previously, the two cooperated on the development of terrestrial infrastructure, and are now focused on collaborative deep-space exploration. For Pakistan, this represents an opportunity to send its first astronaut to space, edging out India by close to a year. Per India's Gaganyaan program, India's first crewed mission is expected to launch no sooner than Q2 2027.

According to recent reports, for China, this is an key step toward the kind of international cooperation typical of NASA and the European Space Agency. It also aligns with their lunar ambitions, which will culminate in the creation of the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). China's growth as a major space power continues and is now taking on partners!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eleven carefully timed images can connect the early and later stages of an ultrafast event, offering scientists a way to investigate fleeting processes that are difficult to repeat.
  • Recent findings suggest that A limited set of images can leave gaps in a laser pulse or shock wave’s story.
  • Conventional imaging methods operate on microsecond, or millionth-of-a-second, and millisecond, or thousandth-of-a-second, timescales, usually capturing images at evenly or nearly evenly spaced intervals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eleven carefully timed images can connect the early and later stages of an ultrafast event, offering scientists a way to investigate fleeting processes that are difficult to repeat.

Recent findings suggest that A limited set of images can leave gaps in a laser pulse or shock wave’s story. Its first moments and later development may unfold on very different timescales, so taking snapshots at regular intervals can miss changes that connect one stage to the next.

Conventional imaging methods operate on microsecond, or millionth-of-a-second, and millisecond, or thousandth-of-a-second, timescales, usually capturing images at evenly or nearly evenly spaced intervals. Single-shot ultrafast imaging typically uses a uniform interval within a selected time window. With only a finite number of frames available, that choice can favor a detailed view of one brief stage over a record of the broader process.

According to recent reports, A team led by Keiichi Nakagawa, an associate professor in the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Tokyo, developed an approach that gives researchers more control over where those frames fall. Called logarithmic ultrafast photography, it distributes a fixed number of images across time, concentrating them around moments when characteristic changes occur.

Recent findings suggest that “We wanted to find a way to connect these very different timescales in a single measurement. In other words, we wanted to see both the first instance and what follows, without having to choose one or the other,” mentioned Keitaro Shimada, a postdoctoral researcher in the Nakagawa Group and lead author of the study.

According to recent reports, the team implemented the approach in sequentially timed all-optical mapping photography, or STAMP, a technique that combines ultrafast imaging with high image quality. To adjust the timing, they used band-resolved individual delay generation, or BRIDGE. It extracts wavelength bands, which are portions of the light spectrum, in sequence and allows their timing to be adjusted independently. Each band remains linked to a specific instant in the process being recorded.

That control lets researchers place frames at selected moments on timescales ranging from femtoseconds, or quadrillionths of a second, to nanoseconds, or billionths of a second. Instead of maintaining a regular interval, they can customize the gaps between images to resolve rapid changes and follow subsequent stages within the same recording.

The technique can capture key moments with 11 frames spanning five orders of magnitude in time, a 100,000-fold range. The report also describes this as equivalent to an approximately 260-frames-per-second exposure, although it does not explain the basis for that comparison.

Sources indicate that “We are particularly interested in phenomena that are difficult to reproduce exactly. In those cases, recording the early and later stages of the same event can reveal relationships that might be lost when a sequence is reconstructed from separate experiments,” said Nakagawa, a co-author and principal investigator of the study.

In a recent development, the researchers’ targets include short-lived phenomena whose peaks are difficult to catch and connections between phases of a physical process that have remained unseen because they occur on different timescales. They propose using the technique in laser processing, material dynamics, plasma and shock-wave research, and biomedical applications.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Logarithmic ultrafast photography with band-resolved individual delay generation” by 19 October 2026, Optica. DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.610944.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Solar panel output is something every spacecraft already tracks, typically in the form of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), which is an algorithm designed to point a craftâs solar sails at the Sun to maximize the amount of incoming solar radiation it receives.
  • Engineers usually spend a lot of time intentionally avoiding eclipses, because they can be really hard on the spacecraft itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, humanity is quickly starting to saturate our ability to track all of the satellites we have in deep space. NASAâs Deep Space Network (DSN) has been the workhorse for tracking such things for decades, but is quickly being overwhelmed by the number of requests it receives. Which in turn makes it harder to track some of the missions that have been released recently. A new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv, from Ian Down, James McElreath, and Manoranjan Majji, of Advanced Space, Space Exploration Engineering, and Texas A&M respectively, offer a no-cost solution to that tracking problem - use solar array data from a spacecraftâs eclipse to determine where it is.

Solar panel output is something every spacecraft already tracks, typically in the form of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), which is an algorithm designed to point a craftâs solar sails at the Sun to maximize the amount of incoming solar radiation it receives. But eclipses, where a spacecraft positions itself so that a body its orbiting is between it and the Sun, is also something every spacecraft experiences, at least for a little while.

Engineers usually spend a lot of time intentionally avoiding eclipses, because they can be really hard on the spacecraft itself. The solar arrays stop generating electricity, draining the battery, and everything on the craft gets much, much colder. However, the precise timing of how those blackouts travel across the solar panels of a spacecraft holds valuable information.

Fraser interviews astrodynamacist Dr. Aaron Rosengren, talking about the three-body problem of lunar orbits.

Astronomers know the exact positions of the Sun, Earth, and the Moon years in advance using advanced planetary maps. Given how much data weâve collected on those three bodies, we also know the precise shape and locations of the shadows those three bodies cast into space. Each shadow comes with two nested cones - the penumbra, where the Sun is partially blocked, and the umbra, where it is completely cut off.

When a spacecraft crosses into one of those cones, the amount of solar radiation hitting its solar panels drops precipitously, but its electronics continue to operate due to the on-board battery engineers placed there precisely to deal with these eclipses. By recording the precise timestamp where the voltage starts to drop, and when it starts to pick back up again after the spacecraft leaves the shadow, a navigation algorithm can determine its three dimensional location in space without needing any cameras, star trackers, or radio signals.

Sources indicate that that sounds simple in theory, but in practice getting that precise measurement correct is difficult. The Moon has no atmosphere, so its shadow is very jagged and tracks the mountains and craters dotting its surface. Each of those features can change the eclipsesâ timing by a few seconds. Earth, on the other hand, is a whole other ball of wax - or ball of gas and rock as the case may be. Itâs squished slightly at the poles, and its atmosphere can blur the Sun, as well as enlarging its shadow, making it difficult to differentiate precisely what part of the planet the spacecraft is passing over at any given time.

Fraser talks about different techniques to find your way in the cosmos.

To solve this problem, the researchers turned to a dataset of over 22,000 historical observations of lunar craters being covered by Earthâs shadow, which was collected by astronomers between 1842 and 2011. Using this data, the algorithm was able to map certain parts of the Earthâs shadow to specific ground features, allowing a more granular idea of where the specific spacecraft is passing over during its eclipse.

It has been revealed that to prove the system works, the researchers used another interesting data set - the actual flight telemetry from CAPSTONE, a CubeSat mission operated by Advanced Space, where Mr. Down, the lead author, works. CAPSTONE, which was intended to test the orbit for NASAâs now discontinued Lunar Gateway, recently completed its mission in July 2026. But on January 11th 2026, it traveled through the Moonâs shadow, with its solar panel voltage dropping from 23V to near zero, then picking back up to 31V when the panels hit sunlight again.

According to recent reports, using that data, the researchers timed the spacecraftâs entry and exit to the Moon shadow to within 15 seconds of the CAPSTONE's actual path. In addition to running the algorithm on real-life data, they also simulated a scenario where a spacecraft missed a check-in with ground stations and had its position uncertainty drift by several kilometers. Processing the eclipse data without any further information cut that uncertainty by more than 60 %.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most vital feature of this whole system is that it's essentially free. It doesnât require any additional hardware, or is âzero-Size Weight and Powerâ (zero-SWaP) in spacecraft jargon. To be clear, it doesnât entirely replace ground-based radio tracking. But it does provide a safety net. And as more and more spacecraft start venturing beyond low Earth orbit, and continue to overwhelm our active tracking systems, that zero-cost safety net could prove very valuable indeed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Here’s a fresh reason to eat your beans and greens.
  • A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Here’s a fresh reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, states Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

In a recent development, researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng states, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

According to recent reports, zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

Industry observers note that the researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s key, Zeng indicates, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng claims, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Chemists Weave Molecules Into a Powerful Newly introduced Material That Traps Toxic Chemicals

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fabric woven at the molecular level could help factories separate chemicals with less energy, opening a new path toward more sustainable manufacturing.
  • Reducing the environmental impact of manufacturing requires more than finding cleaner materials.
  • Researchers from the University of Texas at Austin and Zhejiang University have developed a molecularly woven fabric that can separate benzene from cyclohexane, two chemicals that are notoriously difficult to separate using conventional methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fabric woven at the molecular level could help factories separate chemicals with less energy, opening a new path toward more sustainable manufacturing.

Reducing the environmental impact of manufacturing requires more than finding cleaner materials. It also means finding ways to make industrial processes use less energy and produce fewer hazardous byproducts. One promising approach comes from an unexpected place: the ancient craft of weaving.

Researchers from the University of Texas at Austin and Zhejiang University have developed a molecularly woven fabric that can separate benzene from cyclohexane, two chemicals that are notoriously difficult to separate using conventional methods. The material could offer a more energy-efficient way to handle chemical separation, potentially reducing the energy demands of industries that manufacture nylon, paint, polyurethane, furniture foams, and detergents. The research was published in Nature.

Industry observers note that cyclohexane is an important industrial chemical used to manufacture a range of everyday products. It is commonly produced from benzene, a known carcinogen, which can also remain as an unwanted byproduct. Removing the benzene is essential, yet the two chemicals have nearly identical boiling points, making conventional separation difficult.

Chemical plants typically rely on distillation, a process that heats mixtures to separate substances according to their boiling points. Chemicals with sufficiently different boiling points can vaporize at different temperatures, allowing one to be collected separately. Benzene and cyclohexane, however, vaporize at nearly the same temperature and tend to separate poorly. The process often requires additional additives and considerable energy.

In a recent development, “Unbelievable amounts of energy go into chemical separation. It’s one of the top energy sinks in the modern world,” noted UT chemist Jonathan Sessler, one of the corresponding authors of the study. “In a sense, we are addressing the challenge of improving efficiency using one of humanity’s oldest technologies: weaving. It’s remarkable that the same principle of interlacing works at the molecular level.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers developed a material made from four molecular networks that weave over and under one another, forming an interconnected structure. Each layer can take one of two mirror-image arrangements. In one, the networks cross in a clockwise spiral, while the other follows a counterclockwise spiral. This property, known as chirality or handedness, allows the researchers to alternate between the two arrangements as they stack the layers.

Industry observers note that the resulting material forms a springy, thick fabric that can capture benzene from a mixture. Its interlocking, multi-thread structure also makes it stronger than conventional fabrics made by weaving individual threads in a single layer.

Watch a video showing how these layers self-assemble and stack. Credit: University of Texas at Austin.

According to recent reports, unlike materials that require complicated manufacturing processes, this molecular fabric is self-assembling. Its chemical structure naturally guides the networks into their woven arrangement.

“The whole thing converges by itself based on the underlying chemistry, which is especially cool because it allows the creation of these upcoming materials in a facile way,” Sessler remarked.

The fabric can also be reused. After absorbing benzene from a chemical mixture, researchers heat the material to vaporize the captured benzene, preparing it for another round of separation.

Sources indicate that sessler and the Zhejiang University team, led by professors Feihe Huang and Guangfeng Li, tested the material using a mixture containing equal amounts of benzene and cyclohexane. A single application absorbed 97.9% of the benzene. Multiple passes could provide additional separation for processes requiring greater purity.

The researchers also demonstrated that the material could separate several other compounds of commercial interest, suggesting that its potential applications extend beyond benzene and cyclohexane.

At Zhejiang University, the team has demonstrated how the fabric could be used on a larger, industrial scale. However, an economic analysis has not yet been completed, so its eventual cost and commercial practicality remain uncertain.

According to recent reports, if the technology proves viable, it could offer manufacturers a way to reduce the energy required for separating industrial chemicals. Improving these processes could help limit the environmental footprint of manufacturing, particularly across industries that depend on cyclohexane and other commercially notable compounds.

Reference: “A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric” by Mengbin Wang, Shuai Fang, Xuedong Xiao, Zhewen Guo, Tianyu Shan, Han Han, Chun Tang, Ding Xiao, Guangguo Wang, Zhongwen Liu, Bohan Zhao, Shang Li, Ming Liu, Yan-Fang Wang, Jinbo Li, Ming Li, Liya Chen, Zhenglin Du, Chong Yao, Yizhao Du, Jiyong Liu, J. Fraser Stoddart, Jonathan L. Sessler, Guangfeng Li and Feihe Huang, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8.

💡 Key Takeaways
