📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

It has been revealed that "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, noted in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In a recent development, in its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, noted in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

It has been revealed that the Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

According to recent reports, among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid indicates a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope looks to survey.

Recent findings suggest that this image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

Latest Update: This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves.
  • In a recent development, radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures.
  • One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. The sources of many of these signals are well-understood, and in some cases, special spacecraft have been debuted to monitor them. But some remain unexplained.

In a recent development, radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures. Radio astronomy has been around for decades, so many of these are well-understood. But not all of them. Some of them have only been discovered more recently and are awaiting an explanation.

One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. That's important because it differentiates them from pulsars and their extremely short radio periods. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.

There are different hypotheses invoked to explain them. They could be magnetars, which are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields that rotate very slowly. Or they could be something exotic and speculative, like strange dwarf pulsars.

In a recent development, but at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Astronomers have only been able to confirm the white dwarf's companion in a handful of cases, and in those, the companion is a red dwarf.

Sources indicate that now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. Their results are published in Nature Astronomy in a paper titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion." The lead author is Dr. Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR.

At the time of this research, there were only 12 detected LPTs, and the ones with identified components favoured WD and red dwarf pairs. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write. But this newly-detected LPT, named GPM J071507â114153, bucks that trend. "It is a binary system comprising a low-mass white dwarf and a G-type star identified via optical spectroscopy.".

âWe detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,â said co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker, Associate Professor at the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy.

The MWA detected 214 separate pulses, and the MeerKAT pinpointed its location based on 33 detected pulses. 26 of MeerKAT's pulses were co-detected by the MWA.

The newly introduced LPT has a period of only 7.9âminutes, which is almost certainly from its rotation. The properties of its radio pulses, like its polarization, are modulated by a longer period of about 1.3âdays, which the researchers say is the binary system's orbital period.

Recent findings suggest that follow-up optical observations and spectrometry came from the Keck Telescopes. "The optical counterpart of J0715-1141 was observed with the low-resolution imaging spectrometer on the Keck 1 telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii," the authors write. Those observations were a pair of 1,200 second exposures. They let the researchers determine the nature of the WD's partner star.

This figure from the research demonstrates the optical spectrum of the newly introduced LPT, J0715-1141, compared to model spectra from F-type, G-type, and K-type stars. The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. "As a comparison, hotter F-type and cooler K-type stars show distinct spectral features not present in the data," the authors write. The three panels on the right highlight this in three different elements. Image Credit: McSweeney, S.J., Hurley-Walker, N., Bahramian, A. et al. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. Nat Astron (2026).

According to recent reports, in this case, the WD's binary partner is a star like our Sun, which is far more massive and luminous than the M dwarfs (red dwarfs) found in other LPTs. So this rules out the idea that only WD-red dwarf pairs can generate LPTs.

It has been revealed that astronomers and astrophysicists want to know exactly how these radio pulses are generated. Can any of their observations help researchers determine the exact source of the radio pulses? Not exactly, but the clarity of the pulses helps narrow it down.

âThis is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,â mentioned lead author McSweeney.

"We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.

There's another suprise in these findings. The pulses from the WD let the researchers detect stellar flares from the Sun-like star as it passed in front of the WD.

According to recent reports, âAs a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a âstellar prominenceâ, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a starâs surface,â Hurley-Walker said. âItâs amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.â.

This image reveals a solar prominence from the Sun in 2010, with Earth shown for scale. The researchers were able to detect one of these coming from the main sequence star in the pair, as the white dwarf moved behind it. That's pretty impressive for a star that's 5,000 light years away. Image Credit: NASA/SDO.

One questions astronomers ask is how these types of binaries form, and the researchers have a hypothesis for that. They say the system could've formed through binary evolution. "One possibility is that the present configuration of the system arises through post-common-envelope (CE) binary evolution," they write. The progenitor of the system most likely had an intermediate-mass primary with a lower-mass companion on a wider orbit. "As the primary evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a giant, unstable mass transfer initiated a CE phase, during which orbital energy and angular momentum were transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and substantial orbital shrinkage.".

The primary star was left as an exposed stellar core, and evolved to become a WD, creating the situation the astronomers see today: a WD star with a G-type partner, that are still in a binary relationship, but detached from the common envelope they once shared.

As for the system's future, it could hold a cataclysmic explosion.

Binaries like this that have left their common envelopes, and that consist of a WD and a massive main-sequence star, are potential breeding grounds for eventual Type Ia supernovae. This can happen as their orbit decays and the WD accretes material from its companion. Once enough material builds up on the accreting WD, it explodes and destroys the WD. Or they could created a double degenerate WD-WD merger, if the main sequence companion collapses before the binary orbit decays.

Could the radio signals from LPTs be used to find the progenitors of these supernovae explosions?

"Radio detections of LPTs may offer a route to finding cooler WDs around hotter stars at greater distances than traditional ultraviolet and optical surveys," the authors write.

The upcoming Square Kilometre Array could be the key to this.

"In an era of larger and more sensitive radio surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, this may form a upcoming pathway for investigating the progenitors of type Ia supernovae," the authors write.

Scientists Discover a Giant 66-Pound Rodent That Lived 34 Million Years Ago

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paleontologists have uncovered fossils of an unusually large rodent that lived approximately 34 million years ago in what is now Thailand.
  • Industry observers note that fossilized teeth discovered in a coal mine in southern Thailand have revealed a previously unknown giant rodent that lived approximately 34 million years ago.
  • An international research team, including paleontologists from McGill University, identified the species from two fossilized teeth found at the Bang Mark Pit of the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand’s Krabi Province.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paleontologists have uncovered fossils of an unusually large rodent that lived approximately 34 million years ago in what is now Thailand.

Industry observers note that fossilized teeth discovered in a coal mine in southern Thailand have revealed a previously unknown giant rodent that lived approximately 34 million years ago. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient mammal was substantially larger than other known rodents from its time, suggesting that the evolution of giant rodents began earlier and occurred across a wider geographic area than scientists previously recognized.

An international research team, including paleontologists from McGill University, identified the species from two fossilized teeth found at the Bang Mark Pit of the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand’s Krabi Province. The remains consist of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, providing limited but valuable evidence of an unusually large rodent that inhabited Southeast Asia during the Paleogene period.

By analyzing the dimensions of the fossilized teeth using seven established methods for estimating body mass, researchers calculated that Yakamys weighed approximately 30 kilograms (66 pounds). That would make it roughly twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.

The estimate remains uncertain because scientists must reconstruct the animal’s overall size from just two teeth.

“This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation,” said Virginie Millien, a study co-author and professor of biology at McGill University.

In a recent development, the largest living rodent is the capybara, a semiaquatic mammal native to South America. Although exceptionally large rodents have evolved multiple times, much of the known fossil evidence for rodent gigantism comes from South America, particularly during later periods of rodent evolution.

It has been revealed that “Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems,” stated Millien. “Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an crucial role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents.”.

According to recent reports, the Thai fossils extend the known history of unusually large rodents into Southeast Asia around 34 million years ago. However, the limited remains cannot establish precisely how Yakamys attained its large size or whether its evolutionary path resembled that of giant rodents that appeared elsewhere.

The fossils were recovered through an international research collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand’s Krabi Basin. Participants include scientists from McGill University, Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources, France’s National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), and the University of Poitiers.

The researchers named the new genus Yakamys by combining the Thai word “yak,” meaning giant, with the Greek word “mys,” meaning mouse or rat.

“The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand,” Millien mentioned.

Industry observers note that with only two teeth available, many aspects of Yakamys remain unknown, including its diet, habitat preferences, and evolutionary relationships. Additional fossils could help researchers reconstruct its anatomy and determine how giant rodents emerged in Southeast Asia tens of millions of years ago.

Reference: “A giant eocene ischyromyid from Southeast Asia reveals the early evolution of rodent gigantism” by Yaowalak Chaimanee, Laurent Marivaux, Virginie Millien, Chotima Yamee, Pannipa Tian and Jean-Jacques Jaeger, 4 November 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-76711-6.

The research was supported by CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.

New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming.
  • According to recent reports, I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70!
  • Industry observers note that I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived Newly introduced Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in.

According to recent reports, I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams.

Industry observers note that I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first matter of Upcoming Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman.

It has been revealed that as a pupil in the mid-1960s at a girls’ grammar school in the north of England, one day I picked up a copy of New Scientist in the library. I was mind-blown by an article about Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity and time dilation, including a coloured diagram! I went on to study physical and material sciences at university and worked for eight years in research. But motherhood and misogyny (in those days before equal opportunities legislation) led me to change tack and I’ve been making pottery by hand for over 55 years. I like to think my science education hasn’t been wasted, but handed down to my daughters, one of whom reads New Scientist online in France. Every week, the paper glitch landing on my doormat is devoured with excitement! Anne Rodgers.

Trustworthy science journalism is more essential than ever.

The stories that most interested me were about emerging electronics, the Sputnik satellite and the launch of Laika the space dog. The last of these prompted me to construct a module to house a maggot atop a 3-pence standard firework rocket and launch it. I later recovered the maggot unharmed and used it as fishing bait the next day. Mel.

We are a group of 12 ladies “of a certain age” who meet once a month to discuss three or four articles from Upcoming Scientist. We tackle topics such as AI, quantum computing and cosmology – all of which are quite daunting! We persevere and continue to try to understand topics like these that are very challenging. We look up terms and concepts we don’t understand and then teach each other. We also love to read articles on climate change and medical science, as these feel more relatable. We strategy to get the recordings of the talks from October’s New Scientist Live, so we can watch together and discuss. We want to thank you for making science accessible to us – we all feel that it’s crucial as we get older to not give in to the temptation to ignore all the new discoveries and changes in the world. Diana Currie, Dawn Segrue and the Marlow Science Group.

According to recent reports, an article about Benjamin Libet’s experiments in the 1980s showing there was a time gap between the brain making a decision and conscious awareness of that decision inspired me, as a psychotherapist, to find a way of using that gap in the field of psychological therapy. Two years of exploration and testing later, I taught the first cohort of students, and now it is being employed by psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and psychotherapists all over the world. Terence Watts.

On the eve of New Scientist’s 70th anniversary, newsroom legend Andy Coghlan reveals four of the most dramatic and surprising moments from his storied career.

Back in 2019, I stumbled across an eye-catching magazine on the shelves of a Tesco store. The title-page article caught my eye: “Does this one microbe cause all these conditions… and does that mean we can beat them?” It was at that moment that I truly fell in love with biology. Years have passed, and I have since graduated with a science degree from the University of Edinburgh and am now a returning student at my alma mater pursuing a master of research postgraduate degree in life sciences.

One day, I aim to be able to contribute – even if just a little – to aiding humanity in its endless fight against malady and illness. All of my academic achievements thus far may very well not have been possible had it not been for that magazine that caught my eye, that day in August 2019. And for that, I quite literally owe Latest Scientist all my academic achievements, and all that I have done, to this day. Stephen Wang.

I am 87 and have been reading New Scientist every week since October 1964. I still have a note from my grandson, Maximilian, from when he was 5 years old, thanking me for reading New Scientist with him. He is now studying biology at my one-time college, Merton, at the University of Oxford. In the meantime, he has already succeeded, while travelling with his mother in Amazonia, in identifying, describing, naming and publishing a new genus and species of damselfly. He and I continue to discuss complications like evolution together, though I am a classicist by training. Anthony J. Nieduszynski.

Sources indicate that your magazine is vital to our family. It sparks many conversations at the kitchen table. Our 11-year-old grandson keeps beating us to the latest matter. Our 6-year-old grandson has been enthralled with the cover art since he was 3. I cut out the cartoons and post them on the fridge. They have become the “cartoon of the week”. Often my grandsons see details I didn’t even catch. Krystyna Rodriguez.

From subconscious finger sniffing to rats driving cars, Upcoming Scientist staff have reported on many weird, wild or utterly bonkers discoveries and inventions in the 70 years since we began.

According to recent reports, I have been a reader for almost all the publication’s life, as I first started when I was studying for A level qualifications in 1959/60. The article that really got me was one about the trouble the UK Ministry of Defence was having with dolphins that disrupted its torpedo testing by racing the torpedoes and giving them nudges of encouragement or perhaps challenge, thus putting them off target. I was hooked. It settled my decision to study engineering and, about six years later, I was actually employed as an engineer, working in a team trying to design turbine blades with better efficiency. I am now 83 and retired (well almost), but I still read every problem from cover to cover. Bryan Wilson.

According to recent reports, I met my husband, Simon, on your dating website in 2012. It took me 50 years to find him, and without your mag, I probably never would have. We are two halves of a whole, and have been happily married now for 11 years. He is my heart’s delight, he makes me laugh, wears cravats with his T-shirts and is altogether quirky, like me. I still read New Scientist every week, and hope to be reading it still for many years to come. The quality of articles is outstanding – one day I may even get to understand quantum physics! We both love Tom Gauld’s cartoons, and keep a selection of them on the wall in the toilet, to entertain visitors. Andrea Cohen.

I was delighted when my question about whether anything eats wasps was published in The Last Word (29 January 2005), and even more so when there was a full page of answers. But I was amazed when my question featured in the title of the first Fresh Scientist questions book later that year. Apparently, the book was one of that Christmas’s bestsellers. Not only that, but there were two consecutive reviews in The Times – pretty good for my complete published scientific writing! And what did I get out of this? The original answerers got 25 quid each. Me? Not a penny. Only a fleeting, obscure fame. Fair enough. A great science magazine for the ordinary folks like myself. I will not be cancelling my subscription. Tom Eastwood.

I answered my first two Last Word questions in 1997, when the column was relatively new. Amusingly, both appeared in the same problem, something I gather the rules now prevent. I had always admired New Scientist, but never quite imagined it would publish anything I might write – perhaps a touch of imposter syndrome. Nearly 30 years later, I’m still providing answers. I particularly enjoy questions requiring a back-of-the-envelope calculation or a little mathematical modelling. I like getting absorbed in a problem and trying to explain a tricky concept clearly and concisely. It is one of the few ways I experience mindfulness.

It has been revealed that some questions have spun off in unexpected directions. One, about whether pigeons sweat, led to an email while I was scuba-diving in Thailand asking me to appear on the TV programme BBC Breakfast. Answers have also developed into articles elsewhere, sometimes after reading somebody else’s answer and questioning my own. My favourite? Like the Eye of Sauron, my focus is always on the one I’m looking at right now. Mike Follows.

  • Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
  • The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, notes Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

It has been revealed that chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Recent findings suggest that patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the Latest England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is key because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, claims Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Industry observers note that researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

Industry observers note that the team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

Sources indicate that the researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle notes. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle notes, patients’ damaged kidneys highlighted clear signs of repair.

A Lost World of Hippos and Ancient Humans Emerges From the Arabian Desert

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists from around the world have joined forces to uncover a remarkably detailed picture of how people lived in Arabia 125,000 years ago.
  • In a recent development, around 125,000 years ago, the desert landscape of southern Saudi Arabia looked very different.
  • Industry observers note that the discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in Mundafan, within Saudi Arabia’s Empty Quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists from around the world have joined forces to uncover a remarkably detailed picture of how people lived in Arabia 125,000 years ago.

In a recent development, around 125,000 years ago, the desert landscape of southern Saudi Arabia looked very different. A vast freshwater lake surrounded by vegetation and open grasslands provided an environment where early humans could live, hunt, and gather resources. Archaeologists have now uncovered an unusually detailed record of life along its shores, offering a glimpse into a period known as Green Arabia.

Industry observers note that the discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in Mundafan, within Saudi Arabia’s Empty Quarter. Published in Science, the study was jointly led by the Saudi Heritage Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University, with contributions from several other international institutions. Specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology combined their expertise to reconstruct the environment and human activities during the last Interglacial period, a warm, humid phase around 125,000 years ago.

Using satellite terrain modeling, researchers mapped an ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers (131 square miles), with a maximum depth of 29 meters (95 feet). Sediments, landforms, and aquatic remains indicated that it was a relatively stable freshwater body surrounded by vegetation and grasslands.

Systematic surveys across more than 130 locations documented over 500 fossil specimens of plants and animals, including invertebrates. Animal remains included hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches, revealing the variety of wildlife that inhabited the region when water was far more abundant.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a participating researcher from the Heritage Commission and professor of Paleolithic archaeology, described the discovery in the sands of Lake Mundafan as an notable archaeological find that sheds light on the relationship between humans, animals, and the ancient environment of southern Saudi Arabia.

Researchers also collected 5,511 stone tools larger than 2 centimeters (0.8 inches) from the main study area. More than 98% were made of flint, and their manufacture revealed evidence of Levallois techniques, in which stone is carefully shaped to produce flakes of a desired form. The team used two dating methods on sand and fossil teeth, along with 3D-refitting techniques to investigate how the tools were produced.

Microscopic and chemical analyses of the tools revealed traces of numerous plants, including tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. These residues suggest that people processed plant resources for food and everyday activities. Traces of resin and woody tissue also indicate that some stone points may have been attached to handles or shafts to create hunting weapons.

Recent findings suggest that more intriguingly, some tools contained residues from toxic plants, raising the possibility that early hunters used poisonous compounds in their equipment. Although their precise purpose remains uncertain, the findings represent some of the earliest potential evidence of this practice in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region’s earliest evidence of palm-related vegetation.

The combination of freshwater, animals, plants, and raw materials along the lakeshore supported a range of activities, from stone tool production and hunting equipment preparation to processing food and working with fibers. Because these different traces were preserved together at a single dated site, researchers could examine their relationships in unusual detail.

According to recent reports, “This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today,” said Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. “The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.”.

Sources indicate that reconstructing that ancient landscape required the combined efforts of researchers across several scientific disciplines and institutions. Their work demonstrates how geological evidence, fossils, archaeological discoveries, and microscopic traces can contribute to a more complete understanding of early human life.

“It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past,” noted Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

Industry observers note that the findings add to growing evidence of Saudi Arabia’s deep human and environmental history, with implications for understanding early human movement and technological development across the Arabian Peninsula. They also highlight the importance of international research partnerships and expanding heritage science expertise within the Kingdom.

“Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories,” mentioned Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

Industry News: 12 Years of Research Reveal Something Alarming Happening to Wild Elephants

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair.
  • Sources indicate that asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young.
  • Recent findings suggest that in Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair.

Sources indicate that asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young. Keeping that support network intact requires opportunities to build new relationships as old connections are lost.

Recent findings suggest that in Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system. An analysis of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years found that large, densely connected communities had given way to smaller, more isolated groups. The remaining females were changing their relationships with one another as their numbers fell.

Recent findings suggest that “We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but new individuals are not coming into the population,” said Anastasia Madsen, the postdoctoral researcher who led the study. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.”.

Published November 12 in Science, the research comes from the University of California San Diego’s School of Biological Sciences. Madsen works in Associate Professor Shermin de Silva’s laboratory in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution.

The analysis points to a combination of likely deaths, elephants leaving permanently, and fewer incoming individuals as explanations for the population decline. Poaching and conflicts with humans already cause deaths in many elephant populations. Disrupted connections between habitats and reduced food availability may also contribute as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and its surroundings, though these remain possible pressures rather than established causes of the social changes observed here.

The researchers interpret the shift in community structure as evidence that the population may have crossed a critical threshold, or social tipping point.

“We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study.

Industry observers note that that sequence raises the possibility that losses can build for years before the organization of an animal society changes abruptly. The resulting fragmentation could be difficult to repair.

It has been revealed that “In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” noted Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.”.

The findings add to discussions about conserving elephant populations as people expand into areas where the animals historically thrived. For social species, opportunities to share space and develop relationships are part of what sustains a community.

“We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” said de Silva, who also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.”.

Future studies can use the findings to investigate how animal societies change, how to detect those shifts, and which factors make communities vulnerable.

“We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” said Madsen.

Industry observers note that reference: “Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants” by Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva, 12 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714.

#7134. Breaking: A Deadly Blood Cancer May Begin More Than 50 Years Before Symptoms Appear

Breaking: A Deadly Blood Cancer May Begin More Than 50 Years Before Symptoms Appear

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many older adults carry blood mutations linked to acute myeloid leukemia, yet most never develop it.
  • In a recent development, acute myeloid leukemia can begin developing decades before diagnosis.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery reveals how slowly leukemia can take shape, with mutated blood cells gradually accumulating genetic changes before their growth accelerates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that many older adults carry blood mutations linked to acute myeloid leukemia, yet most never develop it. The difference may lie in how those cells grow.

In a recent development, acute myeloid leukemia can begin developing decades before diagnosis. In two-thirds of women who eventually developed the aggressive blood cancer, researchers traced the first cancer-driving mutation to before age 20. In some cases, more than 50 years passed before the disease was diagnosed.

According to recent reports, the discovery reveals how slowly leukemia can take shape, with mutated blood cells gradually accumulating genetic changes before their growth accelerates. It also points to a possible opportunity to identify people at risk long before they become ill.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) affects around 2,700 people in the UK each year. Only about one in six survive five years after diagnosis. Predicting who will develop it has been difficult because many healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations also found in leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, rarely progresses to cancer, and scientists have not fully understood what separates those who eventually develop AML from those who do not.

It has been revealed that to investigate, researchers from the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL) turned to years of stored blood samples. Their study, published November 11, 2026, in Nature, examined 47 women who later developed AML and 46 matched women who remained free of blood cancer.

Recent findings suggest that the samples came from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), which collected annual blood samples from around 50,000 women for up to 11 years. Some provided a record reaching 15 years before diagnosis. The women who developed AML were diagnosed between ages 53 and 83, at an average age of 72. None of the samples were collected at diagnosis.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led UKCTOCS, explained how the ovarian cancer screening trial created an unexpected resource for studying other diseases.

Sources indicate that “While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.”.

Using ultra-sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical modeling, the researchers reconstructed when mutations appeared and how promptly the affected blood cells multiplied.

According to recent reports, the earliest mutations often gave these cells a decades-long head start. At first, their numbers increased very slowly, taking years to double. Each additional cancer-driving mutation accelerated their growth by roughly two- to threefold. By the time cells carried four cancer-driving mutations, their populations could double in just weeks.

Industry observers note that these expanding populations of genetically related cells are called clones. Once established, they tended to grow at a predictable rate, slowing only when they ran out of room or a faster-growing clone overtook them.

Recent findings suggest that that consistency could make it possible to estimate a person’s future risk from a relatively small number of blood samples. Professor Jamie Blundell of the University of Cambridge’s Early Cancer Institute, who led the study, said:.

“Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood’s evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers also identified a particularly concerning pattern. In at least one-third of the women who developed AML, a mutated cell population had already become dominant in the blood years before diagnosis. This is known as a somatic sweep. None of the women who remained free of blood cancer highlighted the same phenomenon.

Sources indicate that the team found further evidence linking these sweeps to AML risk using UK Biobank data. People with this pattern had a greatly increased risk of developing the disease. However, standard genetic analysis can overlook the warning sign by mistaking these acquired mutations for inherited genetic variants.

There was also an important difference in how early the changes became detectable. In around one in five cases, expanding populations of mutated cells did not appear until just one to two years before diagnosis. This means that the opportunity to identify and monitor high-risk individuals may vary considerably.

Dr. Caroline Watson, a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute and first author of the study, said the findings help explain why AML can seem to emerge so suddenly.

“As a hematologist, I’ve seen how suddenly AML can change someone’s life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.”.

In a recent development, watson is also an Honorary Consultant Hematologist at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, where she sees patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic, Europe’s first clinic focused on leukemia prevention. The clinic already monitors people with blood-cell mutations associated with an increased risk of leukemia.

“At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today’s findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.”.

The researchers now want to find out whether slowing the growth of high-risk clones could prevent them from developing into leukemia. Their mathematical models suggest that even a modest reduction in growth over the decade or more between the second mutation and diagnosis could substantially lower the chance of progression.

Professor Blundell noted: “Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.”.

Testing whether this approach can safely and effectively slow mutated cell populations in people at high risk is the team’s next step.

Reference: “Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia” by Caroline J. Watson, Gladys Y. P. Poon, Hamish A. J. MacGregor, Adriana V. A. Fonseca, Sophia Apostolidou, Aristi Damaskou, Christopher Boniface, Samuel Hackett, Aleksandra Gentry-Maharaj, Usha Menon and Jamie R. Blundell, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x.

Breaking: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
  • Industry observers note that but the dip may not last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

Industry observers note that but the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, states Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite substantial enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.

#7132. Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Newscientist ↗ Open Full Page

Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.
  • “What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a new group of people?” indicates Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.
  • A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.

“What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a new group of people?” indicates Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began.

Recent findings suggest that rødhals Man lived some 6000 years ago, and was discovered on the small island of Sejerø in Denmark in the 1950s, buried in a shell midden – an ancient accumulation of discarded sea shells and other domestic refuse. Previous investigations have indicated he was unusual. He lived some time between about 3800 and 3900 BC, near the start of the Neolithic period in the area, when diets changed to consist predominantly of terrestrial food produced by farmers. And yet Rødhals Man, with his genetic ancestry typical of the local Mesolithic Ertebølle culture of hunter-gatherers, didn’t seem to have eaten that diet: a study in 1981 indicated that he ate mainly seafood.

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something key,” notes Fischer.

Recent findings suggest that to get a better idea of what was going on, Fischer and his colleagues have now looked at the levels of rare isotopes of elements including carbon, nitrogen and sulphur in several of the man’s bones, which renewed at different rates during his life, preserving different snapshots in time. The researchers also analysed the chemical signatures in one of his teeth, which preserve a record of diet from childhood. Collectively, the data gave the team an opportunity to look for clues about how Rødhals Man’s diet changed over the 30 to 40 years of his life.

“You can see that most of the time, the primary food source is what we call the eelgrass biotype. This is not eelgrass itself, but the animals that live in the thick forests of this sea grass in shallow water,” states team member John Meadows at Kiel University in Germany. This could have been animals like molluscs, flatfish or eels, he says.

But from the age of about 11 onwards, Rødhals Man’s diet became unlike that of any Mesolithic hunter-gatherer recorded so far, with increasing amounts of terrestrial, probably farmed, protein.

Rødhals Man’s burial also shares more similarities with burials of Early Neolithic farmers than those of Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, because his bones lacked an added coating of ochre staining and his grave featured a stone frame.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence leads Meadows to suggest that Rødhals Man interacted with the Neolithic farmers and adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his ancestors on the small island. Sejerø is just 12 square kilometres in area, but is only about 5 kilometres from Zealand, which is around 7000 square kilometres.

An analysis of ancient genomes has revealed that the descendants of Stone Age farmers in Europe and hunter-gatherers gained more genes from the latter group than expected.

“He was on a tiny island with very little in the way of wild terrestrial resources to live on,” says Meadows. “He may have spent part of the year living in a farming community on Zealand and part living on the island and only eating fish.”.

Industry observers note that “It is quite amazing that all this information could be retrieved from one single skeleton,” notes Mathias Currat at the University of Geneva. “I think this is an interesting story, which probably represents part of the main story in this area.”.

In a recent development, it would be unusual to change diet in this way, indicates Marcello Mannino at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”.

He indicates it is likely that the Neolithic farmers probably first occupied areas where soil conditions were better, such as in central Zealand, and were slower to inhabit more marginal areas. “We need to find more human remains that span the transition to try to understand how it happened,” he says.

Antiquity DOI: 10.15184/aqy.2026.10476.

Type 2 Diabetes Linked to a 53% Higher Risk of Alzheimer’s, Massive Study Finds

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.
  • People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major research review involving data from more than 27 million study participants.
  • The Curtin University-led systematic review and meta-analysis examined 40 studies and found that approximately five new cases of Alzheimer’s occur annually for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.

People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major research review involving data from more than 27 million study participants. The findings strengthen evidence linking diabetes to Alzheimer’s and provide newly introduced estimates of how frequently the disease develops among people with the condition.

The Curtin University-led systematic review and meta-analysis examined 40 studies and found that approximately five new cases of Alzheimer’s occur annually for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes. Unlike earlier reviews that often grouped different forms of diabetes and dementia together, the researchers focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers screened 9,431 scientific articles before selecting 40 studies with a combined total of more than 27 million data points, calculated from unadjusted sample sizes. Of these, 23 studies provided information on Alzheimer’s incidence, while 26 examined the association between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s risk.

The pooled incidence was 4.71 upcoming Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years. After accounting for other factors included in the original studies’ statistical analyses, people with type 2 diabetes had a 53% higher relative risk of developing Alzheimer’s than those without diabetes. The findings demonstrate an association, not a direct causal relationship.

According to recent reports, studies using administrative health records reported an average of 4.00 latest Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years, compared with 10.24 cases in studies using other methods to identify diagnoses. The substantial difference suggests that how Alzheimer’s is identified can influence reported incidence rates.

Among people with type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s incidence was numerically higher in women than men, at 3.62 versus 2.76 cases per 1,000 person-years. However, the relative risk associated with diabetes was similar between sexes, with increases of 73% in women and 76% in men. Additional analyses generally supported the overall findings, although incidence estimates varied considerably across studies.

Recent findings suggest that study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, stated the research provides a more precise assessment of Alzheimer’s risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

“While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease and estimated how often latest cases occurred,” Dr. Adewuyi mentioned.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often upcoming cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Incidence and risk of Alzheimer’s disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis” by Thi Thu Huong Nguyen, Asa Auta, Emmanuel Agada David, Chinedu I. Ossai, Victory Olutuase, Moulinath Banerjee, Yun Zhao, Davies Adeloye, Gavin Pereira and Emmanuel O. Adewuyi, 9 November 2026, Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy. DOI: 10.1186/s13195-026-02254-7.

Latest Update: A Deadly Brain Disorder Has Baffled Doctors for Years. Researchers May Have Finally Solved the Mystery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering fresh hope for earlier detection and answers to previously unexplained tragedies.
  • Some newborns enter the world with devastating brain abnormalities that can cause seizures, profound developmental difficulties, and life-threatening complications.
  • In a recent development, researchers have now identified a genetic cause behind some of these cases, offering long-awaited answers to affected families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering fresh hope for earlier detection and answers to previously unexplained tragedies.

Some newborns enter the world with devastating brain abnormalities that can cause seizures, profound developmental difficulties, and life-threatening complications. The damage begins before birth, and for some families, the condition has claimed the lives of multiple children without doctors being able to explain why or determine whether it could happen again.

In a recent development, researchers have now identified a genetic cause behind some of these cases, offering long-awaited answers to affected families. A study published in Genome Medicine links changes in a gene called VPS25 to a previously unknown brain disorder, giving doctors a upcoming way to investigate severe neurological conditions that have remained unexplained.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery began with a pattern of illness shared by children from five unrelated families across Saudi Arabia, Europe, and North America. Three families were initially identified through genomic programs in Saudi Arabia, and researchers subsequently connected their cases with others overseas. Although the families were unrelated, their children had similar symptoms and changes in the same gene.

Sources indicate that “When a condition is this rare, one family alone may not be enough to reveal what is happening,” mentioned Professor Fowzan Alkuraya, clinical genetics lead on the study who is affiliated with both King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center (KFSHRC) and King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). “Bringing together clinical experience with genomic data from Saudi Arabia, and connecting it with cases internationally, allowed us to see a pattern that had previously been invisible. This is why building these genomic resources matters: they can help us find answers to diseases that might otherwise remain unexplained.”.

It has been revealed that to understand how these genetic changes might affect the developing brain, scientists at KAUST examined biological processes inside affected cells. The VPS25 gene plays a role in maintaining nerve cells, and laboratory testing revealed disruptions that altered both the number and contents of tiny packages released by cells. Some of these packages were missing proteins involved in protecting and maintaining nerve cells, offering clues about how the disorder develops.

The findings provide the first evidence connecting VPS25 changes to a human disease. Establishing that connection required clinicians at KFSHRC to work closely with affected families, documenting their symptoms and investigating possible genetic causes, while KAUST researchers studied the underlying cellular problems.

Recent findings suggest that for families who have endured years of uncertainty, identifying the cause offers something that was previously missing: an explanation for their children’s illness and information that could help guide future pregnancy decisions. The discovery also gives clinicians a new gene to examine when investigating similar brain abnormalities and may allow the condition to be detected through genetic testing during pregnancy.

“Knowing that this disease has a rare genetic cause can bring comfort to families who have lived for years with uncertainty about their tragic losses,” remarked Professor Jasmeen Merzaban, co-lead of the study at KAUST. “It also enables clinicians around the world to recognize similar cases and detect the disease through genetic testing during pregnancy.”.

Researchers hope that identifying VPS25 as a disease-associated gene will help uncover additional cases around the world. Studying more affected families could reveal how the condition varies between children, improve diagnosis and genetic counseling, and provide a clearer understanding of how disruptions involving VPS25 interfere with early brain development.

In a recent development, reference: “Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy” by Ioannis Isaioglou, Lama AlAbdi, Muhammad Tehseen, Yossef Lopez de los Santos, Mansour Aldehaiman, Gloria Lopez-Madrigal, Norah Altuwaijri, Viviana Hermosilla Aguayo, Anna Pleyers, Maya Ayach, Ashraf Al-Amoudi, Jing Kai, Vlad-Stefan Raducanu, Bader Alhaddad, Edda Hofstätter, Amani Al-Amodi, Mais O. Alkuraya and Jasmeen S. Merzaban, 14 September 2026, Genome Medicine. DOI: 10.1186/s13073-026-01693-z.

Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
  • In a recent development, some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

In a recent development, some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting firm in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

Industry observers note that the ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Industry observers note that joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

Industry observers note that in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

Industry observers note that the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a massive hint, McConnell claims, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Organization. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Tech giant installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data indicated, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell claims, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

It has been revealed that these fresh findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

A Strange Black Hole Gap Could Reveal Stars That Died Without Exploding

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.
  • According to recent reports, some massive stars may end their lives without a supernova, collapsing directly into black holes instead of producing a brilliant explosion.
  • Using observations from the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA gravitational-wave network, researchers analyzed 257 black hole mergers recorded over the past decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.

According to recent reports, some massive stars may end their lives without a supernova, collapsing directly into black holes instead of producing a brilliant explosion. A upcoming Caltech-led study suggests that gravitational waves from colliding black holes may contain evidence of these silent stellar deaths, potentially explaining why certain black holes are far more common than others.

Using observations from the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA gravitational-wave network, researchers analyzed 257 black hole mergers recorded over the past decade. They found a pronounced concentration of black holes with masses around 10 times that of the Sun, accounting for roughly three-quarters of the merger sample. Black holes between 12 and 16 solar masses, however, were unexpectedly scarce.

The researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes spin, a property influenced by the processes that formed them. Black holes near 10 solar masses had a narrower distribution of spin rates than the overall population. Combined with the unusual mass distribution, this suggests they may belong to a distinct group with a shared formation history.

“We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time,” notes Isaac Legred (PhD ’25), the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who conducted the research at Caltech. “But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.”.

According to recent reports, massive stars typically end their lives when their cores collapse and trigger supernova explosions, ejecting much of their material into space. The remaining cores can become neutron stars or black holes. However, theoretical models predict that some massive stars may collapse directly into these compact objects without producing a bright supernova.

According to recent reports, such events, known as failed supernovae, have not yet been conclusively confirmed. Scientists have proposed that they could produce many of the black holes observed in merging binary systems, particularly those around 10 solar masses. In these systems, one or both black holes may have formed through a quiet stellar collapse rather than an explosive death.

“A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun,” says Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and LIGO team member who led the research. “Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin—they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.”.

The National Science Foundation (NSF)-funded LIGO observatories in Louisiana and Washington made the first direct detection of gravitational waves from merging black holes in 2015. These ripples in spacetime carry information about the masses and spins of the objects that produced them. Together with Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan, the network has now detected more than 300 black hole collisions.

Sources indicate that the new study, published in Physical Review D, was led by Chatziioannou, with Legred as lead author and former Caltech researcher Jacob Golomb (PhD ’25), now at Asari AI, as a coauthor. Although the findings agree with theoretical predictions for failed supernovae, they do not directly establish that these events occurred.

“We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it’s challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky,” Legred states. “With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.”.

Sources indicate that reference: “Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10M⊙ peak in the merging black hole mass distribution” by Isaac Legred, Jacob Golomb and Katerina Chatziioannou, 10 November 2026, Physical Review D. DOI: 10.1103/mnzq-w1b5.

In a recent development, funding: U.S. National Science Foundation, DOE/US Department of Energy, Simons Foundation.
