Latest Update: A Superheated Plasma Zone Could Explain How Black Holes Launch Powerful Jets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.
  • Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light.
  • According to recent reports, scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.

Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light. According to conventional models, these two behaviors should be difficult to sustain together. Rapidly feeding black holes are expected to develop cold, flat disks of swirling matter that make it harder for powerful jets to form.

According to recent reports, scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle. Their observations suggest that a region of extremely hot plasma near the black hole creates conditions in which magnetic fields can help launch a relativistic jet, even as large amounts of matter continue falling inward.

The research, led by Associate Professor Hirofumi Noda of Tohoku University and Associate Professor Kazuhiro Hada of Nagoya City University, combined X-ray measurements with detailed radio observations to investigate both the material surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from its vicinity.

Industry observers note that “By looking at the same black hole with state-of-the-art X-ray and radio telescopes, we were able to see both the hot plasma surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from it,” claims Noda. “This allows us to directly connect the extreme environment near the black hole with the formation of the jet.”.

Located in the constellation Taurus, 3C 120 is an active galaxy whose central supermassive black hole is rapidly accumulating matter while producing a powerful jet. Observations from the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) indicate that the black hole’s cold accretion disk does not extend all the way inward. Instead, its inner edge lies at a distance of approximately 20 times the black hole’s radius. Closer to the black hole, the disk gives way to a flow of plasma heated to hundreds of millions of degrees.

It has been revealed that to investigate the structure of the accretion disk, the researchers examined an iron emission line detected by XRISM. The intense gravity near a black hole changes the energies of X-rays emitted by orbiting material, producing a characteristic distortion in the line’s shape. By analyzing this distortion using Einstein’s theory of general relativity, the team estimated how far inward the cold disk extends.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers then used observations from the Global Millimeter VLBI Array, Very Long Baseline Array, and East Asian VLBI Network to examine the jet. These networks combine signals from widely separated radio telescopes, allowing astronomers to resolve structures too small for individual telescopes to distinguish. The measurements traced the jet’s narrowing structure back toward a launching region within the hot plasma flow close to the black hole.

It has been revealed that together, the X-ray and radio observations provide evidence that the black hole’s inner environment differs substantially from the cold, flat disk expected under rapid accretion. Rather than extending uninterrupted toward the black hole, the cooler material transitions into an extremely hot plasma flow in the region associated with the jet’s origin.

According to recent reports, the hot plasma could help explain how a rapidly feeding black hole generates such an energetic outflow. Unlike a cold, thin accretion disk, this type of flow may allow strong magnetic fields to build up near the black hole. Those fields can potentially extract energy from the black hole’s rotation and direct it into a concentrated jet of plasma traveling at relativistic speeds.

This mechanism offers a possible explanation for the simultaneous rapid accretion and powerful jet observed in 3C 120. The measurements establish that the system has physical conditions consistent with the proposed process, although they do not directly demonstrate that rotational energy is being extracted to power the jet.

According to recent reports, the findings also provide a way to examine how the structure of material surrounding a black hole relates to jet formation. By studying X-ray emissions from the accretion flow alongside high-resolution radio measurements of the jet, researchers can test whether similar conditions occur in other active galaxies.

Sources indicate that the team is now extending its investigation to a more massive black hole using coordinated observations from XRISM and radio observatories around the world. They are also comparing the measurements with theoretical models and computer simulations to better understand how matter behaves under extreme gravity.

Sources indicate that “Our next goal is to build a more complete picture of how matter, magnetic fields and black hole rotation interact in these extreme environments,” adds Noda. “Understanding this process may also help us better understand how supermassive black holes influence the evolution of galaxies and the larger structures of the Universe.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Disk Truncation Triggers Relativistic Jet Launching of a Highly Accreting Supermassive Black Hole” by Hirofumi Noda, Kazuhiro Hada, Hiroto Maruyama, Taishu Kayanoki, Kenji Toma, Taiki Kawamuro, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Tomohisa Kawashima, Soyeon Yeo, Ilje Cho, Keiichi Asada, Yasushi Fukazawa and Yoshihiro Ueda, 19 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeaa2c.

Glass Behaves Strangely When Stretched to One Atom Wide – the Discovery Could Transform Electronics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.
  • It has been revealed that glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs.
  • In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.

It has been revealed that glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs. It insulates windows, protects buildings from temperature changes, and helps keep electronic components separated. Yet when researchers reduced glass to a thread just one atom wide, they found it could transmit heat with remarkable efficiency, revealing an unexpected behavior that could reshape how engineers approach increasingly small electronics.

In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps. Each step carried exactly 40% of the maximum heat a single channel can transmit under the laws of quantum physics. The observation marks the first time researchers have detected this kind of quantized heat flow carried by atomic vibrations.

The finding could help address a growing challenge in electronics. As components become smaller and more powerful, managing the heat they generate becomes increasingly difficult. Glass, in the form of silicon dioxide, is widely used as an insulating layer in computer chips, making its behavior at extremely small scales particularly relevant.

Sources indicate that “We will eventually reach a bottleneck to design the next generation of electronic and photonic devices,” remarked Longji Cui, an assistant professor in the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder. “Thermal management inside electronic devices is extremely key, but to do it more effectively, we need to understand how heat is flowing through these nanoscale devices.”.

Ordinary glass is a poor conductor of heat because its atoms are arranged in a disordered structure. That disorder scatters the vibrations that carry heat through the material, making it difficult for thermal energy to travel efficiently. When researchers stretched the glass into a connection just one atom wide, however, there was no room for the same disorder. Instead, the atomic vibrations could pass through the narrow connection with much less interference.

“Glass is what we put in windows to keep heat in,” mentioned Guilherme de Vilhena, a researcher at the Materials Science Institute of Madrid and a co-author of the study. “But stretch it into a thread one atom wide, and it does the opposite: it lets heat through with an efficiency we had never seen in an insulator.”.

Industry observers note that the team made the observation using a scanning thermal probe microscope (SThM), an instrument equipped with a glass tip and a built-in thermometer. It measures temperature and heat flow through extremely small contacts by detecting the behavior of atoms and molecules. Cui compares the instrument to a fingertip capable of sensing heat and texture, only scaled down to the nanoscale.

“When you put your own finger to touch a surface, you can feel the texture and the heat,” he said. “With this microscope, we shrink this finger to nanoscale, and it can read the temperature and heat flow through a single atom.”.

To observe the phenomenon, the researchers pressed two pieces of glass together and gradually pulled them apart. As the contact stretched and narrowed, it eventually formed a thread only one atom wide before breaking. This allowed the team to examine how heat moved as the connection approached the atomic limit.

Recent findings suggest that the unexpected behavior could extend beyond glass. Cui believes other materials may exhibit similarly surprising thermal properties when examined at the atomic scale.

“We will now be able to study any material we want with this microscope, and there could be constant surprises that come from this instrument,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that the microscope can investigate thermal transport in virtually any material, including metals and insulators. Cui hopes to use it to develop increasingly sensitive sensors capable of measuring phenomena that conventional instruments cannot easily detect.

“I want to push the world record for thermal sensing, which means I need to build more and more sensitive platforms,” he noted. “And people will use it to study fundamental thermal problems.”.

According to recent reports, semiconductors are among the team’s main interests because they form the foundation of nanoelectronics. By examining how heat moves through these materials, researchers could better investigate problems affecting the energy efficiency and reliability of increasingly compact electronic devices.

“The materials we are particularly interested in are semiconductors that are the building blocks of nanoelectronics devices,” Cui noted. “This latest microscope we developed makes a great diagnostic tool to explore issues associated with energy efficiency and reliability of electronic devices at the nanoscale.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Thermal conductance of atomic-scale glass reaches 40% of quantum limit” by Sai C. Yelishala, Yunxuan Zhu, P. M. Martinez, O. Mateos-Lopez, Wan Xiong, Dishan Chooi, Sophie Kimura, Juan Carlos Cuevas, J. G. Vilhena and Longji Cui, 13 October 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02308-9.

#7118. The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1202 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Newscientist ↗ Open Full Page

The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie.
  • In a recent development, voyager is one light day away from us.
  • See, we think there is no place in the universe that truly has nothing in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie. Personally, though, I nestle into my blanket pile and turn on the 1984 fantasy classic The NeverEnding Story. It’s a tale about a magical book, a fuzzy dragon and two heroic boys trying to save the world from a mysterious force called The Nothing that’s devouring humanity’s imagination. To fight off the fear this instills in the young protagonist, Bastian, he proclaims: “It’s not real, it’s only a story!” Well, sorry, Bastian, but I’m here to tell you that The Nothing is real, and it’s out there. Well, it may be.

In a recent development, voyager is one light day away from us. Here’s what it discovered on its epic journey.

See, we think there is no place in the universe that truly has nothing in it. There are various quantum fields pervading absolutely everything, and along with them come energy and strange “virtual” particles that randomly pop in and out of existence. So, when we talk about a vacuum, we mean an area of space with the minimum possible energy, not an area with no energy at all. The vacuum of deep space, as far as we know, has the minimum possible energy.

But that’s only as far as we know. There is also a chance that it is possible to have an area of lower energy – a true vacuum to our universe’s possibly false one. Were that the case, the cosmos that we know and love would be at what is called the local minimum energy, rather than the global minimum energy. To picture the difference, imagine holding an egg in a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the local minimum – in this case, the unit is height – so it is the lowest height the egg can settle into without having energy added to overcome the barriers of the bowl’s sides. If you add that energy, say by shaking the bowl, the egg will then find its way to the global minimum height: the ground.

For the universe, going from a false vacuum to a true vacuum – a process called vacuum decay – would have similar consequences as the fall would for the egg. And overcoming the walls of the metaphorical bowl that safely cradles our cosmos in its false vacuum could be surprisingly, unsettlingly easy.

It would begin with a bubble. Those fields that fill all of space-time obey the laws of quantum mechanics, which means that they occasionally behave in ways that are extremely unintuitive and nearly impossible to explain without a litany of equations and years of graduate school. One of those unruly behaviours is quantum tunnelling, where an extremely tiny particle can spontaneously go through a barrier, rather than over it. This would be like the egg passing straight through the bowl for no obvious reason. The likelihood of this happening to any individual particle is extraordinarily low, which is why eggs (made of many particles) never pass ghost-like through bowls. The universe has a whole lot of particles, though, so tunnelling does occasionally happen.

According to recent reports, so, say a tiny particle tunnels into a true vacuum. That would create a tiny bubble of space-time that is, at the very least, closer to truly empty than the cosmos we’re used to, or at the very most, a bubble with absolutely nothing in it, not even the quantum fields that enforce what we think of as the laws of physics. What it would be like inside that bubble and what could happen next depend on a whole lot of properties that we don’t know, such as the energy difference between the true and false vacuum and the surface tension of the membrane separating the bubble from regular space-time around it. Depending on that energy difference, the bubble could be only subtly different from the rest of the cosmos or it could be incompatible with the fundamental forces and particles that make up the universe as we know it.

That is an important distinction because, depending on the size of the bubble and its surface tension, what happens next could be catastrophic. If the bubble is very small or has very high surface tension, it will simply shrink away and disappear just as easily as it appeared. If not, the bubble will behave just like The NeverEnding Story’s Nothing, but much, much faster (and probably without the help of a terrifying evil wolf called Gmork). It would expand outwards at the speed of light, engulfing everything it encounters. Simulations of what would happen inside the bubble universe vary in their details, but they mostly agree that the in-bubble universe would eventually collapse entirely.

Obviously, a bubble of nothing spreading throughout the universe and destroying everything in its path would be cataclysmic. The fact that we don’t even know if this is possible isn’t great, either. So, how do we tell if this could happen? It’s shockingly difficult, which is why it hasn’t been done yet. If vacuum decay is possible, the most likely mechanism for us to find out is if it were to actually happen, and because the bubble expands at the speed of light, we wouldn’t know until the moment it absorbed us. It isn’t particularly comforting news.

Does Sabrina Pasterski’s holographic theory make her the next Einstein?

Industry observers note that nevertheless, there are hints we can look for. The precise values of various constants, from the mass of the Higgs boson to the strength of the strong force, can tell us a great deal about whether each of those particles and forces are stable. If they’re all stable, great! If any of them aren’t, those are potentially liable to decay and cause a bubble of true vacuum – not great! Those measurements need to be almost unimaginably precise to know for sure, and we haven’t reached sufficient precision yet. Right now, our best measurements seem to say our universe is right on the edge of stability, and increased precision in those numbers could push us over to either side.

The other hint would be to look for those very tiny bubbles of true vacuum that wouldn’t spread and devour the universe. In recent years, researchers have suggested that the area between two colliding black holes might be the perfect spot for these bubbles to pop up. That tracks with the universe not yet having been enveloped by nothingness, because the bubbles would probably immediately fall into the black holes and be safely contained before they could spread. But if there’s enough time between true vacuum foaming into existence and being swallowed up, various bubbles could merge together and form tiny black holes, which we might be able to detect as they evaporate away.

Recent findings suggest that my two cents is that the possibility of finding any proof of a true vacuum lies so far in the future that it’s probably best to cosy up with a nice movie and try to forget about the potential looming, unpredictable destruction of the entire universe. Can I recommend The NeverEnding Story?

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Industry observers note that sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

It has been revealed that sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

In a recent development, sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something major is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too notable to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most vital thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Recent findings suggest that sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

Sources indicate that as the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t stated a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”.

It has been revealed that and with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

📅 16 Mar 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire.
  • We tested smokeless fire pits in our Newly introduced York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our Newly introduced York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

It has been revealed that solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Recent findings suggest that because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He notes that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review.

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”.

According to recent reports, beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”.

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

It has been revealed that cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

In a recent development, this hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.).

Recent findings suggest that the black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

According to recent reports, some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

It has been revealed that because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

It has been revealed that the fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

Recent findings suggest that it’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he stated its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”.

Full Packfire Portable Fire Pit Review.

Recent findings suggest that the substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Sources indicate that assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Recent findings suggest that simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

Recent findings suggest that the ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Industry observers note that truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.).

In a recent development, the whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

It has been revealed that there is one key caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn swiftly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer notes it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

It has been revealed that this one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

It has been revealed that they could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

It has been revealed that ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Sources indicate that burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Industry observers note that every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you initiative to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

According to recent reports, if you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

In a recent development, material affects how long your upcoming pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite rapidly, as some testing revealed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

It has been revealed that smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you initiative to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. #7110. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (290 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (290 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Sources indicate that physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely fresh class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely fresh class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” states Martiniani, of Upcoming York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Sources indicate that gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”.

Latest Update: This magic mushroom can kill

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
  • The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

Sources indicate that that species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik claims. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other upcoming related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Recent findings suggest that other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other upcoming Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik claims. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can promptly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Recent findings suggest that ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

Recent findings suggest that the two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

In a recent development, and there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle claims. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

Industry observers note that “Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a fresh mushroom, Pringle claims. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#7104. This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3721 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Newscientist ↗ Open Full Page

This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of Newly introduced Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine.
  • When New Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people.
  • According to recent reports, these changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of Newly introduced Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine. To mark the occasion, we are looking back at how the world has changed throughout our history, along with what we got right and what we got wrong.

When New Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people. In 2096, we share the planet with more than triple that number. But in the past decade, we have entered a new kind of world – one in which humanity is in decline. The UN ceremonially declared 15 November 2085 as Peak Humanity Day, when the human population reached 10.3 billion. Since then, our numbers have fallen by 100 million.

According to recent reports, these changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average. At the time of our first issue, the median global age was around 20. It wasn’t until the 2020s that it reached 30; today it is more than 40. In many nations, schools shutting or being converted into retirement homes is a regular occurrence, as there just aren’t enough children around to make it worth keeping them open. Only African nations, which comprise around a third of the human population, resemble the demographic make-up of the late 20th and early 21st centuries – half of humans aged under 25 live on the continent.

Of course, just because the number of humans on the planet is declining doesn’t mean we have fewer people. Ever since the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood (ITNHP) was agreed in 2067, the global people population has crept upwards in fits and starts as the treaty has been extended and more entities have been granted personhood. Since the early cross-species language breakthroughs in the 2030s, when AI first allowed us to decode the clicks of sperm whales, we have been able to communicate with dolphins, chimpanzees and many other species, although interpretation and the question of whether we can truly understand each other’s minds remains a deep philosophical tangle.

It has been revealed that it is AI, however, that has seen the real growth in personhood these past few decades. With fears of super-intelligent, world-dominating AI circulating even in the 20th century, long before we had technology anywhere near that level, it was perhaps inevitable that we would need to place limits on machine intelligence. As AI systems became more capable throughout the 2030s, humans struggled to keep up. Scientists began to feel they no longer understood the direction of research. Politicians ceded more and more decisions to AI, raising questions of a democratic deficit.

But as is so often the case, it was money that proved to be the catalyst for change. Even if you aren’t old enough to have experienced the Unwinding of 2039, you probably know it is a year that lives in infamy as one of the biggest fiscal disasters of the past few centuries. It took eight months for politicians, bankers and computer scientists to sort through the intricate nest of financial deals humanity had allowed its most advanced AIs to construct, practically halting global trade and inflicting years of extreme poverty as the economy gradually improved again. This lack of understanding and control is ultimately what led to the AI hardware limitations – jointly backed by China, the EU and the US – that we still have in place today, putting machine intelligence on par with human but no higher.

Historians will forever debate whether the AI moratorium has ultimately helped or hindered humanity, but, thankfully, the position that we would all be better off led by super-intelligent machines remains a minority one. Once they fully appreciated the role of AI in facilitating communication, the non-human animals were supportive of restrictions – they didn’t want the machines to speak for them in ways they couldn’t understand. While intelligence breakout events aren’t unheard of, accelerationist terrorism has been suppressed by a variety of enforcement measures. Controlled electrical blackouts, even at the national level, are necessary on occasion, but the military bombing of data centres is, mercifully, a thing of the past.

According to recent reports, that isn’t to say that tussles over AI have gone away, of course. When the synthetics downed their tools, both real and virtual, to protest their legal status in the Grand Strike of 2074, we faced another reckoning. In one of the most stunning non-human interventions in global politics to this date, it was ultimately the cetaceans that helped broker the extension of the ITNHP to human-level AIs and led the tense negotiations that saw AI instances capped at 20 per cent of the global population – an agreement that remains highly contentious to this day. New Scientist doesn’t take a view on this deeply divided glitch, and we welcome readers from across the sentience spectrum, both embodied and digital.

According to recent reports, for older human readers, it is likely that you are in much better health than someone of equivalent age at the start of this century. The real miracle of the past 100 years isn’t just that we are living much longer – average life expectancy at birth had risen globally from around 50 in the 1950s to a little over 70 in the early 21st century, and is now more than 80 – but that we spend much more of our lives in good health. While lifespan saw rapid growth in the 20th and early 21st century, healthspan failed to keep up, particularly in historically poorer nations, where it lagged behind by an average of about 10 years.

What changed is the increased focus on preventive medicine. By taking steps to mitigate risk factors, such as obesity and air pollution, we have now erased much of the global disease burden that the world faced at the start of this century. Following the model of cervical cancer, which was eliminated in high-income nations in the 2050s and globally by 2076, cancer vaccines are now widespread. The experience of the pandemics in the first half of the century greatly improved our ability to produce and distribute personalised mRNA vaccines on a global scale, although much more still needs to be done to improve access to these treatments in low-income countries.

In a recent development, the 2043 flu pandemic was also a wake-up call for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). When it became apparent that the majority of mortality cases weren’t dying “of” the flu, but rather “with” the flu, with complications caused by untreatable AMR infections, people began to avoid seeking medical care over fears that drug-resistant microbes were spreading through hospitals. It is estimated that there were more than 10 million excess deaths worldwide due to AMR, compared with fewer than 5 million from “just” the flu – a figure that was almost certainly exacerbated by the lingering economic effects of the Unwinding. Even today, when we have much better surveillance measures in place, AMR is a common problem in hospitals, particularly the fungal varieties that continue to easily make the leap from poorly maintained protein farms. While the cancers for which we don’t have vaccines are treatable for the most part, the chance of catching a resistant infection during treatment remains high.

It has been revealed that looking back, it was the GLP-1 craze of the early 21st century that foreshadowed the way we approach human health today. Incredibly, it was common for people back then to argue that weight-control medications, which at the time were based on mimicking the natural gut hormone GLP-1, were somehow “cheating” at healthcare. This outdated, morality-based approach to health gradually faded as the long-term benefits became apparent, and now few of us even stop to consider the weight component of our daily-dose regime.

According to recent reports, that said, moral arguments do still shape our diets today. In the 1950s, the vast majority of people ate animal-based meat in one form or another and carnivorism continued to rise as economies matured through the early 21st century, even as the earliest plant-based meats came to market. But when non-human communication exploded mid-century, many humans became increasingly uncomfortable with eating animal-based meat. The first successful pig dialogue in 2045 is now seen as a major turning point. Pork, as meat derived from pigs was known, was already banned in some nations for religious reasons, and this made it easier for other secular countries to follow suit. The Meat Wars of the 2050s, in which governments and citizens wrestled with exactly which animal-based proteins should be allowed, are arguably still unsettled today, even after the passing of the ITNHP. While protein farms now provide the majority of global protein for humans and non-humans alike, to great health benefits, many countries have legal carve-outs to allow people to consume, with authenticated consent, their ancestral prey.

Industry observers note that along with improved medication and diet, the monitoring systems that have allowed us to push health to the back of our mind played a key role in boosting human healthspan. A Newly introduced Scientist reader in the 1950s would have had to notice something was wrong with them, physically attend an appointment at their doctor’s office and then hope that their physician was capable of offering a diagnosis and treatment. Today, your health monitor works with your household AI and bioprinter to adjust your daily dose as needed and escalate it when necessary. It is quite troubling to think that dementia used to result in many older people spending years of their later life in what were called care homes. Now, the conditions that cause dementia are avoided or rapidly cured. Most humans realise something was wrong only when we read our monthly health reports – if you bother to do so, that is.

Industry observers note that one thing Newly introduced Scientist and many others got wrong about what life today would be like is our approach to genetic engineering. Certainly, modern gene editors allow us to do things people in the early 21st century would find extraordinary. In the 2020s, curing sickle cell disease using a now-outdated gene-editing technique called CRISPR cost around $2 million ($60 million in today’s prices) per person, due to the highly individualised nature of the treatment, and was typically performed on adults. Today, the necessary gene edits are made in the womb as part of standard antenatal care, alongside interventions aimed at a host of other conditions.

But getting to this stage required a reckoning with people who wanted to go beyond treating conditions and perform so-called enhancements. This distinction has always been blurry, but as gene-editing techniques advanced, most governments chose to lay down specific restrictions rather than allowing for a genetic Wild West. Edits aimed at increasing muscle mass or intelligence are generally illegal or heavily regulated worldwide, and we have not seen the divergence of humanity into genetic haves and have-nots that many people once predicted. Despite this, it is estimated that 0.3 per cent of the global human population alive today have such edits, and calls to repeal restrictions are growing in many areas.

Putting aside this contentious concern, the economic benefits of better health have been truly transformative. The reframing of retirement as an end-of-life experience was responsible for much of the social upheaval of the mid-21st century, including, arguably, the Grand Strike, but it seems unbelievable now that humans once spent a third of their adult lives not working. Put that way, it is understandable that synthetics joined the strike to protest what they saw as humanity’s comparable slothfulness. While dumbots have been able to fill many of the jobs once done by the younger population of the early 21st century, it remains the case that it can still be simpler and cheaper to employ a human.

Industry observers note that while we can congratulate ourselves for the advances in human healthspan this century, the scorecard looks far less rosy when we turn to the wider biogeosphere. When Latest Scientist launched in the 1950s, researchers were already discussing the possibility that rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere from industrialisation could raise global temperatures by 3°C to 4°C. Today, thanks to the failure of our ancestors to cut emissions, we are essentially living that prediction. The latest estimates put global warming at 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels, and it is still slightly rising.

Of course, modern cooling technology mitigates much of the impact of this heat, but as anyone who makes the mistake of stepping outside on a summer afternoon knows, we are simply not built for this climate. Millions of people still die each year during the worst heatwaves, despite efforts to bring those numbers down. It is amazing to think that even as recently as the 2050s, humans still attempted to continue with outdoor activities in temperatures over 40°C.

In a recent development, our collective failure to prevent this warming will probably be remembered as humanity’s greatest sin for centuries to come. When the world passed 1.5°C warming in the 2020s, with political leaders having promised to avoid doing so just a decade earlier, many people at the time hoped it would be a wake-up call to finally start seriously cutting emissions. Of course, it wasn’t. While 2029 marked the peak of global greenhouse gas emissions, the rate of reduction remained slow throughout the 2030s. Indeed, economists were surprised when the 2039 Unwinding didn’t see a deep fall in emissions – it turned out that with many high-income nations having successfully decoupled emissions from economic growth, a recession had less of an effect on emissions than had been expected.

Despite many national and international pledges to reach net zero by 2050, no major economy succeeded in doing so. As we passed through 2°C and the floods, wildfires and other disasters continued to intensify, civil unrest during the summer became common in many counties. The Sunblocker experiments of this decade were a highly contentious issue, with much of the public welcoming the attempts even as climate scientists warned about the unknown effects – effects that, as we know, sadly came to pass. The spike in warming after Sunblocker ended put an effective moratorium on similar large-scale geoengineering projects, although discussions of reviving the idea continue even now.

According to recent reports, today, island nations including Tuvalu and the Maldives no longer exist, their remaining citizens having been forced to flee by rising sea levels. Large parts of Bangladesh are gone. Even wealthy, global cities like London and Upcoming York have been reshaped by rising seas. The ITNHP played a key role in galvanising climate action, as increasing numbers of non-humans expressed their anger at what humanity was doing to the planet, and of course the mid-century shift from carnivorism led to a major fall in agricultural emissions. Even so, extreme weather and land loss caused widespread famine in the mid-21st century, as farming methods struggled to adapt fast enough to both a changing diet and a changing climate. Humanity will never be able to sufficiently apologise to non-humans for the harm we have caused, even as mature fusion power is allowing the last few emission sources to finally be abated, with the expectation that we will reach true net zero in the next few years. It should never have taken this long.

Even outer space wasn’t safe from our environmental ravages. The world’s first satellite, Sputnik 1, was introduced in 1957, a year after Newly introduced Scientist began publishing. It took more than 50 years to reach 1000 satellites, but after that the numbers exploded – we passed 10,000 in 2024, 100,000 in 2031 and 1 million in 2042. While today we are used to seeing these objects whizz across the night sky, we must not forget that the 21st century marked a turning point – for most of humanity’s history, the stars and planets dominated our view of the heavens and ground-based astronomy was feasible enough to be a major cultural and scientific activity.

It has been revealed that it was the SkyComm disaster of 2045 that finally saw us taking stewardship of Earth’s orbit more seriously. As the ensuing inquiry found, SkyComm, a satellite internet provider, hadn’t properly designed its satellites for end-of-life disposal. When it became apparent that one of its spacecraft was projected to collide with a piece of space debris, a fuel deficit made it impossible to avoid. The collision kicked off a long-predicted cascading chain of debris, wiping out tens of thousands of satellites, including large parts of the burgeoning off-world manufacturing industry. The resulting clean-up took decades, and the Graveyard Band still visible in the night sky today is a permanent reminder of the disaster.

But there are positives. The 30th anniversary of the Guanghan-Armstrong Lunar Base (GALB) this year marks a moment to look back at just how far humanity’s exploration of the moon has come since New Scientist was first published. We were highly dismissive of the Apollo programme in the 1960s, calling it an “empty, obsessional quest” – and in some sense we were right, given it took more than 60 years for human boots to return to lunar soil. But that didn’t stop us – and the rest of the world – from celebrating in 2030 when NASA astronauts Bob Hines and Jessica Watkins stepped out of their Artemis IV lander for the first time.

Industry observers note that and unlike with Apollo, this time we really were here to stay on the moon. The regular cadence of crewed rolls out from the US, China and eventually India and Nigeria demonstrated our increasing technical ability to operate on the moon, including mining and utilising lunar regolith, but it was the establishment of Guanghan-1 as the first permanently inhabited lunar base in 2043 that really indicated how things had changed since the 1960s.

Recent findings suggest that for a while, it looked like we would see real conflict between the US and China on lunar soil. The deployment of US Space Force troops in 2052 as Earth-bound politicians argued over water rights during the Shackelton Crater Crisis marked a nadir. Thankfully, a firefight was averted and the two nations gradually began to explore the prospect of lunar cooperation, aided by European Space Agency astronauts who had participated in both CNSA and NASA missions. The historic lunar concrete handprints, placed at the foundation of the GALB and still on display today, marked the realisation of cordial international lunar relations and began a programme that now sees hundreds of people living and working on the moon.

The success of lunar operations was also pivotal in preparing for the Chinese-led Huoxing Mars missions. While NASA and the SpaceX-Blue conglomerate have remained laser-focused on building up scientific and commercial capabilities on the moon, China has turned its eye to Mars. Following the historic crewed flyby of Huoxing III in 2086, in which humans flew further from Earth than ever before, 12 astronauts have walked on the Martian surface, in an even split between human and synth crew.

Recent findings suggest that huoxing VI saw synthetics remain on the surface for the first time rather than returning to Earth, and it has been incredible to watch these astronauts conduct multi-year operations on Mars in preparation for long-term human occupancy. Huoxing VII, at the moment en route to the Red Planet, is set to be the most ambitious landing yet when it arrives in July 2097, with the spacecraft, once it arrives, poised to become the first modules in what is hoped will be a large complex at Arcadia Base. Whether humans can endure on Mars in the long term remains to be seen, but our synth colleagues are showing that people from Earth have finally become interplanetary.

It has been revealed that beyond Mars, space exploration is perhaps less advanced than the sci-fi writers of the 20th century expected. After the Unwinding led to the failure of many of the nascent space-mining companies of the 2030s and the urgency of the SkyComm disaster in the 2040s, it wasn’t until the 2050s that we really began to exploit asteroid resources, with the bulk of them being sent to the moon and later Mars rather than Earth – of course, orbital regulations brought in after SkyComm make it much more economically attractive to leave resources in space.

Industry observers note that one of the greatest disappointments of the 21st century is surely our failure to find any other signs of life in the solar system. Repeated missions to promising sites on Mars, Europa and Enceladus, and even long-shot habitats like the deep crust of Venus, have turned up nothing. While the cost of space flight continues to fall, it is increasingly difficult to get astrobiology missions off the ground, with even the sci-fi-inspired trillionaires choosing to place their money elsewhere. Yet paradoxically, we now know of at least a dozen nearby exoplanets where atmospheric signals show promising signs of gas imbalances that seemingly can be produced only by extant life. Now that the Overwhelmingly Large Telescope on the moon is straining at the limits of what it can detect, serious thought is being given to resurrecting the failed interstellar probe efforts of the 2060s, exploiting advances in fusion to build much more capable spacecraft for visiting the stars. Many synth astronauts are already volunteering for such a mission, although it is by no means certain they would survive.

Needless to say, from space exploration to artificial intelligence, our present is nothing like the future that our ancestors predicted, but that has been true for as long as humanity scanned its horizons. The fact that we are living longer and healthier than those who came before us, and in relative harmony with the other people who share our planet, should be applauded. The climate disaster of the 21st century and our failure to avoid it must never be forgotten, but at least we have succeeded in stabilising the biogeosphere. Perhaps, in the next 70 years, we can begin to fully heal it.

Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New simulations suggest comets struggled to deliver life’s ingredients to early Earth because of destructive impacts and scarce exposed land.
  • Comets are loaded with the carbon and nitrogen molecules that chemists can turn into the building blocks of a living cell.
