📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New simulations suggest comets struggled to deliver life’s ingredients to early Earth because of destructive impacts and scarce exposed land.

Comets are loaded with the carbon and nitrogen molecules that chemists can turn into the building blocks of a living cell.

For more than a century, that has made comets a possible source of the ingredients that helped life begin on Earth. The trouble is the arrival.

A comet hits Earth at around 17 miles (28 kilometers) per second. The heat of that impact destroys most of the fragile molecules on board.

In newly introduced computer simulations that replayed Earth’s first 500 million years 100,000 times, the usual outcome was that not one comet delivered a useful dose.

Richard Anslow of the Institute of Astronomy at the University of Cambridge led the work, with colleagues at Cambridge and the University of Edinburgh. The result is a model rather than a measurement.

“It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely,” Anslow mentioned.

The authors trace the idea to a 1908 paper, and it has lasted because comets really do carry the right molecules.

Anslow’s team focused on one of them, hydrogen cyanide. In the lab, a strong enough solution of it can be turned into sugars, fats and the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

Comets carry hydrogen cyanide at about a tenth of a percent of their water ice.

It’s the only such raw ingredient, or feedstock molecule, found in comets at a level that would matter, and it holds up to heat better than most of them.

If comets struggled to deliver hydrogen cyanide intact, delivering more fragile molecules would be even harder.

Comets are porous and weak, and a planet’s atmosphere breaks them apart.

Anything smaller than about 330 feet (100 meters) across explodes high in the air, spreading whatever it carried over a wide area.

A shallow angle means more air to cross, and even some comets more than half a mile (1 kilometer) wide never reach the ground.

Losing the shallow ones matters, because a shallow, slow impact is exactly the kind that lets hydrogen cyanide survive the heat of the crash.

Fewer than 7% of comets arrive at an angle shallower than 15 degrees, and only the largest of those get through the atmosphere.

The team ran Earth’s comet bombardment 100,000 times, each with a different random mix of comet sizes, speeds and angles.

A hit counted as a success only if it landed on exposed land and left hydrogen cyanide at the concentration the lab experiments need.

Every uncertain assumption was chosen to favor the comets.

Across those runs, the median number of successful impacts was zero. In 54% of the runs, not one comet qualified, out of more than 100,000 comets striking the planet in each run.

When a run did produce a success, it came early, most often around 4.4 billion years ago.

That is more than 100 million years before the last common ancestor of all living things, which other researchers place at about 4.2 billion years ago.

In an interview with Earth.com, Anslow was asked what surprised him most when the simulations ran.

“It was a surprise how strongly our simulations – building on recent advances in the modeling of cometary impacts – disfavored this long-standing hypothesis in origins of life research, finding in most cases no comets delivering sufficient feedstock molecules for the origins of life,” he said.

By the team’s count, all the hydrogen cyanide that comets delivered intact over the whole period, spread through the oceans, would be more than 10,000 times too dilute to matter.

So the only version of the idea that works is a local one: a single comet landing on dry land and leaving a concentrated pool.

A comet strike shatters and melts the ground, groundwater floods into the latest crater, and rain and runoff dilute the cyanide within days to weeks.

Industry observers note that the chemical reactions needed to start life would have to occur within that window. By the authors’ rough calculation, the expected wait for such an event is longer than the age of the Universe.

“We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way,” Anslow mentioned. “But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”.

The team ran the same model for Mars and Venus, and the picture changed. Mars is smaller, so comets arrive more slowly, and its thin air lets almost every comet reach the ground.

Industry observers note that in the model, Mars took about one-fifth as many comet hits as Earth. Even so, the simulations gave it 744 successful deliveries on average, against 87 for Earth and 24 for Venus, before land was taken into account.

“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” Anslow mentioned.

“Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked where Earth’s first building blocks came from if not from comets, Anslow remarked he wouldn’t speculate. He pointed instead to research he finds promising.

Molecules might have been made and concentrated on Earth’s own surface, or made after large asteroid impacts, or delivered by carbon-rich asteroids such as Ryugu and Bennu.

It has been revealed that several of the model’s inputs are still open. The formula for how much hydrogen cyanide survives an impact leaves out a comet’s internal strength and porosity, and the authors wrote that this probably makes their estimates too generous.

Early Mars was modeled with today’s atmosphere. If its atmosphere was once thicker, fewer comets might have reached the ground intact.

Recent findings suggest that the team expects the same physics to hold for exoplanets, the planets around other stars. Bigger planets pull comets in faster, and most rocky planets found so far are bigger than Earth.

“Exoplanets significantly larger than the Earth are expected to be much poorer candidates for the successful cometary delivery of these key feedstock molecules,” Anslow told Earth.com.

Astronomers could use that to shorten the list of targets when NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory begins its search for Earth-like planets.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

In a recent development, fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Recent findings suggest that children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, states archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

In a recent development, the purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

It has been revealed that davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he indicates. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Early on March 30, 2026, a SpaceX rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Caltech robot released on March 30, 2026 assembled one bay of a truss in orbit with no astronauts, in what Caltech calls a first.

Early on March 30, 2026, a SpaceX rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base. On board was a Caltech robot packed into a box about 35 cubic feet (1 cubic meter) in size.

On the ground, Jaden Suh, then a Caltech postdoctoral scholar on the team, watched the launch with tears in his eyes.

Industry observers note that months later, that box built a structure in orbit without help from astronauts, a first according to Caltech. Its robotic arm picked up struts and joints from nearby dispensers. It then assembled a fresh section of a truss in orbit.

Sources indicate that the demonstration, called ASTRA, was meant to build an entire reflector antenna. The team ran short of time and built only the initial section. The mission ends in December, according to Caltech.

ASTRA, short for Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly, flew as one of 10 payloads on Vigoride 7. That orbital vehicle was built by Momentus Inc. Vigoride 7 itself rode to low Earth orbit on SpaceX’s Transporter-16 mission.

It has been revealed that inside the payload were two truss sections, or bays, that had been built on the ground, plus an armlike manipulator. Motorized dispensers held the rest of the parts needed to finish the structure.

Recent findings suggest that the team leader is Sergio Pellegrino, a professor of aerospace and civil engineering at Caltech. He is also a senior research scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. He called it “the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space.”.

The payload was completed, tested and handed over to Momentus in less than 12 months. Pellegrino said that schedule was an enormous undertaking for a small team.

Once ASTRA reached orbit, the team sent commands to its computer through the Vigoride vehicle. First, the restraints that held the parts in place during launch were released.

Industry observers note that next, the robot pushed the two prebuilt bays out of the builder. Then it assembled the third bay on an assembly plate.

Three team members sent the commands. They were Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer, Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer, and graduate student Tara Venkatadri.

Sources indicate that after each step they checked the result against photos downloaded from orbit. The payload carries 11 cameras.

Contact with the payload was limited to about seven or eight windows a day, each lasting roughly 15 minutes. Operations were repeated to get around unforeseen problems, of which Caltech said there were many.

To fix them, the engineers kept a twin of the payload, a flight spare, in Pellegrino’s Caltech lab. They tested possible fixes on the spare and then sent the working version up to orbit. When an matter is confirmed in space, Sommer remarked, the team tries “to mimic the problem on the ground.”.

In a recent development, ASTRA was meant to build a reflector antenna about 4.6 feet (1.4 meters) across from composite fiber tubes, aluminum joints and Kapton, a thin, heat-resistant plastic film. DARPA calls the robot a relatively simple gantry, able to move along three straight axes.

In a recent development, on a normal cycle the arm builds one bay on an assembly plate, attaches the reflective film and pushes the bay out into space. Springs keep the two film nets under tension. Then it starts on the next bay, until all 11 are done.

In a recent development, igor Bargatin’s group at the University of Pennsylvania co-invented the perforated film with the Caltech team. Per Caltech, it needs less built-in tension than the knitted metal mesh normally used in foldable reflectors, so engineers can design lighter structures.

Andrew Detor, the DARPA program manager for the project, compared the approach to building with Tinkertoys or K’Nex construction toys in the agency’s statement.

It has been revealed that ASTRA belongs to DARPA‘s Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design program, known as NOM4D. DARPA started it in 2022.

Sources indicate that until now there have been two ways to put a large structure in space. One is to fold it for launch and unfurl it in orbit. The other is to piece it together by hand from sections sent up over several releases.

Recent findings suggest that caltech describes building the structure in orbit as a third option. Detor said NOM4D is aiming at structures “hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale.”.

NOM4D was not first planned around a flight test. After good results from teams in phase 2, Detor changed the last phase to a space demo. He noted the program went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype in 15 months.

Sources indicate that ASTRA is one of two projects that reached phase 3. The other comes from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Later this year it will test a new resin for composite structures on the International Space Station.

It has been revealed that the team considers it unlikely that ASTRA will finish the full truss before December. Two bays were built on Earth and one in orbit, so eight of the 11 remain unbuilt.

Recent findings suggest that caltech mentioned the engineers learned enough to show that the assembly approach is viable. They also learned that the design needs to be simplified and refined.

Recent findings suggest that suh is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin. He noted orbit differs from the ground in many ways, and that is the reason for proof-of-concept flights.

Even complete, the ASTRA antenna would span only 4.6 feet (1.4 meters). DARPA’s target is hundreds of meters or more, and Detor remarked nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.

Industry observers note that caltech video on the ASTRA assembly demonstration for DARPA’s NOM4D program. Credit: Caltech.

Pellegrino said the method fits structures too large to be built on the ground and unfolded. Large reflectors could serve as mirrors for space telescopes, like the big optics planned for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, or as wide radio antennas.

In a recent development, pellegrino also co-directs Caltech’s Space Solar Power Project, which aims to collect solar power in orbit and send it to Earth without wires. He remarked the same approach could help build very large solar arrays for that work.

Industry observers note that detor listed large space depots, habitats, solar arrays and radio antennas as things a future space economy will need. Robots also appear in prepares for building on the Moon, such as NASA’s plan to use 3D printing and robots for a lunar base. Any such economy would share orbit with the millions of pieces of debris that already circle the planet.

It has been revealed that suh joined ASTRA at the start, as a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech. He stated many of his original ideas are in the system, and that “sending your stuff to space is what I’ve been dreaming of my entire life.” Part of that system is now a truss bay in orbit, photographed by the payload that built it.

The information was obtained from Caltech and DARPA.

Tech Report: A 5th-century boat burial held a carved alder chair, and its owner carried a leprosy branch new to northern Europe

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA from a 5th-century boat burial at Fallward, Germany, points to a man of about 50 with Danube roots and a leprosy branch latest to northern Europe.
  • Between 1995 and 1998, the archaeology service of Germany’s Cuxhaven district excavated a boat burial at Fallward, near the North Sea coast.
  • Recent findings suggest that his skeleton then went into storage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA from a 5th-century boat burial at Fallward, Germany, points to a man of about 50 with Danube roots and a leprosy branch latest to northern Europe.

Between 1995 and 1998, the archaeology service of Germany’s Cuxhaven district excavated a boat burial at Fallward, near the North Sea coast. In grave 265, a man of about 50 lay in an oak boat more than 13 feet (4 meters) long, with a carved chair outside it.

Recent findings suggest that his skeleton then went into storage. Nearly three decades later, a genetics lab in Kiel sampled his heel bone and a molar. It found leprosy bacteria, plus DNA that points to the Danube region.

The strain sits on a branch first known from an Egyptian mummy and had not been found in central or northern Europe before. His exact homeland is still not pinned down, the researchers say.

Recent findings suggest that fallward was a village on a terp, an earth mound raised on a beach ridge to keep homes above storm floods. There were no dikes yet. The study lists it among eight mound villages between the Elbe and the Weser founded in the 1st century BCE.

It has been revealed that the village was probably abandoned by the end of the 5th century CE. Its cemetery was used from the late 3rd century onward and held about 200 cremations and 60 burials of bodies. Some pits went 6.5 feet (2 meters) down into old marsh clay.

Industry observers note that the wet clay kept wood, furs, cloth and plant mats from rotting. Several graves were lifted as whole blocks and frozen. A German Research Foundation project at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research (NIhK) in Wilhelmshaven is now opening them in the lab.

The man died in the second quarter of the 5th century. Wooden panels closed his boat like a roof. Inside, he lay on a reed mat, and fish bones turned up in the boat with him.

In a recent development, the chair outside the boat was cut out of one alder trunk, with notched patterns, and was probably painted when upcoming. The NIhK calls it the Throne from the Marsch.

A maple footstool lay by his feet, with a runic inscription and a hunting scene on its underside. Rolf Kiepe of the NIhK photographed both pieces.

According to recent reports, diggers also found a game board, a bronze basin, a clay pot and a little box in the shape of a water bird. A late Roman military belt lay in the grave too.

Many of these things show wear and old repairs. The authors think they belonged to him or his family and were not made for the grave.

Hauke Jöns of the NIhK said the belt had already suggested that the man “had had connections across great distances.” The wood came from local trees, but the decoration indicates the influence of late Roman art.

In Kiel, the Ancient DNA Working Group of the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) got 12 bone samples from 11 people buried at Fallward. It read the DNA on a high-throughput sequencing machine. Seven males and one female could be identified.

Three people had enough DNA to compare with other ancient groups. The adult man in grave 14 and a 3-year-old girl in grave 250 matched northwestern Europe, closest to Anglo-Saxons in England. Their relatives may have joined the North Sea crossings of the migrations of the first millennium AD.

Industry observers note that the man in grave 265 grouped elsewhere. His DNA fell among Roman-era people from the Danube frontier in present-day Croatia, Slovenia, Hungary and Serbia.

A mapping program called mobest placed the most likely location of genetic similarity more than 870 miles (1,400 kilometers) southeast of Fallward, near the old Roman border.

His Y chromosome, passed from father to son, belongs to a lineage called haplogroup G, which today is most common in the Caucasus.

It has been revealed that A scan for germs found Mycobacterium leprae, the bacterium that causes leprosy, in both the tooth and the heel bone. There was more bacterial DNA than human DNA. The team read over 99 percent of the bacterial genome at least four times.

Lead author Daniel Myburgh, a doctoral researcher at the IKMB, and his colleagues built a family tree of 44 ancient and 185 modern leprosy genomes.

The Fallward strain landed near the root of branch 4. Only one genome on that branch is older, from a mummy at Abusir in Egypt dated to the 4th to 2nd centuries BCE.

Myburgh noted the man “is the first individual from this group to have been identified in Europe.” Earlier work on medieval graves tracked other strains, such as one from central or western Asia in a pilgrim’s skeleton found by Winchester researchers.

Recent findings suggest that according to the World Health Organization, leprosy mainly harms the skin and the nerves. The Fallward man’s bones show no leprosy damage.

Either he had no symptoms or the infection had only reached soft tissue. Almut Nebel, a professor at the IKMB, mentioned, “He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease.”.

The authors give more than one possible life story. He may have been a foederatus, a hired soldier who served in the Roman army.

Ben Krause-Kyora, who leads the study at the IKMB, remarked the man could have been a mercenary who later “settled between the Elbe and the Weser,” or a long-distance trader.

The paper adds that the belt does not necessarily mean army service. Such belts were also traded, inherited or taken as war booty. Roman soldiers carried habits and symbols across provinces, as a study on what held Roman soldiers together found.

In a recent development, his bones suggest a third option. His upper arm muscles were very well developed. Together with the boat, the reed mat and the fish bones, that could point to a boatman or a fisherman.

In a recent development, most of the human DNA was in bad shape. The three usable genomes covered only 32,000 to 67,000 of the roughly 1.24 million genetic markers that ancient DNA labs usually check. The man’s sample also showed less ancient damage than the girl’s.

Recent findings suggest that other statistical ancestry models could not set him apart from the two local people. The authors write that his origin needs caution and that three people do not speak for all of Fallward.

Sources indicate that two children in graves 224 and 282 read as boys in the DNA, though they were buried with brooches and beads. Their data were too weak to be sure.

In a recent development, the raw sequences sit in the European Nucleotide Archive. The ROOTS Cluster of Excellence paid for the work, Kiel University mentioned on November 3, 2026.

According to recent reports, many Fallward grave goods ended up in museum cases while the bones stayed in storage. A sample from one heel now links the man with the alder chair to the Danube frontier and to a leprosy branch whose earliest known member comes from Egypt.

The full study was published in the journal iScience.

Four volunteers spent 378 days inside a windowless NASA Mars habitat

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four NASA CHAPEA volunteers left a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston on Oct.
  • Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery walked out of NASA’s Mars habitat in Houston on Saturday, Oct.
  • In a recent development, ellis, the crew’s medical officer, later told NASA that on most days she did not feel isolated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four NASA CHAPEA volunteers left a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston on Oct. 31, 2026, after 378 days.

Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery walked out of NASA’s Mars habitat in Houston on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. They had gone in on Oct. 19, 2025, and stayed 378 days with no windows and no live calls home.

In a recent development, ellis, the crew’s medical officer, later told NASA that on most days she did not feel isolated. She mentioned she relied on her three teammates every day to get through the mission.

In a recent development, the year inside was CHAPEA Mission 2, NASA’s second yearlong simulation of life on the surface of Mars. NASA posted the crew’s reflections on Nov. 9. The health data are still to be interpreted in two weeks of post-mission evaluations.

The habitat is called Mars Dune Alpha. It was 3D-printed, covers roughly 1,700 square feet (158 square meters) and sits inside a building at Johnson Space Center.

On entry day in October 2025, the crew rode to the habitat in the Space Exploration Vehicle, a prototype pressurized rover, according to NASA’s Human Research Program.

In a recent development, suzanne Bell, the mission’s co-principal investigator, spoke to them at the door. Two alternate crew members posed with them for photos before the start.

Sources indicate that CHAPEA is short for Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog. The first mission used the same habitat and ended on July 6, 2024.

Before the second crew went in, the prepares for a second yearlong rehearsal in the printed habitat put crew autonomy at the center.

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway spoke about the time they were away. While they were inside, he flew a 237-day mission on the International Space Station and came back. The Artemis II crew also traveled around the Moon in that period and set a distance record for humans.

Hathaway said the year required “immense physiological and psychological strength, teamwork, and human grit.”.

Messages between the habitat and mission control took up to 22 minutes each way. The crew spoke with their families only by email, with a Mars-like delay, NASA said in a one-year upgrade on Oct. 19.

In a recent development, on May 7 the crew reached day 200. That week they were in a two-week loss of signal, a planned blackout like the one when Mars passes behind the Sun, according to a NASA update from May. They worked with no contact with mission control and used preplanned procedures.

The crew also had to handle simulated equipment failures and limited supplies. Michael Stenger, chief scientist of the Human Research Program, said the mission was starting to show NASA what year-long missions need, including medical and psychological care across communication delays.

Elder was the commander, Ellis the medical officer, Montgomery the science officer and Spicer the flight engineer. As part of their personal item allowance, the four brought musical instruments into the habitat.

In a recent development, elder is a former U.S. Air Force experimental test pilot. According to NASA, he found the Marswalks and robotic work very similar to working as part of a flight.

For a Marswalk, the crew put on suits, went through an airlock and walked on red sand outside the habitat. That area is still inside the building. From inside, crew members also ran a drone and a rover to survey the ground and find or collect rock samples.

Elder stated that getting suits ready, doing airlock procedures and making long traverses took time and stamina. He said food, exercise and rest were needed to keep up that pace.

Sources indicate that montgomery helped identify the rocks brought back from the walks. One NASA photo highlights Ellis and Elder doing a maintenance task outside during a simulated walk. Another shows photos the crew placed around a boot print in the sand.

Spicer worked in satellite communications and spacecraft development before the mission. At the exit, he was thanked for keeping the habitat’s systems running and was called the crew’s resident data scientist.

Recent findings suggest that he compared the year to living on a submarine or a boat. The crew counted supplies from dish soap to respirator filters, and they rationed food and water.

Recent findings suggest that spicer said he was surprised by how little he missed the news and social media, even though the crew could get news. He told his crewmates they made the year “not a chore, but a joy.”.

According to recent reports, montgomery had worked in hardware engineering, robotics, tech startups and independent films. He set up the habitat’s 3D printing capabilities and ran a seed germination test with simulated Martian soil and a control.

He also grew vegetables in a hydroponic system. NASA has run other work on growing lettuce, peppers and tomatoes in microgravity, because packaged food can lose flavor and vitamins.

Sources indicate that ellis is a U.S. Space Force officer and has worked at the National Reconnaissance Office. Inside the habitat she helped organize biological sample collections and prepare supplies for the health studies.

It has been revealed that she said it was hard to explain to other people what life inside was like. “It would be difficult to convince someone who has never lived in isolation that most days, I don’t feel isolated,” she said.

Industry observers note that ellis thanked the exercise, behavioral health, nutrition and medical specialists on the ground. She mentioned the main lesson for her was that a Mars crew will need a closely integrated ground team.

Isolation has also been studied at Concordia Station in Antarctica, where researchers linked living in close quarters to more conflict and mistrust.

Sources indicate that the crew started two weeks of tests and debriefs with NASA scientists after the exit. Scientists will compare the data with what the crew reported. Mission 2’s results are still to come, and each crew has only four people.

In a recent development, grace Douglas, the principal investigator, noted the results will help NASA weigh health risks against crew time, communication capacity and food and water systems. She also said many of the resource problems in space are like problems on Earth.

Sara Whiting, the project scientist, noted the data will feed into intends for NASA’s Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. “This is really the now moment for this kind of data,” she said.

NASA’s live broadcast of the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew leaving the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, 2026. Credit: NASA Johnson.

On Oct. 31, the four stepped outside for the first time in 378 days, where family, friends and colleagues met them. Ellis had said that on most days inside, she did not feel isolated.

The information was obtained from NASA.

Sea otters are adorable and iconic, but few people understand how important they are to ocean ecosystems

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp.
  • Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp, so otters are famous for bringing kelp forests back.
  • Around San Nicolas Island, off Southern California, otters, urchins, and kelp lived together for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp. On Southern California reefs, a study suggests, competition among grazers and seaweeds weakened that chain.

Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp, so otters are famous for bringing kelp forests back. Off Vancouver Island, it happened so fast that a reef was almost always one or the other: covered in urchins or covered in kelp.

Around San Nicolas Island, off Southern California, otters, urchins, and kelp lived together for years.

A study of both coasts suggests that on the southern reefs, competition among other species weakened the otters’ effect on kelp.

In a recent development, the fur trade wiped out sea otters across most of the places where they once lived. Otters were brought back to Vancouver Island from 1969 to 1972 and to San Nicolas Island from 1987 to 1990.

Researchers surveyed the same marked sites year after year, eight off Vancouver Island and six around San Nicolas. The records run through 2017.

A team led by Ryan Langendorf of the Department of Environmental Studies at the University of Colorado Boulder built a statistical model from those records. The study was published in March 2025.

The model’s numbers are estimates of how strongly species affected one another, not direct measurements.

Ecologists call the sea otter a keystone species. That means it has an unusually large effect on the other species around it.

“We always thought keystone species control their ecosystem the same way, regardless of where they are or what else is in the ecosystem,” Langendorf stated.

“A more modern view is that they are still very crucial, but they can have different effects in different places.”.

Otters reduce urchins, and urchins reduce kelp. Two negative effects in a row make a positive one for kelp.

Competition can add a third negative step, and three in a row make a negative one.

In a recent development, at San Nicolas, one of the strongest chains of that kind involved turban snails. Otters eat the snails, and the snails compete with red urchins. With fewer snails, red urchins can do better, and red urchins eat giant kelp.

Sources indicate that the model estimated that these extra chains often made little difference. In some years at some San Nicolas sites, though, they reduced the otters’ effect on giant kelp by 15% to 20%.

Off Vancouver Island, the extra chains made almost no difference.

Fish aren’t in the model, because the team lacked the data. Records of what the otters ate are missing too.

Around San Nicolas, grazing animals didn’t eat giant kelp down to nothing, even before otters were brought back. The authors wrote that their models don’t adequately explain why.

Future analyses could include otter diets, the authors wrote. That may help explain how much the mix of urchin species shaped the otters’ effect.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#7096. Tech Report: Scientists built a wearable device meant to let a friend in another city smell your coffee

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists built a wearable device meant to let a friend in another city smell your coffee

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An electronic nose names a food from its fumes, a message crosses the internet, and a wearable puffs out the matching scent, so far only in a lab.
  • In a recent development, sending a friend a picture of your coffee takes a second.
  • Recent findings suggest that A sensor sniffs the coffee and software recognizes it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An electronic nose names a food from its fumes, a message crosses the internet, and a wearable puffs out the matching scent, so far only in a lab.

In a recent development, sending a friend a picture of your coffee takes a second. The smell stays in the kitchen, however, because phones carry pictures and sound but nothing for the nose. A new wearable device now gets around that.

Recent findings suggest that A sensor sniffs the coffee and software recognizes it. Then a short message tells a device on your friend’s wrist to release a coffee smell that it already holds.

What crosses the internet is a label rather than the smell itself, and that is both the trick and the limit. The system is a laboratory prototype.

Sources indicate that it knows five smells so far: beer, cake, coffee, orange, and red wine. It reproduces each one from a scented liquid loaded into the device ahead of time.

Sources indicate that engineers at Ohio State University built the system and named it Scentronic. Chunyu Yang, a doctoral student in the University’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering, is the first author.

Jinghua Li’s group ran the work with colleagues at Zhejiang Laboratory in China.

In an interview with Earth.com, Yang described what the device is for. “Scentronic has the potential to allow people to share smells with others over long distances, much like we right now share images, sounds, and videos,” he said.

“For example, someone could share the aroma of their coffee with a friend in another city.”.

It has been revealed that the sniffing end is a ring of six gas sensors around a spot where the food sits. Each sensor is a heated chip of tin dioxide.

Vapors from food, such as the alcohol in beer and wine, change how easily electricity flows through the sensor. Engineers call a sensor array like this an electronic nose.

It has been revealed that no single sensor can tell coffee from cake. The six together produce a pattern, so the team trained a pattern-matching program on it.

They recorded each of the five foods 50 times, for 200 seconds at a stretch. That made 250 recordings, one brand of each: the cake was a bag of King’s Hawaiian sweet rolls.

On recordings the program had not seen before, the best version named all five foods correctly.

Coffee gave the faintest signal, and the authors wrote that many of the compounds behind its aroma may not be the kind that these sensors detect well.

Industry observers note that once the program decides on coffee, that word is all that travels. It goes to a program on a cloud server and on to the wearable, a trip that took about 65 thousandths of a second in the team’s tests.

Recognizing the food takes longer, from several seconds to a few tens of seconds.

The wearable is built around a thin disk that vibrates about 110,000 times a second. A cotton pad feeds it scented liquid from a small chamber, and the vibration pushes that liquid through tiny holes as a fine mist.

Switching the vibration on and off sets how much mist comes out.

Sources indicate that A wristband version of the device holds two smells. A necklace holds five, lined up, as the authors wrote, “like pearls on a string.” Run flat out, a cartridge empties in under five minutes, and at the lowest setting it lasts more than 35 minutes.

After an hour of continuous use, the warmest spot on the device measured 96.4°F (35.8°C), below body temperature.

Sixteen volunteers from the University kept their noses 8 inches (20 centimeters) from a device while a smell of orange rose through ten strength levels, and stated when they noticed it.

The middle level was where the most volunteers first noticed it, and the spread formed a bell shape, which told the team which settings people can actually smell.

Recent findings suggest that fourteen volunteers then took tests built like a standard smell exam. After learning the five food scents from labeled tubes, they identified single scents from the device about 73 percent of the time.

They named both parts of a two-scent mixture about 71 percent of the time. The hardest test was ranking five strengths of an alcohol scent from weakest to strongest, and they got about 59 percent of those right.

Sources indicate that the volunteers were smelling scents released in the same room. Earth.com asked Yang what surprised him when volunteers first received a smell sent from a distance.

“These were separate experimental evaluations, and we did not specifically investigate volunteers’ reactions to receiving odors transmitted remotely,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that medicine is the use the authors focus on. Head injuries, infections, and diseases of the brain can dull, distort, or erase the sense of smell, and smell problems became a common aftereffect of COVID-19.

Today’s clinic tests use scratch-and-sniff cards or scented pens at a few fixed strengths.

An adjustable device, the authors wrote, could let a clinician raise an odor step by step, over the internet, until a patient notices it. That would find the threshold without an office visit.

A patient who needs a strong puff to notice anything has a weakened sense of smell, the kind of loss seen after COVID-19.

Sources indicate that one who notices a faint puff that others miss may be oversensitive, which happens during migraines and pregnancy. The National Institutes of Health describes these smell disorders.

The team also built a cup with five scent cartridges in its lid and five small pumps in its wall, each pump holding a flavoring liquid.

When the electronic nose smelled beer, coffee, or the two together, the cup released the matching aroma and dripped the matching flavor into the water inside.

In a second demonstration, a person wearing a Meta Quest 3 headset reached for a virtual beer or coffee on a virtual shelf. The real cup then dispensed that drink’s flavor and smell.

The authors wrote that today’s virtual reality headsets focus on sight and sound, while smell and taste shape how real an experience feels.

The authors also wrote that making food seem to taste better could matter for patients with nutritional problems, for astronauts facing unappealing food supplements, and for soldiers eating field rations.

Five smells is a small vocabulary, and the authors wrote as much. The device reproduces a category, coffee rather than this particular coffee, from a liquid chosen in advance, and it doesn’t match the chemistry of the original.

Yang told Earth.com that the number of odors was limited mainly by the time it took to collect training recordings. Adding more, he said, depends on how sensitive and selective the sensors are and on how complex the mixtures get.

The human tests were simple, with few control conditions, and the authors wrote that this could introduce bias. Each food came from a single brand, so whether the program would recognize a different coffee is untested.

Next steps the team listed include working with smell researchers under controlled conditions and recording brain signals while the device delivers a scent.

“Scentronic is at the moment a laboratory prototype,” Yang noted, and “we expect it will take several years, potentially longer, before such devices become commercially available.”.

Until then, every smell the device has sent was sent and received inside a lab.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#7094. Paying down debt can leave a country more exposed when the next hurricane hits

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Paying down debt can leave a country more exposed when the next hurricane hits

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica borrowed about 18% of its economy to recover, and researchers say lenders reward debt cuts but not seawalls.
  • According to recent reports, paying down debt is supposed to make a country safer.
  • The reason, four researchers argue, is that the rules rewarding a country for paying off loans offer nothing comparable for building seawalls and drains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica borrowed about 18% of its economy to recover, and researchers say lenders reward debt cuts but not seawalls.

According to recent reports, paying down debt is supposed to make a country safer. Lenders reward it with better credit ratings and lower borrowing costs. Jamaica spent more than a decade doing exactly that, but one hurricane undid much of the progress in a matter of weeks.

The reason, four researchers argue, is that the rules rewarding a country for paying off loans offer nothing comparable for building seawalls and drains.

In a recent development, hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica as a Category 5 storm in October 2025. It caused an estimated $12.2 billion in damage, losses, and costs.

In a recent development, this represents about 57 percent of the country’s entire economic output for 2024. Insurance covered about 2 percent of that, and Jamaica borrowed roughly $3.6 billion to recover.

Sources indicate that aayushi Mishra, a doctoral candidate at Northeastern University, traced what happened next. Her co-authors are Advait Arun of the Center for Public Enterprise and Northeastern’s Evan Kodra and Auroop Ganguly.

In a recent development, the paper is a policy analysis built on Jamaica’s public finance and disaster-loss figures, not a latest data study. It argues for changes at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the development banks, and the rating agencies.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mishra noted the people running those institutions are not the villains of the story. “No one here is acting in bad faith: every institution is doing exactly what its own rules ask of it,” she said.

“The problem is that those rules, once taken together, leave resilience underfunded.”.

It has been revealed that in 2013, Jamaica owed about 144 percent of its yearly economic output in debt. By 2023 it had cut that to about 72 percent, and it was on track for 60 percent by the 2027 to 2028 budget year.

The country did this through years of tight budgets and strict spending rules that it adopted on its own, not as a condition set by the IMF.

Lenders noticed. In September 2025, the rating agency S&P Global upgraded Jamaica’s credit rating. A few weeks later, Melissa made landfall.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Mishra pointed to the speed of the reversal. “Honestly, how little time it took for Jamaica’s hard-won progress to get diluted by just one storm, albeit a massive one,” she stated.

The team projects Jamaica’s debt will now peak at about 68.5 percent of its economy, roughly 8.5 points above the path it was on. New borrowing makes up most of that increase, and the storm’s damage to output accounts for the rest, shrinking the economy against which analysts measure the debt.

It has been revealed that jamaica had done the things disaster experts recommend. It held a catastrophe bond through the World Bank, which pays investors’ money to the country if a storm crosses set thresholds for wind speed, track, and pressure.

It also bought insurance from a regional pool, the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF), that pays on the same measurements rather than on assessed damage.

Both paid swiftly. The bond paid its full $150 million, and with the insurance and other aid the total reached about $242 million, within 3 to 14 days of landfall. Jamaica waited about three months for its IMF money to be approved.

According to recent reports, but $242 million against $12.2 billion in losses is 2 percent. Speed was never the problem; scale was.

In a recent development, the year before, Hurricane Beryl had caused about $1 billion in damage, and the bond paid nothing because the storm’s measured strength fell short of its trigger. The insurance pool covered $26.6 million of Beryl’s damage, under 3 percent.

According to recent reports, the instruments worked exactly as specified, the team wrote. Insurers have a name for the gap between what a storm measures and what it costs: basis risk. For a whole country, that gap was about 98 cents of every dollar lost.

The country is paying for the rest of the recovery with roughly $3.6 billion in new loans, about 18 percent of Jamaica’s pre-storm output in a single year. That is above the level the IMF treats as a warning sign for emerging economies.

The loans come from the IMF, the World Bank, and three regional development banks, mostly on terms that have not been made public.

In a recent development, so the team modeled a range, from low-cost development lending to near-market rates. The team put total repayments, including interest, at $4.9 billion to $5.7 billion.

Industry observers note that what matters to Jamaica’s budget is the yearly cash payment. At peak repayment, the team estimates, servicing the new debt alone would approach or exceed Jamaica’s entire annual budget for public investment.

Jamaica’s investment budget was already small. In the 2024 to 2025 budget year, Jamaica spent about $3.15 billion servicing debt and about $510 million on public capital projects.

Industry observers note that that second budget is the one that pays for coastal defenses and drainage. “So for every $1 the country spent on things like public infrastructure, it paid $6 in debt service,” Mishra told Earth.com.

According to recent reports, how much would it have taken to avoid the borrowing? Using cost-benefit ratios from disaster research, the team estimates that spending $360 million to $900 million a year on protection before the storm could have offset the new debt entirely.

In a recent development, the IMF’s own 2025 review of Jamaica’s economy found the country could afford only $40 million to $80 million a year on climate adaptation without straining its debt path. That is 4 to 22 times less than the estimated need.

The gap narrows if private investors cover most of the cost, as the researchers assume they would.

The government’s share would then be about $120 million to $300 million a year, still 1.5 to 7.5 times what the IMF considered sustainable.

The team wrote that these figures can’t say which investments would have worked best, or how long they would have taken to build.

Researchers have modeled this pattern before and call it a climate-debt doom loop.

A disaster hits an underprepared country, and the country borrows to recover. The repayments then crowd out spending on protection, so the country is just as exposed when the next disaster arrives.

The authors wrote that no one had documented the loop unfolding in real time inside a single country before.

Industry observers note that rating agencies grade countries on budget surpluses, how fast debt falls, and how strictly budget rules are followed. Some have begun adding climate risk to side reports, but the authors wrote that it stays peripheral to the core decision. Nothing in that system changes when a country builds a seawall.

In a recent development, the IMF’s health check on a country’s debt added climate risk guidance for some programs in 2024. The authors wrote that it is still not part of the core method.

According to recent reports, jamaica’s 2025 review asked how much adaptation the country could afford without hurting its debt path. It didn’t ask the reverse: what happens to the debt when adaptation falls short and a catastrophe follows.

Sources indicate that the paper’s four proposals aim at the lenders, not at Jamaica. Resilience spending should count in the IMF’s debt analysis as something that lowers the odds of a catastrophic loss.

An IMF trust fund created in 2022 for low-cost, long-term climate lending should be scaled up for the most indebted small island states.

Storm insurance triggers should use rainfall and surge as well as wind, and development banks should back the pools so they can pay more.

According to recent reports, the fourth is a clause in loan contracts. Mishra said countries can add these now, while their finances are strong, as Barbados has.

“Simply put, these clauses let debt payments pause for up to two years after a disaster, so the country doesn’t have to take on new debt to cover them,” she remarked. Seventy-three countries and the major development banks have committed to them.

Ganguly, Mishra’s doctoral advisor, said much of the underlying data in this field is kept behind institutional walls or never disclosed.

“We would like to see funders and multilateral institutions to treat disclosure of these terms as standard practice (and not a courtesy), since the public and researchers alike are left to trust conclusions that they can’t necessarily check independently,” he said.

It has been revealed that nearly a year after Melissa, many of the terms of Jamaica’s recovery loans have still not been disclosed, Mishra said. Until they are, the cost of one storm to Jamaica is a range, not a number.

The next test is whether pause clauses get written into loans before the next hurricane arrives, rather than after.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#7093. Breaking: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

📖 Baca

Breaking: Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
  • On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Sources indicate that didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

Recent findings suggest that the cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

Industry observers note that “Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” indicates planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.).

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” notes planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

In a recent development, juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Industry observers note that juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” notes planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer fresh avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

Industry observers note that for example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always indicated the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Sources indicate that similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

📖 Baca

Breaking: One of the dodo’s closest relatives was seen in Samoa for the first time in five years, but no one got a photo

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five sightings of Samoa's critically endangered manumea, a rare relative of the dodo, offer hope for a bird threatened by hunting and habitat loss.
  • It has been revealed that the manumea, or tooth-billed pigeon, is Samoa’s national bird and one of only three surviving relatives of the extinct dodo.
  • During a survey from October 17 to November 13, 2025, the Samoa Conservation Society recorded five manumea sightings in Upolu’s Uafato rainforest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five sightings of Samoa's critically endangered manumea, a rare relative of the dodo, offer hope for a bird threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

It has been revealed that the manumea, or tooth-billed pigeon, is Samoa’s national bird and one of only three surviving relatives of the extinct dodo. Its scientific name is Didunculus strigirostris, and the genus name means “little dodo” in Latin.

During a survey from October 17 to November 13, 2025, the Samoa Conservation Society recorded five manumea sightings in Upolu’s Uafato rainforest.

No photograph was taken, the society mentioned. The bird’s call is also easily confused with that of the more common Pacific imperial pigeon.

Recent findings suggest that like the dodo, the manumea is a pigeon. It is stout and short-toed, about 12 inches (31 centimeters) long.

Its head and neck are a glossy blackish green, and its back and wing coverts are chestnut brown.

The bird is named for several notches along the cutting edge of its lower bill. Its bill is adapted to saw through the tough seeds of Dysoxylum trees, relatives of mahogany, according to the EDGE of Existence program.

Recent findings suggest that it flies clumsily and slowly along a low path, which helps set it apart from other Samoan pigeons. The only nest ever recorded sat about 82 feet (25 meters) up in a banyan tree.

Recent findings suggest that the bird prefers the large, hard-coated fruits of Dysoxylum. Hunters interviewed for the conservation effort said it also feeds on several other fruiting trees, and it may forage on the ground.

The species has been listed as Critically Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) since 2014. It had been listed as Endangered from 2000 to 2014.

Samoa’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society published a recovery plan for the species in March 2020. At that time, the last definite, confirmed sighting dated from August 4, 2017, in the Uafato forest.

A juvenile photographed on Savai’i in December 2013 was the first certain record of the species this century. It also showed that the manumea was still breeding.

The species is known from ten localities on Savai’i, and remote areas of forest on that island have never been surveyed.

Earlier fieldwork suggested that one definite sighting was possible every three to five years, even with medium to intensive search effort.

The 2025 observers saw only adult birds, and the society has noted it is unclear whether the sightings involved one bird or several.

The manumea’s advertising call is nearly identical to one of the calls of the Pacific imperial pigeon, or lupe. Even local hunters and experts struggle to tell the two apart.

A 2020 study in Pacific Conservation Biology tested whether hunters’ traditional knowledge could help. Recordings at nine forest sites on Upolu and Savai’i yielded 104 clear call sequences.

It has been revealed that two top hunters each identified the species behind 80 sequences. They agreed on 54 of them, or 67 percent.

Sound analysis found that the manumea’s coo calls are lower in pitch and more regularly spaced than those of the lupe. The regular rhythm may help observers recognize the bird in the field.

The study also described the manumea as actively hiding in the dense canopy when it hears people moving through the forest.

Surveys in the late 1980s put the population at 4,800 to 7,200 birds across Samoa.

Recent findings suggest that A later estimate of about 500 birds, from 2005 and 2006, is now considered far too high. It relied on calls that are easily confused with the lupe’s.

Surveys in 2012 and 2013 estimated fewer than 50 birds on each of Samoa’s two main islands, Upolu and Savai’i.

Sources indicate that the recovery strategy names three main threats: habitat loss and degradation, hunting and invasive predators. In recent decades, it appears that manumea have been killed mainly by mistake or as bycatch during lupe hunts.

Black rats and feral cats may also harm the species, though there is no direct evidence of it yet. Cyclones Ofa in 1990 and Val in 1991 reduced forest canopy cover by an estimated 27 percent, and the population appears never to have recovered.

Samoa has banned hunting all endemic pigeons, doves and fruit bats since at least 2004, but the rule has never been enforced nationally.

Recent findings suggest that the ten-year plan sets out eight objectives and 26 activities, with an estimated budget of about $1.8 million. Its goal is to improve the species’ status from Critically Endangered to Endangered by 2029.

Early priorities included a conservation working group, a two-year fundraising campaign and a dedicated manumea coordinator.

A 2019 to 2020 national campaign strategy called the manumea “highly threatened and at risk of extinction in our lifetimes.”.

Surveys of remote forest areas are still needed to find any undiscovered groups of the bird.

The information was obtained from the Samoa Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society.

#7091. Malaria mosquito bites aren’t one quick jab but five separate moves under the skin

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Malaria mosquito bites aren’t one quick jab but five separate moves under the skin

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under the skin, a malaria mosquito bite runs in five steps, and the researchers who filmed it say the first two are the ones to stop.
  • Sources indicate that A mosquito bite feels like a single stab.
  • In a recent development, then she spends about 20 seconds pushing a flexible needle in and out, searching for a blood vessel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under the skin, a malaria mosquito bite runs in five steps, and the researchers who filmed it say the first two are the ones to stop.

Sources indicate that A mosquito bite feels like a single stab. Beneath the surface, however, it’s a sequence. A malaria mosquito pierces the skin in a fraction of a second.

In a recent development, then she spends about 20 seconds pushing a flexible needle in and out, searching for a blood vessel. Only then does she start to drink.

Researchers who filmed and recorded that process on a living human arm counted five separate steps, and the mosquito’s legs and mouthparts move in time with each one.

The experiments were done in Christopher Potter’s lab in the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.

Joanna Konopka, who is at the Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute, and Danny Poinapen, who also works at Western University’s Robarts Research Institute in Canada, led the work.

Every bite happened on the right forearm of one volunteer, and the mosquitoes were lab-raised Anopheles coluzzii, a malaria carrier from sub-Saharan Africa.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Konopka was asked whether any of the five steps could be interrupted to stop a bite or an infection. Her answer named the first two.

“The first two stages of the bite (skin piercing and blood vessel searching) are most crucial for disease transmission, because this is when the pathogen is most likely to be introduced via mosquito saliva,” she said.

The volunteer wore a small, clear acrylic box strapped to her forearm with sports wristbands. It left a window of skin about an inch (2.5 centimeters) square.

One female mosquito at a time was released onto that patch while a high-speed camera recorded at up to 250 frames per second. A tracking program followed the legs, the mouthparts, and the two feelers beside them, which are called palps.

What happens below the surface can’t be filmed, so the team recorded it electrically instead. Each mosquito was glued at the back to a gold wire finer than a human hair while the volunteer held an electrode.

The moment the needle broke the skin, the circuit closed, and every movement underneath demonstrated up as a change in voltage.

“We were fascinated by the coordinated and synchronized movements that female mosquitoes exhibit above and below our skin when they are biting us,” Poinapen told Earth.com.

“And some of these movements occur as fast as an eye blink yet they are finely coordinated!”.

Five stages stood out in the voltage traces: piercing the skin, searching for a vessel, drinking blood, pulling the mouthparts back, and withdrawing them.

In a recent development, A full bite took about 160 seconds on average. Roughly 128 of those seconds went to drinking and about 21 to the search for a vessel.

Sources indicate that above the skin, the body kept pace. As the mosquito pushes the needle deeper, her front legs bend and lift off the skin.

When she pulls back, the legs straighten and press down, and the bend begins a fraction of a second before the mouthpart moves.

A mosquito repeated that push and pull about three times before settling into a steadier search. Her palps changed with each stage too. During the hunt for a vessel they swung side to side above the skin, 10 to 25 times a second.

According to recent reports, the moment blood began to flow, the palps stopped swinging and started a faint up-and-down vibration. The team suspects that vibration matches the pumps in the mosquito’s head that draw blood in.

The team ran the same recordings on Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that spreads yellow fever and dengue.

The two groups split about 150 million years ago, and the traces highlighted it. The malaria mosquito stabbed its needle in abruptly, while Aedes worked it in gradually, with a steady rhythm.

Industry observers note that once inside, Anopheles found a vessel about 17 seconds sooner, with shorter and more targeted probing. Even so, both finished a meal in about the same time, roughly 160 seconds for Anopheles and 165 for Aedes.

According to recent reports, the volunteer reported that every Anopheles bite was noticeable whereas the Aedes bites were painless. Whether that holds for anyone else is still an open question, and Earth.com asked the researchers whether the abrupt stab is why malaria mosquito bites seem to hurt more.

“This is not an established phenomenon – different people can have different experiences and reactions to the bites of these two mosquitoes,” Konopka and Poinapen said.

Industry observers note that they added that the different piercing patterns might relate to when each mosquito is active. Malaria mosquitoes bite mainly at dusk and at night, while yellow fever mosquitoes bite mostly in the daytime.

Mosquitoes taste and smell with their legs and mouthparts as well as their antennae. To test how much the bite depends on that, the team bred Anopheles that lacked one of two genes.

Whole families of taste and smell receptors need those genes in order to work.

One gene, called IR76b, is active in nerve cells of the legs, the mouth tip, and the needle itself, the three parts that touch the skin. The other, orco, is active in the mouth tip but not in the legs or the needle.

Sources indicate that mosquitoes missing both copies of IR76b mostly didn’t bite at all. More than half made no attempt in 20 minutes on the volunteer’s arm. Of the 14 tested, six probed and only four managed a partial meal.

Mosquitoes missing orco still bit, some of them a little later than normal, and 98 percent of their probes ended in a blood meal.

Industry observers note that mutants that did bite kept the same timing through all five steps. The one difference was in the drinking itself, which ran in a more regular, repetitive pattern than in normal mosquitoes.

“We found that some malaria mosquitoes with impaired sense of taste and smell had difficulty initiating and completing bites,” the two researchers wrote.

“This indicates that mosquitoes heavily rely on their ability to flavor us during the biting process.”.

All of this rests on one volunteer’s arm and on lab strains of each species. So the team can’t yet say how much a bite changes on a different person’s skin, or with wild mosquitoes.

According to recent reports, the mosquitoes with no working IR76b never fed while wired up, so there are no recordings of their bites. A third family of taste receptors couldn’t be switched off at all, because no shared gene controls it.

According to recent reports, the biggest gap is under the skin. One possibility the researchers raise is that the needle itself senses chemical cues on the way to a blood vessel, and that mosquitoes without IR76b can no longer aim it.

Following the needle’s movements inside the skin, and finding those cues, is the work the team states is needed next. The same setup, they wrote, could also test how repellents, skin microbes, and different hosts change a bite.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.
