#7090. Standing desks may change how people work, even while sitting

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Standing desks may change how people work, even while sitting

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Workers with sit-stand desks logged more active computer time, but researchers could not determine whether standing explained the difference.
  • According to recent reports, sit-stand desks are meant to get office workers out of their chairs.
  • The comparison was with coworkers who used fixed-height desks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Workers with sit-stand desks logged more active computer time, but researchers could not determine whether standing explained the difference.

According to recent reports, sit-stand desks are meant to get office workers out of their chairs. A large study has now linked the desks to roughly 43 extra minutes of active computer use each day.

The comparison was with coworkers who used fixed-height desks.

It has been revealed that more than 10,000 employees of one manufacturer were included in the analysis. The company never recorded whether any of them actually stood up.

In a recent development, the analysis was led by Tricia Salzar, a regional ergonomist with the U.S. Army Public Health Command. Mark Benden, a professor at the Texas A&M University School of Public Health, co-led the work.

Benden also directs the school’s Center for Worker Health.

The records were drawn from a workplace wellness program. They cover workers who joined that program between 2012 and 2014.

Desks were not assigned by the researchers. The study can therefore show that the desks and the extra computer time went together.

Recent findings suggest that the firm is a California energy firm that employs about 24,000 people. Under its wellness program, keypresses and mouse clicks were logged by software on each worker’s computer.

A worker was counted as active only while the keyboard or mouse was in use. If 30 seconds passed without a keypress or a click, the clock stopped.

Workers were also asked in a survey whether they used a height-adjustable desk. That is another name for a sit-stand desk.

Recent findings suggest that salzar’s team identified 3,404 workers who answered yes on two surveys taken a year apart. They were compared with 6,741 workers who answered no both times. Anyone who switched desks during the year was left out.

Industry observers note that over the year, workers at fixed desks averaged 2.95 hours of active computer use a day. An average of 3.66 hours was recorded for workers with sit-stand desks.

Recent findings suggest that the difference between the two groups did not take a year to appear. A gap of about 40 minutes a day in active computer time was already present in the first month.

Industry observers note that across a work year, the authors calculated, the daily difference comes to about 171 hours. That is more than four full-time weeks.

The sit-stand group also typed more. They averaged about 860 more keypresses a day than the fixed-desk group. They also typed roughly 80 more words.

Sit-stand users also made slightly more typos. This remained true after the team adjusted for the number of words typed. The authors wrote that this difference in typos may be too small to matter.

Long hours of uninterrupted sitting have been linked to health risks and to muscle and joint pain.

Recent findings suggest that the survey therefore also asked how often workers felt physical discomfort at work. Soreness, tired muscles and eye strain were given as examples.

It has been revealed that more discomfort was reported by sit-stand users, not less. In the first month, 30.1% of them said they never felt discomfort. The figure for workers at fixed desks was 35.7%.

Industry observers note that the two groups then moved closer together. By the end of the year, 32.5% of sit-stand users noted they never felt discomfort. Among fixed-desk workers, the share was 34.3%.

The change was described by the authors as negligible. In a group this large, they wrote, a difference can pass a statistical test. It can still be too small to matter in practice.

Why would workers with sit-stand desks report more discomfort in the first place? Some may have requested the desks because they were already in pain, the authors wrote.

The records do not show why any worker had one.

Salzar’s team converted the extra time into money. The federal Office of Personnel Management standard for a work year was used. The average wage was set at $52.04 an hour.

Industry observers note that the authors put the value of the added computer time at about $8,900 per worker per year. A fully adjustable sit-stand desk costs about $2,200 delivered and set up, they estimated. It could therefore pay for itself in under three months.

The estimate assumes that computer activity can stand in for productivity. It also assumes that giving a worker the desk would produce the extra minutes.

Benden stated the findings suggest that the desks “can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity.”.

The paper he co-wrote is more cautious. The authors wrote that “the only thing that we can truly determine” is an association. Workers who had the desks also used their computers more.

Benden has worked on standing desks as an inventor as well as a researcher. He founded Stand2Learn, a firm that made standing desks for classrooms. It was acquired by the desk maker Varidesk in 2018.

He is also the named inventor on patents for adjustable-height desk accessories. Those patents are held by the Texas A&M University System. No outside funding and no conflicts of interest are listed in the paper.

The two groups were not matched. Sit-stand owners were younger, with an average age of about 43.

Recent findings suggest that the average for the fixed-desk group was 49. A larger share of the sit-stand users were women.

Salzar’s team also had no record of any worker’s job.

An administrative worker might spend more time typing, the authors wrote. An engineer might instead spend time at the computer reading reports and specifications.

Reading without typing or clicking does not register as active time.

In a recent development, suppose sit-stand desks went mostly to workers in keyboard-heavy jobs. The job, not the desk, could then account for the gap.

The manufacturer’s records are also more than a decade old, and they come from its offices. They cannot show what the desks do for people working from home.

How often a desk was raised was not recorded in the survey. Neither was how long a worker stood or how many times a day the worker changed posture.

Standing may not explain the 43 minutes. The authors cited an earlier study from Benden’s group on this point. They wrote that fewer than 10% of people with these desks choose to stand.

People who do stand may spend only 10% to 20% of the day on their feet.

Industry observers note that the authors offered another explanation. A standard desk is fixed at a height of 29 to 30 inches (74 to 76 cm). A sit-stand desk can be set to fit the person sitting at it. The benefit may come from that fit.

Benden noted his group is also interested in how AI tools could change the physical workspace.

Future studies should record how often workers raise their desks and how long they stand, the authors wrote. Until one does, the extra 43 minutes cannot be credited to standing.

The full study was published in the journal Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics.

#7088. Childhood health problems may share hidden environmental links

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Childhood health problems may share hidden environmental links

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study following children into adolescence links early environmental exposures to overlapping patterns in physical and mental health.
  • The environment children grow up in can shape their health in more ways than we might realize.
  • From the air they breathe to the food they eat, everyday exposures may be connected to several health problems that continue into adolescence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study following children into adolescence links early environmental exposures to overlapping patterns in physical and mental health.

The environment children grow up in can shape their health in more ways than we might realize.

From the air they breathe to the food they eat, everyday exposures may be connected to several health problems that continue into adolescence.

In a study of 586 European children, some exposures were linked to several problems at once.

A mother’s smoking during pregnancy was tied to a higher body mass index in her child and to more aggressive, impulsive behavior. Both links were still there in the teen years.

The findings suggest that a single early exposure may be tied to several parts of a child’s health.

Studying several health outcomes together can help reveal these overlapping links.

Augusto Anguita-Ruiz of the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) and the University of Barcelona led the work with colleagues at Inserm, France’s national institute for health and medical research.

From pregnancy into the teen years, the researchers observed families and changed nothing about how they lived.

Xavier Basagaña, an ISGlobal researcher, is a senior co-author of the study.

“The study does not establish that these exposures cause the observed health outcomes,” stated Basagaña.

Industry observers note that all of the children came from six long-running birth studies in the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Lithuania, Norway and Greece. The six studies belong to a European project called HELIX.

For each mother and child, the team had 69 measures from pregnancy and 129 from childhood. Scientists have a name for that full mix of what a person eats, breathes and lives around: the exposome.

Blood and urine samples provided measures of tobacco exposure, metals, pesticides and other chemical pollutants.

Other exposure measures came from home and school addresses, which the team used to estimate outdoor air pollution, traffic and nearby natural spaces.

Questionnaires covered diet, sleep, physical activity and pets.

Industry observers note that the team compared those measures with 11 health outcomes in four areas: weight and blood pressure, mental health, breathing, and allergies. Each child was examined twice, at an average age of about 8 and again at about 15.

Researchers behind a recent US atlas compared 619 exposures with 305 health traits, but their survey data captured each person at a single point in time.

Six pregnancy exposures and 42 childhood exposures were linked to more than one health outcome. The researchers call these four health areas domains.

Valérie Siroux is an Inserm researcher and senior co-author.

“Although no exposure was associated with all four domains, around one in three of the selected exposures was linked to more than one, suggesting that certain exposures can have broad and multisystemic effects on health,” said Siroux.

Smoking during pregnancy was one of those exposures. It was also tied to more ADHD symptoms in the teen years.

Among childhood exposures, fine particles in indoor air, known as PM2.5, were linked to worse results for weight and blood pressure and for mental health.

Higher copper levels in a child’s blood were linked to worse results in the same two areas.

Secondhand smoke and benzene in indoor air were each linked to higher BMI or blood pressure at both exams.

It has been revealed that why would one exposure be tied to such different problems? The authors suggested that the four health areas share biological pathways, most notably inflammation throughout the body. The team didn’t measure inflammation here.

Of those 42 childhood exposures, 16 were linked to outcomes across more than one health area, and 12 of those involved diet.

Diet also appeared when the team analyzed weight and blood pressure alone. There, following a diet closer to the Mediterranean pattern and eating more fruit were each linked to lower BMI and blood pressure.

In the team’s models, childhood exposures explained up to about 15% of the variation in mental health and in weight and blood pressure.

Pregnancy exposures explained up to about 7% of the variation in mental health and about 1.5% in weight and blood pressure.

Recent findings suggest that so the measured exposures left most of the differences among children unexplained. Allergy outcomes were scarcely related to the exposures.

Some results were the reverse of what the team expected.

Higher blood levels of certain long-lasting chemicals, including PCBs and the PFAS chemical PFOA, were linked to lower BMI and blood pressure in children.

The authors didn’t read that as protection. These chemicals are stored in body fat, so a child’s body fat and growth are expected to affect how much of each chemical appears in blood.

Body size may be shaping the blood reading rather than the chemical shaping body size, the authors wrote, and they urged caution with those results.

The team also repeated every analysis six times, each time leaving out the children from one of the six birth studies.

Most links appeared again, in the same direction, in more than four of the six runs.

Sources indicate that A few links didn’t meet that standard. One tied how much meat a mother ate during pregnancy to asthma and wheezing in her child. Another tied fast food in childhood to worse mental health.

Such links may reflect conditions in one region or one group of families rather than a general pattern, the authors wrote.

It has been revealed that among the 1,301 mother-child pairs in HELIX, the 586 in this study were those with data from every stage. About 87% of the children were white, and 53% of their mothers held a university degree.

The authors described the group as highly selective, so the links may not apply to other populations. The group was also too small to analyze boys and girls separately.

Some chemicals with highly variable levels were measured in only one or a few urine samples, which could make a link look stronger or weaker than it is.

Industry observers note that the bacteria, viruses and fungi a child encounters weren’t measured. The authors suggested that could be why breathing and allergy problems were less clearly tied to the exposures.

Every association is posted in a free interactive online atlas that anyone can search or download.

“Further studies in larger and more diverse populations will be needed to better understand these relationships and determine whether modifying some of these exposures can alter health trajectories during childhood and adolescence,” Basagaña stated.

Future research could also add outcomes this study lacked, such as thinking skills and metabolic health, and examine children at other ages.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#7087. Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state

Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.
  • The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.
  • But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.

But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.

SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike.

It has been revealed that together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she claims.

The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington.

This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants.

In a recent development, the findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao, a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.”.

But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns.

Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that “There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],” notes Dominici. She wants to see data centre developers and operators be more transparent about the environmental impacts and energy use of their facilities. “My frustration is that as we are moving forward, this narrative is not informed by rigorous scientific data, and data-driven decision making,” she says.

Public resistance to data centres has increased sharply in the US over the past year, with a recent poll suggesting 76 per cent of Americans would oppose the construction of a latest data centre in their community.

At the same time, the industry is developing rapidly, with many new facilities now reliant on private gas power generation rather than grid electricity, which increases their climate impact.

Hundreds of millions of people live close enough to data centres used to power AI to feel warmer average temperatures in their local area.

According to recent reports, hyperscale data centres reduce the cost of computing power to companies by harnessing economies of scale to run their servers as efficiently as possible. But the larger the data centre, the greater the impact on local communities.

Alongside high levels of power demand, hyperscale data centres also require large volumes of water to cool their servers, and take up a lot of land. In Utah, a proposal to build a data centre that would cover land twice the size of Manhattan and almost double the state’s annual peak electricity demand has triggered fierce backlash from residents.

“People might notice increasing land prices, electricity prices, water prices,” notes de Vries-Gao. “They might notice an increase in air pollution, waste pollution. This is why people are ultimately protesting. The hyperscale data centres are probably the most painful type of facility simply because of the sheer size of them.”.

Nature Sustainability DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7.

Diabetes and Alzheimer’s share a link that scientists are still trying to explain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review of 40 studies examines the link between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s, offering fresh estimates of risk and unanswered questions.
  • Industry observers note that how many people with type 2 diabetes go on to develop Alzheimer’s each year?
  • The estimate comes from a review of 40 studies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review of 40 studies examines the link between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s, offering fresh estimates of risk and unanswered questions.

Industry observers note that how many people with type 2 diabetes go on to develop Alzheimer’s each year? Five in every 1,000, according to a latest estimate.

The estimate comes from a review of 40 studies. In it, people with type 2 diabetes were about 53% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s than people without it.

Diabetes has been tied to dementia for years. Trouble is, most earlier reviews threw several kinds of diabetes or dementia into one pot.

This one was limited to type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease, and a link between the two was still found. Yearly case counts, rarely reported before, were worked out as well.

Emmanuel Adewuyi is a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health at Curtin University in Australia.

Adewuyi worked on the review with lead author Thi Thu Huong Nguyen and colleagues in Australia, the UK, and Nigeria.

Sources indicate that the 53% figure describes the relative increase in risk. The rate of upcoming cases over time is called incidence.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes,” Adewuyi said.

According to recent reports, every study in the review was observational. People’s health was recorded, and no treatment was assigned.

It has been revealed that research like that can show that two conditions go together. It can’t show that one causes the other.

Sources indicate that dementia affects more than 57 million people worldwide. Alzheimer’s disease accounts for about 60% to 70% of those cases.

Type 2 is by far the most common form of diabetes, accounting for more than 90% of cases.

Sources indicate that both conditions become more common with age. Many of the same heart and metabolic risk factors are shared by the two.

According to recent reports, type 2 diabetes has a stronger link to vascular dementia than to Alzheimer’s. Vascular dementia follows damage to blood vessels in the brain.

Industry observers note that mixing the two, the authors wrote, blurs how much of the risk belongs to Alzheimer’s. Adewuyi’s team therefore kept only studies in which both type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s were clearly identified.

According to recent reports, studies that mixed type 2 with type 1 or pregnancy-related diabetes were dropped. Studies that could not separate Alzheimer’s from other dementias were dropped as well.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers searched four medical databases for studies published through April 2026. They found 9,431 articles, but only 40 met their criteria.

Industry observers note that those 40 studies were published between 1997 and 2026 and covered 12 countries. South Korea contributed 10 studies, the United States eight, and the United Kingdom seven.

It has been revealed that in 38 studies, researchers followed participants over time, with average follow-up periods ranging from two to 15 years. In most studies, the average participant age was between 55 and 75.

The combined study samples totaled more than 27 million people, though some people may have appeared in more than one study. For example, all seven UK studies used data from the same source, the UK Biobank.

Industry observers note that in 26 of the studies, people with type 2 diabetes were compared with people without it. New Alzheimer’s cases were counted in each group.

The results had already been adjusted for other factors, most often age and sex, the authors wrote.

When the 26 were pooled, Alzheimer’s risk was 53% higher for people with type 2 diabetes. With any single study taken out, the increase stayed between 50% and 57%, the authors wrote.

Across subgroups such as region, age, and study date, the increase ranged from 40% to 66%.

Industry observers note that separate results for men and women were given in only a handful of studies. Similar increases were seen there: 76% for men and 73% for women.

The authors wrote that the sex-specific figures should be treated with caution.

Industry observers note that the International Diabetes Federation’s Diabetes Atlas has its own, lower estimate. In the atlas, the increase for Alzheimer’s was put at 34%.

According to recent reports, the authors wrote that the two estimates are compatible with each other. Different sets of studies in the two reviews may explain the gap, they wrote.

Across 23 of the 40 studies, covering about 9 million people, the pooled rate among people with type 2 diabetes was about 4.7 fresh Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 people a year.

Recent findings suggest that from study to study, it swung from under 1 case per 1,000 people a year to almost 14. Much depended on how a study went looking for Alzheimer’s.

Where hospital or national health records were combed, about 4 cases per 1,000 people a year were found.

Sources indicate that where participants were diagnosed using clinical criteria or memory tests, the figure was about 10. Health records probably miss milder cases, the authors wrote.

The yearly rate per 1,000 people varied by region. It was about 7.5 in North America and 5.8 in East Asia and the Pacific. In Europe and Central Asia, it was 1.2.

Recent findings suggest that health, access to care, and diagnosis may all differ by region, the authors wrote. Those explanations still need to be tested.

It has been revealed that only a few studies split their results by sex. In that small set, the yearly rate was 3.6 per 1,000 women and 2.8 per 1,000 men.

In a recent development, the authors used a standard scale to assess the evidence behind both main estimates. They rated its certainty as very low.

None of the 40 studies tested a treatment, and their results varied widely.

The team rated 38 studies as having a low risk of bias and two as having a moderate risk. But those ratings did not account for how often participants visited a doctor.

According to recent reports, people with type 2 diabetes may have more medical appointments. That could give doctors more chances to notice and diagnose Alzheimer’s.

Earlier research by Adewuyi and colleagues found that the two diseases share some genetic influences. However, it found limited evidence that genes linked to type 2 diabetes directly increase Alzheimer’s risk.

According to recent reports, insulin resistance, high blood sugar, and inflammation could also help explain the connection, the authors stated. But the 53% higher risk highlights a pattern across groups of people, not proof that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer’s.

Sources indicate that in 11 of the 40 studies, researchers relied on participants to report whether they had diabetes. Most studies also took place in high-income countries.

The review could not determine whether better diabetes management changes a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s.

Studies inconsistently reported how long participants had lived with diabetes, how well their blood sugar was controlled, and which medications they used.

Metformin, pioglitazone, and acarbose have each been tied to lower dementia risk in earlier research. So have other diabetes drugs, GLP-1 drugs among them, in people with type 2 diabetes. Cause is as hard to pin down there as here.

Adewuyi’s team described the fresh figures as a benchmark for future studies testing whether diabetes treatment changes Alzheimer’s risk.

In the meantime, the team sees a case for watching memory and thinking as part of long-term diabetes care.

The authors mentioned that future studies would be better if researchers combined individual patient data from multiple studies instead of relying on published summaries.

This would help them account for other risk factors more accurately.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy.

Tropical cyclones may follow a hidden winter pattern months before they form

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A February weather pattern may offer clues to East Asia’s summer typhoon activity, providing information beyond El Niño.
  • In a recent development, predicting how many tropical cyclones will reach East Asia months ahead is difficult.
  • New research suggests that this pattern could help researchers anticipate summer tropical cyclone activity beyond what El Niño alone can explain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A February weather pattern may offer clues to East Asia’s summer typhoon activity, providing information beyond El Niño.

In a recent development, predicting how many tropical cyclones will reach East Asia months ahead is difficult. But a weather pattern that develops in late winter may offer an early clue.

New research suggests that this pattern could help researchers anticipate summer tropical cyclone activity beyond what El Niño alone can explain.

The study was led by Zeming Wu from Zhejiang University and examined more than 40 years of observations.

This year, many blamed the strong El Niño for the storms.

El Niño is a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can influence where tropical cyclones form and how they travel.

But the researchers argue it may not be entirely El Niño’s fault this time.

The team focused on the Pacific–North American pattern, or PNA, a large-scale pattern of atmospheric pressure variations over the North Pacific and North America.

It operates in phases. Its “positive phase” brings warmer temperatures across the western United States and Canada and cooler temperatures across the central and southeastern United States. The negative phase is the reverse.

The researchers found that the February PNA pattern was linked to tropical cyclone activity over East Asia the following summer.

The relationship remained after accounting for the influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring climate pattern that includes El Niño and La Niña.

“Our findings suggest that late-winter atmospheric variability may provide valuable information about East Asian summer tropical cyclone activity beyond the influence of ENSO,” Wu noted.

“This highlights the potential importance of atmospheric circulation outside the tropics as an additional source of seasonal predictability.”.

The positive phase of PNA in late winter is linked to fewer tropical cyclones forming over the western North Pacific and fewer storms reaching East Asia several months later.

But how does a February pattern stay connected to summer storms?

The original atmospheric anomalies may have weakened or vanished. Ocean temperatures kept the events linked.

“Through interactions between the atmosphere and ocean, sea surface temperature anomalies can preserve and transmit climate signals across seasons,” stated co-author Chundi Hu from the same university.

The team found two complementary pathways, both mediated by the ocean and linking late-winter PNA variability to summer tropical cyclone activity.

“The ocean appears to act as a bridge between winter atmospheric variability and summer tropical cyclone activity,” Wu remarked.

“More importantly, our results suggest that this connection involves not only the familiar ENSO-related pathway but also another pathway associated with atmospheric variability beyond preceding-winter ENSO.”.

Industry observers note that the first pathway involves ENSO. A positive PNA pattern in late winter is associated with warming in the tropical North Atlantic and a relatively rapid weakening of El Niño in the tropical Pacific.

According to the researchers, these temperature changes match shifts in large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Those shifts favored the development and persistence of an anomalous anticyclone over the western North Pacific into summer.

The second pathway works beyond the linear influence of preceding-winter ENSO. Hu pointed to a mechanism called seasonal footprinting.

This pattern lets anomalies in atmospheric circulation leave a lasting and developing imprint on ocean temperatures.

In this case, the anomalies were wind changes over the subtropical North Pacific and were associated with cooling in the central tropical Pacific.

“Despite their different origins, both pathways converge on a similar atmospheric response: an anomalous anticyclone, or unusual system of high pressure, over the western North Pacific,” Wu remarked.

“This circulation pattern suppresses conditions favorable for tropical cyclone formation and modifies the winds that steer storms, reducing the number of tropical cyclones reaching East Asia during summer.”.

Next, the researchers initiative targeted climate model experiments to investigate these pathways further.

“Ultimately, our goal is to better understand the sources of tropical cyclone predictability and contribute to more reliable seasonal risk assessments for East Asian coastal communities,” Hu mentioned.

Industry observers note that seasonal forecasts give coastal communities time to plan for storm risks. The findings suggest that February’s PNA pattern could provide useful information alongside ENSO.

Further testing will help establish whether this winter signal improves forecasts of summer tropical cyclone activity.

In a recent development, the PNA pattern is large scale. It distributes air and heat across the North Pacific and North America. Its late-winter phase may offer a clue months before the storms arrive.

For coastal communities in East Asia, better forecasts could mean better preparation and more reliable seasonal risk assessments. That could help people get ready before the storms hit.

The study is published in the journal Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
  • Recent findings suggest that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Recent findings suggest that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

Sources indicate that the study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, indicates neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

Sources indicate that although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

According to recent reports, “You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman states. The newly introduced study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their upcoming role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Sources indicate that patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team indicated that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao indicates, a medical conundrum for which there are presently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao indicates. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao notes.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Two billion individuals. That’s economist and demographer Dean Spears’ forecast for our human population in 300 years. The last time we belonged to that small of a group was 1927. Now there are eight billion of us, and in 2080, we’re expected to hit our peak—around ten billion people. Yet, for the first time in history, demographers estimate that the average dropping birth rate over the past several decades means our species will no longer be able to replenish our numbers.

Civil engineers say this will cause major instability worldwide, including to the man-made structures of our world—roadways, buildings, safe water pipelines, and more. All of them will likely deteriorate without city residents who can pay to maintain such structures.

According to recent reports, but we don’t have to fully reimagine what our infrastructure would look like under extreme population collapse; we can look to a swath of the industrial Midwest, known as the Rust Belt, which saw immense population decline when the steel industry cratered in the 1970s and ’80s. The fallout meant shedding at least 75 percent of the 350,000 jobs lost nationally, and massive population decline in cities from St. Louis, Missouri to Buffalo, Fresh York. For example, in Cleveland, Ohio, 46 percent of the residents exited between 1970 and 2000, a typical scenario.

It has been revealed that depopulation on this scale is an unprecedented situation, but also an inevitable one, explains civil and environmental engineer Sybil Derrible, PhD, a professor at the University of Illinois Chicago. He calls himself an urban engineer, because he focuses on studying how population loss will affect multiple urban infrastructure systems over the coming century. “As far as I know, there's no policies about how to deal with depopulating cities,” he says. “No one’s going to give you $2 million to shrink.”.

The total mass of all infrastructure systems humans have built over the past 200 years is truly mind-boggling; it exceeds all living biomass, which is 545.8 gigatons, according to the World Economic Forum. “So when the population goes down, infrastructure will go from being a thing we really need to being a burden. And it's already happening in many cities where there was a lot of infrastructure investment,” claims Derrible.

Industry observers note that in the 1970s, a massive exodus began in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, when the steel industry collapsed. The city of nearly 700,000 residents shrunk to about half its size between 1970 and 2025, and today more than 20,000 housing units sit vacant.

The engine that keeps a city running is its infrastructure, a vast, interconnected network of housing construction, roadways, public transit, electrical grids, and safe drinking water. But multiple factors, including job loss and a higher cost of living, have been pushing people—including upcoming migrants—out of thousands of American cities for decades, leaving the infrastructure with little financial support. The problem will only worsen as the population fails to replace itself, Derrible believes.

Right now, about 40 percent of the nearly 30,000 U.S. cities are losing their people. In a century, it will be more like 50 percent. The larger ones, like New York City or Chicago, are likely to weather changes in population in the long run. It’s the smaller ones, home to about 10,000 to 20,000 people, that will truly suffer, Derrible says. About 12,000 cities, many of them in the Midwest, are facing infrastructure problems, but at least another 3,000 will be experiencing them by 2100, according to Derrible and his team’s 2024 paper in Nature. While the overall U.S. population is increasing due to immigration, people coming to this country don’t usually move to “small, rural cities,” he says. Instead, they settle in the suburbs.

It has been revealed that yet, policies designed to help people living with weakened infrastructure don’t yet exist, Derrible notes. “Those people are completely being neglected. So I'm worried about that. I really want to make sure that we have some policies to be able to help them.”.

Recent findings suggest that but Derrible believes the solutions will come. Policymakers, engineers, scientists, city planners, and residents need to put their heads together and do the work, he says.

Here are three core parts of city infrastructure that are already being hit the hardest.

The most dire consequence of a shrinking population is the inability to maintain massive but increasingly derelict water distribution systems, Derrible says. If you don’t have money for upkeep, the result can be crises like Flint, Michigan’s untreated toxic water disaster, which happened after the cash-poor city switched its municipal water source from Detroit’s system to the Flint River to cut costs in 2014. The city has seen a mass departure of people since the 1980s, when the U.S. auto industry closed many plants and downsized operations. By 2010, four years before the water crisis, Flint’s population had dropped to nearly half its former peak.

Industry observers note that “[The water problem] is especially overlooked because people don’t think about it too much,” Derrible states. Figuring out solutions to the lurking water crises in cities has to happen now, he says, but no easy solutions exist. Questions about how to deal with water contamination or shortages are many, though: “Do you go back to wells? Are there aquifers?” Derrible asks. And if you need to cut off a totally depopulated part of a city, how do you even do that?

Industry observers note that according to industry organization Empowering Pumps and Equipment, aging water infrastructure is the biggest enemy of water, wastewater, and stormwater professionals who maintain and run these systems. The group cites the 2017 American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) Infrastructure Report Card, which states that pipes leak 6 billion gallons of treated drinking water each year, and that about 240,000 water main breaks happen annually. Upgrades and replacements require greater investment—to the tune of $670 billion, the ASCE’s 2025 infrastructure report says—but funding doesn’t come close to meeting need. With two million miles of drinking water pipes across the country, many of which were laid in the early- to mid‐20th century and are now technically at the end of their lifespan, it will take an estimated 200 years to replace the entire system at the current replacement rate of 0.5 percent of pipes per year, according to the 2017 report.

In a recent development, underutilized roads are cracking and becoming harder to drive on, but also harder to fix in cities with far fewer people. A 2021 paper by Derrible and his team in the journal Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability reported that driving on rough roads in New Orleans cost about $685 per person each year. The city has lost half its population since Hurricane Katrina.

Instead of stretching thinning budgets to maintain underutilized roads, cities could consider current and future traffic patterns and potentially abandon some roadways. They could even rip out surfaces and turn them back into dirt roads, Derrible notes. Each city must look at its individual needs and create its own solution.

Japan is implementing a similar kind of solution, where denser patches of houses and services keep their maintained roads and public transit areas, but in areas with few residents, the mostly unused streets are closed or repurposed.

Several cities in the U.S. have been choosing to remove the interstate highway sections that slice up their cities, most of which entered urban areas in the 1950s and destroyed and divided neighborhoods. One such city is Detroit, Michigan, which looks to replace the wide gray strips with roomy, walkable neighborhoods, in hopes of reconnecting residential areas.

Sources indicate that because fewer people means less tax revenue, cities that are being abandoned have less money to deal with aging or empty infrastructure like buildings. The other side of the coin is that fresh businesses don’t want to occupy old buildings. “New Costco? They’ll want new land to build it,” Derrible notes. “At the same time we have all those abandoned buildings that we're not doing anything with, because it's just cheaper to build on new land than to retrofit an existing building.”.

The picture of abandoned buildings doesn’t have to look like a post-apocalyptic nightmare of neglect. Existing buildings that are still in good shape could meet housing needs or become community spaces. For example, urban malls could be turned into apartments that are already conveniently located.

“At the very least, what I think we could be doing when a building is being abandoned is remove all the hazardous equipment, material, appliances, all of that,” Derrible indicates. Similar to the cleanup after a natural disaster, all furnaces and power and electrical hardware must come out to prevent fires and toxic materials.

Then you could either bulldoze the building and remove the debris, or you could strip the structure for useful parts, such as wood, metal, pipes, and electrical wire. Even skyscrapers could become rich sources of material that the civil engineering industry could mine. “Instead of going to quarries and getting new material, we could go to old skyscrapers or old concrete buildings. We crush them, so we have the aggregates to build new buildings,” Derrible indicates. The wood could also be reused, or it could become a source of fuel when burned. Derrible foresees abandoned city infrastructure as a potential source of new jobs that mine and process material for reuse. “Isn't that like the core of the American system, to turn any challenge into an opportunity, right?”.

According to recent reports, before joining Popular Mechanics in 2022, Manasee Wagh worked as a science journalist, a newspaper reporter, a technical writer, and an engineer. She has a bachelor's degree in computer engineering and a master’s degree in journalism. Her favorite stories are about the discoveries that unearth even deeper mysteries, and she enjoys helping people understand the science behind the remarkable world we live in. She lives in the Northeast with her two favorite people and one curious, feisty feline, but always seeks to combine her love of food, nature, and travel into memorable journeys away from home.

Instagram posts may reveal subtle clues about loneliness

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Instagram habits may reveal loneliness in college students but cannot reliably show their support networks, according to a new study.
  • Instagram users carefully choose what they share, but their posts may still reveal signs of loneliness.
  • college students found that posting habits, captions, and photos offered clues about how lonely students felt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram habits may reveal loneliness in college students but cannot reliably show their support networks, according to a new study.

Instagram users carefully choose what they share, but their posts may still reveal signs of loneliness.

A new study of U.S. college students found that posting habits, captions, and photos offered clues about how lonely students felt.

Those same accounts revealed far less about how many friends or relatives students could turn to for support.

The work was led by Sherry (Yueyi) Jiang with psychology professor Piotr Winkielman at the University of California San Diego. Jiang completed a doctorate in experimental psychology there in 2025.

All of the students attended that one university, and most of them were women. The results describe patterns across a group. They are not presented by the authors as a way to screen any single person.

Loneliness is difficult for other people to see. The authors also described it as a serious risk factor for early death. The effects are comparable in size to those of smoking and obesity, they wrote.

Each student completed questionnaires, then downloaded a full archive of their Instagram account and uploaded it to a secure server.

Industry observers note that in total, 541 students took part, and 415 of them were kept in the analysis. A total of 93 students were excluded by the team because posts, likes, or comments were missing from their archives.

A further 33 students were removed since their questionnaires had been left unfinished.

Only part of an account can be seen on a public profile. About 62% of the students had private accounts.

Posts, likes, and comments that remain invisible to strangers on the app could therefore be studied by the researchers.

The archives contained 9,353 captions and 353,407 comments, together with the photos and the time of every post.

Faces in the photos were detected by one program, and the expression and head tilt of each face were estimated.

According to recent reports, the tone of captions and comments was scored by other programs. Words were also sorted by these programs into themes, such as family or the past.

The share of each student’s posts made late at night, defined as 11 p.m. to 5 a.m., was also calculated.

Computer models were subsequently trained by the team to identify the lonelier students from those Instagram measures alone.

Data from 80% of the students were used to build the models, which were tested on the remaining 20%.

From the questionnaires, five scores were obtained for every student, and four of these reflected how lonely the student felt.

Industry observers note that the fifth score addressed a separate matter. It reflected how many relatives and friends a student contacted regularly and could ask for help.

The main loneliness questionnaire included 20 statements, among them “I feel isolated from others.”.

According to recent reports, model performance was judged on a scale where 0.5 equals a coin flip and 1 is perfect. A value of 0.77 was reached by the best model for this main questionnaire.

According to recent reports, for each of two more specific loneliness scores, the models achieved 0.74, while a single-question score was predicted at 0.68. The first three results were described by the authors as moderate, and the last one as modest.

Weaker performance was recorded for the fifth score, which concerned support.

The best model reached 0.61, with an uncertainty range of 0.42 to 0.79. Because that range included 0.5, the result did not clearly establish performance better than chance.

Two kinds of loneliness have been separated by researchers since the 1970s.

Industry observers note that emotional loneliness is the distress of having no one close. Social loneliness is dissatisfaction with a person’s wider social circle.

On Instagram, students with higher social loneliness scores tended to be less active with other people.

These students liked fewer posts. They also commented less often and posted less on weekends.

In a recent development, A different pattern was seen in students with higher emotional loneliness scores. More of their posts went up late at night.

Their captions were more negative in tone, and sad or angry facial expressions were more common in their photos.

Industry observers note that the emotionally lonely students also posted more often, not less. Frequent posting, the authors suggested, might be an effort to find emotional connection when close ties are missing.

Word choice was examined as well. Students who wrote “we” more often tended to score lower on emotional loneliness. Those who wrote “I” more often tended to score higher on social loneliness.

“Loneliness isn’t a one-size-fits-all experience, and neither are the solutions,” Winkielman said.

Two ideas were proposed by the authors for future testing. Social loneliness might be eased by more chances to engage with others.

For emotional loneliness, help with low mood and disrupted daily routines was suggested instead.

Lonely people are often depressed or anxious as well, and the same was true of these students.

It has been revealed that the team therefore checked each Instagram sign again. This time, each student’s depression and anxiety scores were taken into account.

Only one sign was still linked to loneliness: fewer faces per post. Students whose photos contained fewer faces were more likely to score high on two of the loneliness measures.

In a recent development, according to the authors, fewer moments shared with other people may be reflected in photos that contain fewer faces. The same link between loneliness and the number of faces had been reported in an earlier study of Instagram users.

It has been revealed that past-focused words in captions were tied to two of the loneliness measures. Profile photos with the head tilted upward were tied to three.

That tilt is probably no accident, Jiang’s team wrote, given how carefully people pick their photo angles. But once depression and anxiety scores entered the analysis, neither sign was still tied to loneliness.

Nobody in the study was followed over time. Each of the 415 students filled out the questionnaires once and handed over an archive.

So the order is unknown: the Instagram habits may have come first, or the loneliness, or both.

According to recent reports, the group itself was narrow. About 85% of the students were 21 or younger and about 79% were women.

Asian students (43.9%) and White students (38.8%) made up the two largest groups.

Age and culture change how loneliness is felt, the authors wrote, and they change posting habits on social media too.

Patterns found among San Diego undergraduates need to be tested in other populations.

There is also the question of misuse, which the authors raised themselves.

Flag the wrong person, and the result may be stigma or outreach that was never wanted. Miss the right person, and support does not arrive.

For that reason, the team limited its suggestion to consent-based research and to support services that people opt into.

Covert screening built only on these signs was advised against.

Two kinds of follow-up were proposed. One would measure the same people’s loneliness repeatedly while their Instagram activity is collected.

The other would briefly change how lonely people feel in an experiment, then record what they do online afterward. Cause is easier to isolate that way, according to the authors.

The full study was published in the journal npj Mental Health Research.

Having just started its maiden season in North America, Royal Caribbean’s upcoming Legend of the Seas was one of the ships that operated on a revised schedule.

Norwegian Cruise Line also adjusted its schedule, delaying the departure of vessels such as the Norwegian Luna.

According to a statement shared with guests onboard, the ship started its seven-night cruise to the Caribbean four hours later at 8:00 PM.

Other vessels delaying their departures from PortMiami included the Carnival Magic, which sailed for an eight-night cruise to the Caribbean two hours later than scheduled at 5:30 PM.

Royal Caribbean’s Icon of the Seas started a seven-night cruise to the Western Caribbean two and a half hours later at 7:00 PM.

MSC Cruises also postponed the departure of the MSC World America from Miami by two hours to accommodate passengers impacted by flight delays.

In addition to delaying departures for arriving guests, companies stepped up for passengers disembarking this weekend.

Disney Cruise Line offered free Wi-Fi for passengers arriving on Saturday who would like to contact airlines for the latest flight information.

Breast cancer leaves signs in blood that may hint at its return

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new blood test revealed promise for spotting breast cancer and predicting relapse, but larger studies remain essential.
  • Recent findings suggest that mammograms can sometimes miss breast cancer in women with dense breasts.
  • The test also found signs linked to cancer returning within five years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new blood test revealed promise for spotting breast cancer and predicting relapse, but larger studies remain essential.

Recent findings suggest that mammograms can sometimes miss breast cancer in women with dense breasts. A newly introduced blood test called EPINUC demonstrated promise in detecting breast cancer regardless of breast density.

The test also found signs linked to cancer returning within five years.

Larger studies are needed to confirm whether it can help detect cancer early and predict its return.

The test was developed in the lab of Efrat Shema at the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Recent findings suggest that for the fresh study, her team worked with Guy Ron, a physicist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Ron’s group belongs to the university’s Racah Institute of Physics.

Sources indicate that the cancer status of every woman was already known when her blood sample was analyzed. The test has not yet been applied to women undergoing routine screening.

In a recent development, inside a cell, DNA is wound around protein spools. Each spool, with its loop of DNA, is called a nucleosome.

Small chemical tags are added to the spool proteins. These tags help set which genes the cell uses, and biologists call them epigenetic tags.

Recent findings suggest that dying cells, whether healthy or cancerous, release nucleosomes into the bloodstream. The tags stay on.

Industry observers note that tumor DNA is the target of several blood tests for cancer. In Shema’s method, the tagged spools are instead examined individually under a microscope.

Industry observers note that each type of tag is marked with a fluorescent label of a different color. Tags that occur together on a single spool can therefore be identified.

The test needs less than 1 milliliter of plasma, the liquid part of blood – about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

Colorectal cancer was detected by an earlier version of the test.

Two further tags and three proteins related to breast tissue were added for the present study. A total of 29 measurements is now obtained from each sample.

It has been revealed that the relevant tags were first sought in tumor tissue. Twelve women who had not yet received any treatment provided the samples.

It has been revealed that the operations were performed at Kaplan Medical Center in Israel. Noa Furth, a researcher in Shema’s lab, is one of the study’s lead authors.

“Once a tumor is removed, there’s only a short window of opportunity before its epigenetic tags begin to deteriorate,” noted Furth.

Recent findings suggest that “So as each surgery began, the doctors would alert me. I would rush the tissue sample from the hospital to our lab on ice, and we’d start analyzing it that very day.”.

The team measured the tags in more than 1.1 million individual cells.

Eleven of the 12 tumors were luminal. Hormone receptors are present on the cells of luminal tumors, which generally respond well to hormone-blocking drugs.

Recent findings suggest that each luminal tumor also contained a minor population of unusual cells. These cells resembled a different form of breast cancer, known as basal-like. A worse outlook is associated with that form.

Hormone signaling was reduced in the basal-like cells.

The same pattern of tags was observed in these cells across patients. In laboratory cultures of breast cancer cells, greater movement was recorded for cells of this kind.

The researchers then investigated whether genetic differences could explain the aggressive cells.

Latest colonies were established in the laboratory, each from a single cell.

“The differences appear to be mainly epigenetic,” Shema said.

“When we grew breast cancer models in the lab starting with nonaggressive cells, an aggressive population always emerged eventually.”.

The test was then applied to stored blood from 77 women with luminal breast cancer. All had been treated at Mayo Clinic in Florida. Blood from 30 healthy women was also tested.

A computer model was trained to distinguish cancer samples from healthy samples. Its performance score was 0.95, where 0.5 indicates chance-level performance and 1 indicates perfect separation.

An identical score was obtained for the 42 patients with tumors in the smallest size class. Such tumors measure about 0.8 inches (2 centimeters) or less.

It has been revealed that no change in performance was seen across density scores, which are assigned by radiologists from mammograms. This was also true of women with extremely dense breasts.

Samples from two Israeli hospitals and a second Mayo batch were subsequently included. The combined set comprised 137 patients and 51 healthy women.

Three-quarters of these samples were used to train a latest model, and the remainder served as a test.

In the test group, 92% of the 13 healthy women were correctly identified as cancer-free.

Cancer was detected in 85% of the 34 patients and missed in 15%.

The test did about as well in 22 women with triple-negative breast cancer, which lacks hormone receptors.

Industry observers note that luminal breast cancer usually responds to treatment, but in many women it comes back. Differences among the cells within a tumor are suspected to be one reason tumors return.

Industry observers note that all 77 Mayo patients gave blood before surgery. The women were then followed for at least five years. Cancer returned in 33 of them within five years, while 44 remained disease-free.

Two tags characteristic of the basal-like cells were elevated in the blood of women who later relapsed.

Sources indicate that A model built on the blood measurements separated the two groups. It scored 0.81 on the same scale. Models based on age, tumor stage, grade, and other standard measures scored lower.

A score of 0.92 was recorded in a second, smaller set of 30 patients.

These differences in blood markers were also present in women with early-stage or low-grade tumors. Such tumors are rated as lower risk by standard measures.

Recent findings suggest that the team also looked at Oncotype DX scores. Oncotype DX is a gene test performed on tumor tissue to estimate the risk of relapse.

Its scores did not differ between 40 women who stayed disease-free and nine who relapsed.

All samples had been collected earlier and were analyzed once the outcomes were known. The group to which each sample belonged was not concealed from the analysts.

Industry observers note that the groups were small as well. Cancer returned in only 10 of the 30 patients in the second set.

Recent findings suggest that blood from healthy women was collected at the Weizmann Institute. Blood from patients was supplied by hospitals in the United States and Israel.

In a recent development, nearly all of the tumors examined were luminal. Triple-negative tumors are usually treated with drugs before surgery, and few untreated ones were available.

The authors wrote that the tumor findings may not extend to other types of breast cancer.

Signals from tumor cells, damaged healthy tissue, and the immune system are combined in blood. A tag found in blood therefore cannot be attributed to the basal-like cells alone.

Both tumor tissue and blood were available from ten women. For most tags, higher levels in the tumor were accompanied by higher levels in the blood.

Recent findings suggest that the blood-test method is covered by a patent application on which Shema is a named inventor. The exclusive license is held by a organization called Epivision Genetics. Four of the study’s authors are affiliated with that company.

Sources indicate that larger studies of the blood test are still required, the authors wrote. In such studies, blood would be collected first and each woman’s outcome learned afterward.

A separate question concerns the basal-like cells. It remains to be tested whether tumor cells can be kept from switching states by epigenetic drugs.

“We’re now looking for treatments that could deprive cancer cells of their epigenetic flexibility – and perhaps even coax cells that have already turned aggressive into adopting less aggressive traits,” Shema stated.

No such treatment was tested in this study.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#7076. The rise of oxygen on Earth may have unfolded differently than we thought

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The rise of oxygen on Earth may have unfolded differently than we thought

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient rocks suggest major rises in Earth’s atmospheric oxygen occurred earlier than thought, while the deep ocean took longer to catch up.
  • For most of Earth’s history, the planet lacked enough atmospheric oxygen to sustain wildfires.
  • Charcoal preserved in rocks indicates that oxygen had reached levels capable of supporting wildfire by about 420 million years ago – roughly three-quarters of today’s atmospheric level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient rocks suggest major rises in Earth’s atmospheric oxygen occurred earlier than thought, while the deep ocean took longer to catch up.

For most of Earth’s history, the planet lacked enough atmospheric oxygen to sustain wildfires.

Charcoal preserved in rocks indicates that oxygen had reached levels capable of supporting wildfire by about 420 million years ago – roughly three-quarters of today’s atmospheric level.

Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology, reviewed evidence suggesting that major increases in atmospheric oxygen preceded corresponding changes in the ocean.

Their review suggests that two major atmospheric oxygen increases occurred earlier than traditionally thought.

Many widely used clues to ancient oxygen levels come from marine rocks, including their minerals, isotopes, and trace metals.

These records primarily reflect ocean chemistry, providing indirect evidence of atmospheric conditions.

Ocean chemistry is highly complicated. It answers to nutrient supply, biological productivity, how water circulates, even the shape of the basin.

Sulfate offers a more direct connection to the atmosphere. Atmospheric oxygen carries a distinctive isotopic signature that can pass into sulfate when sulfide minerals oxidize.

Preserved in sedimentary rocks, that signature helps researchers reconstruct ancient atmospheric conditions.

The Great Oxidation Event, 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago, still holds. Cyanobacteria had been quietly making oxygen in shallow coastal waters for ages before that.

According to recent reports, oxygen concentrations in these shallow waters may have reached levels sufficient to support oxygen-using microbes. Reactions with minerals and gases consumed much of that oxygen before it could accumulate in the atmosphere.

Then production finally outran consumption and the atmosphere flipped.

Steps two and three are where the textbooks take the hit. Wang and Li date them to 1.3–1.0 billion and 0.44–0.41 billion years ago.

Those dates precede the conventional timings of the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event, around 800–500 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event, around 420–360 million years ago.

But according to the sulfate record, those weren’t the atmosphere oxygenating.

They were the ocean catching up to atmospheric changes that had already happened – about 200 million years late in the first case, and 30 million years late in the second.

Between about a billion and 410 million years ago, the carbon isotope record is peppered with sharp excursions that generations of scientists read as oxygen rising.

Sources indicate that the sulfate evidence suggests that some ocean oxygenation events temporarily lowered atmospheric oxygen. As oxygen entered the ocean, reactions with stored organic carbon and sulfur compounds consumed it.

Recent findings suggest that the “boring billion” suddenly looks less boring. Modeling pegged to the sulfate data puts mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at 0.1–1% of today’s atmospheric oxygen level.

At those low atmospheric levels, local photosynthesis likely supplied much of the oxygen in shallow waters, while the deep ocean remained largely oxygen-free.

According to recent reports, two oxygen modes coexisted through most of this history. The first was local: cyanobacterial mats producing oxygen in shallow, sunlit patches.

The second was global: oxygen dissolving from the atmosphere into surface water and being shoved deep by circulation.

The local mode is older than three billion years. The global mode becomes more influential as atmospheric oxygen levels rise.

Widespread oxygenation of the deep ocean developed around 410 million years ago.

Oxygen-poor zones persisted, however, and episodes of widespread ocean oxygen loss occurred later.

Strangely, the ancient local mode still runs today. Redox-stratified lakes in Antarctica and Venezuela sustain oxygenated pockets above anoxic bottoms.

There, they are powered by the same benthic microbial photosynthesis that kept tiny patches of Earth’s ocean alive for two billion years.

Low oxygen availability initially restricted the habitats available to oxygen-dependent life.

During the Proterozoic, fluctuating oxygen levels helped shape opportunities for more complex organisms.

Eukaryotes appeared, and multicellularity got its start. Organisms also evolved ways to respond to low oxygen levels.

Later increases in oxygen helped expand the habitats available to large, active organisms.

Major increases in atmospheric oxygen came before widespread oxygenation of the deep ocean. In the long interval between them, life evolved amid uneven and changing oxygen supplies.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Industry observers note that when I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in conscious patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

In a recent development, in 2018, when my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

In a recent development, with a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that highlights that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.
