Light and sound could change how we measure blood pressure

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A wrist sensor read blood pressure beat by beat from laser-made sound in an artery, matching a cuff within a few mmHg in two volunteers.
  • In a clinic, a blood pressure check usually means a cuff squeezing an arm to produce a reading for that moment.
  • A sensor pressed to the wrist has now read blood pressure beat by beat, with no cuff at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A wrist sensor read blood pressure beat by beat from laser-made sound in an artery, matching a cuff within a few mmHg in two volunteers.

In a clinic, a blood pressure check usually means a cuff squeezing an arm to produce a reading for that moment.

A sensor pressed to the wrist has now read blood pressure beat by beat, with no cuff at all.

Recent findings suggest that the sensor flashes pulses of light into the skin and picks up the faint sound an artery gives off in response. That sound tells it how wide the artery is with every heartbeat.

In two volunteers tested over three months, its readings differed from a clinical finger-cuff monitor by only a few points on average.

Two people make a proof of concept rather than a finished product, and the researchers wrote that a full clinical trial is still to come.

Amir Rosenthal and Daniel Lange of the Technion in Haifa, Israel, led the work with doctoral student Gil Gelbert.

Rosenthal runs a lab for biomedical imaging and sensing at the university’s Viterbi Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

Blood pressure is one of the most important indicators of heart health. Yet it is still usually measured with an inflatable cuff, which gives a reading at a single point in time.

The alternatives have been a catheter inside an artery or repeated cuff readings, and neither suits daily life.

Recent findings suggest that wrist sensors have tried to fill the gap with stand-in signals, such as the pulse that light-based sensors read through the skin. Those signals shift when the device moves and need frequent recalibration.

A more direct route is the artery itself. Each heartbeat widens an artery slightly, and the amount it widens tracks the pressure inside.

Ultrasound patches can follow that widening, but they need rows of transmitting elements and careful alignment over the artery.

The wrist’s radial artery is only about 0.08 inches (2 millimeters) across and sits about 0.16 inches (4 millimeters) deep, which makes that alignment hard to hold in a wearable.

The Technion team turned to an effect in which light makes sound. Near-infrared laser light pulses through the skin 100 times a second.

Blood absorbs that light far more than the tissue around it, so the artery warms and expands by a tiny amount and sends out an ultrasound wave.

A detector on the skin records the wave. The gap between the sound from the artery’s near wall and its far wall gives the artery’s inner width, and that width changes with every beat.

In a recent development, what makes the device unusual is its detector. It is a channel for light etched into a silicon chip and coated in a soft silicone layer.

The channel is about a thousandth of a millimeter wide, far thinner than a human hair.

Pressure from the sound wave changes how light moves through the channel, and a readout system measures the change.

Sources indicate that because the detector is so small, it picks up sound from almost any direction, so it doesn’t have to be aimed at the artery. A single element does the job that patches need arrays for.

An established formula then converts the artery’s width into blood pressure, calibrated once per person.

The team first tested the sensor on artificial arteries built to mimic the wrist.

Shifting the sensor up to 0.4 inches (10 millimeters) off center, or rotating it up to 30 degrees, changed the measured width by only about a hundredth of a millimeter.

A conventional piezoelectric detector element, tested the same way, worked only within half that range and lost the artery’s edges when turned by just 5 degrees.

On a 29-year-old man’s wrist, finding the artery took less than 10 seconds. The team then slid the sensor across his arm while it recorded, and the readings held steady.

A standard pulse-echo ultrasound element, by contrast, produced an error of roughly a fifth of a millimeter when moved just 0.3 millimeters.

The blood pressure test used two volunteers. One was the 29-year-old man, whose pressure ran slightly high. The other was a 42-year-old woman, whose pressure ran slightly low.

Over three months they sat for 120 measurements of 10 seconds each, some at rest and some while tensing their core muscles, which raises blood pressure.

A finger-cuff system approved for clinical use recorded the reference pressure at the same time.

The sensor was calibrated once per person at the start. For every later session it was taken off and put back by hand, with no markers to guide its position, the way a watch goes back on a wrist.

Averaged across all 120 measurements, the sensor’s readings differed from the cuff system by 2.6 mmHg on the lower, diastolic number. On the upper, systolic number, the gap was 4.7 mmHg.

The authors wrote that this matches the accuracy reported for the leading wearable ultrasound patches in studies of similar size.

In one session, the sensor tracked the man’s pressure continuously for more than 30 minutes, several days after it had been calibrated.

According to recent reports, two people are enough to show the idea works, not to show it works for everyone. The authors wrote that a full validation study would need more than 85 participants.

Only a study that size, they wrote, could tell whether the sensor performs differently in men and women.

According to recent reports, every reading was also taken sitting still. The authors wrote that sliding the sensor didn’t disturb the signal, but blood pressure during walking or exercise has not been tested.

Both lasers, the one that fires the pulses and the one that reads the detector, still sit on a lab bench.

The team wrote that compact laser diodes could replace them, and that the readout electronics could eventually be built into the chip itself.

It has been revealed that the sensor also records the full shape of each pressure pulse, beyond the high and low numbers. The authors wrote that this information was not used in the study.

The researchers believe the technology could eventually go into smartwatches and medical patches.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

Webb reveals a stellar nursery with secrets even infrared cannot reach

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that why does Sagittarius B2 produce so many stars?
  • Today’s Image of the Day reveals a crowded stretch of the Milky Way where bright stars and orange clouds surround patches of almost complete darkness.
  • Those dark areas may look like gaps in the scene, but they contain some of its most intriguing material: dense clouds concealing the birth of stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that why does Sagittarius B2 produce so many stars? Webb’s infrared observations offer a closer look at an unusually active region near the Milky Way’s center.

Today’s Image of the Day reveals a crowded stretch of the Milky Way where bright stars and orange clouds surround patches of almost complete darkness.

Those dark areas may look like gaps in the scene, but they contain some of its most intriguing material: dense clouds concealing the birth of stars.

The James Webb Space Telescope captured this view of Sagittarius B2 with its Near-Infrared Camera, or NIRCam.

Released on September 24, 2025, the image offers a detailed look at a vast stellar nursery near our galaxy’s center.

Its brilliant points of light are only part of the story. Understanding what remains hidden could help astronomers explain why this particular cloud produces stars so much more actively than its surroundings.

Sagittarius B2 lies a few hundred light-years from Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way’s heart.

This central neighborhood contains crowded star fields, thick clouds and complicated magnetic fields.

Yet an abundance of gas does not automatically translate into abundant star formation.

According to NASA’s release, Sagittarius B2 contains about 10 percent of the gas in the galactic center but accounts for roughly half of its star formation.

That imbalance makes it a valuable place to investigate what allows some clouds to become especially productive stellar nurseries.

Astronomers Adam Ginsburg and Nazar Budaiev of the University of Florida led the observing program.

The team used Webb to examine how massive stars emerge within this unusually dense environment.

Stars begin inside cold molecular clouds, where gas gathers into denser pockets.

Recent findings suggest that as a clump gains material, its gravity strengthens. Eventually, gravity can pull it inward, beginning a collapse that heats the material and produces a developing star called a protostar.

At first, the object draws much of its energy from that collapse. Later, if its core becomes sufficiently hot and compressed, hydrogen nuclei begin combining to form helium.

This process, nuclear fusion, supplies the energy that allows a star to shine through the longest stage of its life.

It has been revealed that the cloud surrounding a developing star can make that transition difficult to observe. Astronomers must examine stellar birth through the very material that makes it possible.

A bright, mature star may announce itself across space, while a much younger object remains buried in its original supply of gas and dust.

Webb’s instruments reveal different parts of this environment.

In the NIRCam image, stars crowd the field, interrupted by luminous clouds and dark structures.

Near-infrared light can pass through some of the obscuring dust, bringing objects into view that would be harder to distinguish in visible light.

A companion image from Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument, or MIRI, changes the emphasis.

Warm dust becomes much more prominent, while far fewer stars remain visible. Only the brightest stars emit strongly enough at these longer wavelengths to stand out through the clouds.

Together, the views show why one image cannot provide a complete inventory of a stellar nursery.

According to recent reports, changing the wavelengths changes which objects and structures dominate the scene. The same cloud can appear rich in stars in one view and rich in glowing dust in another.

Even Webb’s sensitivity has limits in Sagittarius B2.

The team’s observations used 14 filters covering wavelengths from 1.5 to 25 micrometers.

They revealed a layered cloud containing both exposed massive stars and deeply obscured populations.

The researchers also identified candidate regions of gas energized by massive stars that earlier radio observations had missed.

Elsewhere, MIRI detected radiation escaping from the embedded cluster Sagittarius B2 North along cavities associated with outflows.

These openings provide routes for light to emerge from an otherwise heavily concealed environment.

But many young stellar objects previously detected with the ALMA radio telescope remained invisible to Webb.

Their absence from the infrared images illustrates how effectively the surrounding material can conceal ongoing star formation.

The result gives today’s image a second way to be read. Its bright stars reveal what has emerged into view.

Its dark clouds mark places where the next part of the story is still unfolding beyond Webb’s sight.

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

It has been revealed that in 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

In a recent development, when the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

According to recent reports, this chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

It has been revealed that these fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston indicates. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

It has been revealed that angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston notes.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The oldest-known comb, fashioned from animal bone, dates back nearly 8,000 years to mesolithic Syria. But in those intervening 10,000 years, the comb hasn’t seen much innovation. Sure, plastics have long since replaced bone as the material of choice for this particular piece of grooming gear (though animal bone combs are still a thing). But the comb’s overall shape and function—individual tines and all—has remained remarkably unchanged.

In a recent development, “The basic design evolved from the fingers of the human hand,” the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford writes on its website. “From Bronze-Age man to Cleopatra, to Napoleon's wife, Josephine, all would recognize these items as such.”.

But just because something’s remained largely unchanged for millennia doesn’t mean there isn’t room for innovation. Take, for instance, the “Detangle,” an experimental comb developed by Beihang University in China as a tool for tackling androgenetic alopecia (AGA), or just simply baldness. At first glance, the comb looks much like any other hand-inspired comb—there’s a long handle and the recognizable tines. However, that’s where the similarities end, because this comb has teeth packed with embedded electrodes as well as small compartments for delivering molecules designed to stimulate hair growth. Researchers published a study detailing the efficacy of this experimental comb in the journal Nature Communications.

“Androgenetic alopecia affects over 1.5 billion individuals, causing progressive hair loss with psychological and quality-of-life burdens,” the authors write. “This system features electronic teeth embedded with height-differentiated electrodes and integrated drug-loading modules, which generate an enhanced electric field penetrating up to ~9 times deeper into hair follicle regions than conventional external application.”.

This “Detangle” device, whose name the authors admit was inspired by the Disney animated film Tangled, isn’t a newly introduced hair-loss treatment so much as a revolutionary way to deliver one. One of its most high-tech features is a control circuit that creates pulsed electric fields across two types of electronic teeth. These teeth have different heights that generate a stronger electric field than if the teeth were aligned. That generates a positive environment for the transmembrane delivery of a therapeutic molecule into the impacted follicular cells, increasing uptake by more than three times, the authors report.

According to recent reports, the authors tested the comb on mouse models and found hair growth recovered near 100 percent within a month, a steep increase from the approximate 70 percent recovery rate of typical minoxidil treatments—one of the go-to FDA-approved treatments for hair loss. To achieve this impressive recovery rate, the authors relied on the SRD5A2 siRNA molecule and a VEGFA plasmid. The first molecule inhibits dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone that causes hair follicles to shrink, while the latter boosts blood vessel growth around the impacted follicles.

“By co‑delivering VEGFA plasmid and SRD5A2 siRNA, the Detangle system promotes hair follicle regeneration via a dual mechanism that synergizes electrostimulation with molecular regulation,” the authors write. “Given the multifaceted signaling abnormalities in AGA, the Detangle system presents a versatile platform for co‑delivering therapeutic agents beyond metabolic modulation.”.

After 10,000 years, the comb finally gets a serious glow up.

Amadeus River Cruises has unveiled the itinerary and shore excursion program for its newest vessel, the Amadeus Douro.

Purpose-built for the Douro River and marking the company’s entry to Portugal, the ship will make its debut in May 2028, with the inaugural season continuing through November.

The firm highlighted its eight-day “Portugal & the Golden Douro River” itinerary that will take guests through the Douro Valley, operating seasonally from March through November, sailing roundtrip from Porto/Vila Nova de Gaia.

According to recent reports, “We are delighted to introduce the next chapter of the Amadeus experience with our first sailings on the Douro River. This itinerary is about more than experiencing the remarkable scenery of the Douro Valley,” said Amadeus President Marcus Leskovar.

“Through our carefully curated excursions and cultural experiences, guests will have the opportunity to connect with Portuguese traditions, meet the people behind the region’s winemaking heritage, savor its cuisine and discover the history that makes this part of Europe so special.”.

The tech giant has shared that the ship will be able to accommodate 107 guests in 52 staterooms featuring floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors with French balconies and three suites with private wraparound balconies.

Public spaces will include an expansive Sun Deck with a swimming pool and lounge, as well as Café Vienna.

Unlike on other ships in the fleet, shore excursions on the Amadeus Douro will be included in the cruise fare, including guided sightseeing, vineyard visits, wine tastings and culinary experiences.

After setting sail from Porto, the ship sails east through the Douro Valley and guest visit Quinta de São Luiz, a historic wine estate where a guided tour of terraced vineyards and traditional wine cellars concludes with a tasting of selected Port wines.

Further into the valley, guests will discover Castelo Rodrigo, a historic hilltop village overlooking the Portuguese countryside.

The itinerary also crosses the Spanish border for a full-day excursion to Salamanca, and continues with a visit to Lamego in Portugal, home to the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Remedies and its staircase of 686 steps, decorated with traditional Portuguese tiles.

Guests will also sample regional specialties, including at Quinta da Pacheca, surrounded by historic vineyards.

After exploring Guimarães, considered the birthplace of Portugal, the journey concludes in Porto, where guests get a guided sightseeing tour and a visit to one of the city’s historic Port wine cellars, complete with a guided tasting.

Beyond shore excursions, the itinerary features a collection of Amadeus Experiences designed to bring Portuguese traditions and flavors to life, including a Portuguese language class, traditional folklore performance, discovering the art of opening vintage Port and watching how pastéis de nata custard tarts are prepared.

Children’s brain responses to food may help predict later fat gain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Children who ate more ultra-processed foods indicated stronger brain responses to food pictures, which were linked to greater body fat gain later.
  • Breakfast cereal, packaged bread and instant soup get blamed for childhood weight gain because of what’s in them.
  • A upcoming study links children’s ultra-processed food intake to how their brains respond to pictures of food.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Children who ate more ultra-processed foods indicated stronger brain responses to food pictures, which were linked to greater body fat gain later.

Breakfast cereal, packaged bread and instant soup get blamed for childhood weight gain because of what’s in them.

A upcoming study links children’s ultra-processed food intake to how their brains respond to pictures of food.

A year later, the children with stronger reactions had gained more body fat. Every child was a healthy weight when the study began, and this kind of study can show a link but not prove a cause.

According to recent reports, dr. Kathleen Page, a physician and professor of medicine and pediatrics at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, is the study’s senior author, and Jasmin Alves is the first author.

“Children’s brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It’s an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment,” Dr. Page remarked.

The 46 children were 7 to 10 years old and part of the BrainChild study.

That long-running project follows children whose mothers did or did not have diabetes during pregnancy, and it recruits them through Kaiser Permanente Southern California.

Each child had a BMI below the 85th percentile for their age and sex.

On two separate days, each child and a parent walked trained staff through everything the child had eaten in the previous 24 hours.

It has been revealed that the researchers then sorted every food by how processed it was. On average, ultra-processed foods supplied about 68% of the children’s daily calories, close to the 67% a 2021 analysis found for American kids as a whole.

About a month later, each child lay in an MRI scanner after a 12-hour fast and then a glucose drink.

The scanner recorded how active two deep brain areas were during the food photos.

Both areas are part of a structure called the striatum, which handles motivation, learning and reward.

The ventral striatum is involved in anticipating and experiencing rewards. The dorsal striatum helps link cues with learned actions and habits.

Children who got more of their calories from ultra-processed foods had stronger dorsal striatum responses to the food photos.

According to recent reports, the ventral striatum indicated no clear pattern. The association with dorsal striatum responses remained after accounting for each child’s age, sex, body size and whether their mother had diabetes during pregnancy.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dr. Page emphasized that the association held even after the researchers accounted for total calorie intake, suggesting that how much children ate did not fully explain the pattern.

The children also consumed a standardized drink before their scans, “so the stronger response to food cues wasn’t simply due to hunger,” she noted.

Rodent studies had already shown that a steady diet of sugar-rich food changes how the dorsal striatum works.

No earlier study had looked directly at how much ultra-processed food people habitually eat and how their striatum responds, the authors wrote.

The children came back for measurements roughly a year later, with an average gap of about 15 months.

Their BMI had risen by one point on average, their body fat by close to one percentage point, and their waists by about 1.5 inches (3.9 centimeters).

In a recent development, children whose dorsal striatum had reacted more strongly to the food photos gained more in BMI and body fat. Eating more ultra-processed food was linked to a bigger waist a year later.

Ultra-processed food intake’s links to BMI and body fat were weak enough that chance could explain them.

The team then asked how much of the link between diet and fat gain involved the brain.

Once the dorsal striatum response was in the model, the association between ultra-processed food and body fat gain shrank by 44%, and the one with BMI by 31%.

Dr. Page said the result does more than repeat that these foods are tied to weight gain, because it points to a pathway in the brain.

“It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time.”.

Recent findings suggest that what stood out most to Dr. Page was that every child was a healthy weight when the study began.

“This suggests that the link between ultra-processed foods and the brain’s response to food cues may be detectable before obesity develops, rather than simply resulting from excess weight,” she told Earth.com.

Added sugar is in most ultra-processed foods, so the team checked whether sugar was driving the result.

Children who ate more added sugar tended to have stronger striatum responses too, but the pattern wasn’t clear enough to rule out chance.

When the team accounted for added sugar, the link between ultra-processed food and the dorsal striatum weakened and was no longer statistically clear.

Still, the authors wrote that sugar is unlikely to be the whole story.

In a recent development, forty-six children is a small group, and the authors wrote that this limited their power to detect modest effects. Brain scans of this kind are also hard to reproduce in small groups.

Each child was scanned only once, so no one knows yet whether the stronger responses persist or fade as children get older.

An observational study like this one can’t say which came first. Children whose reward circuits already react more strongly to food may be the ones who reach for ultra-processed foods, rather than the other way around.

And because every child started at a healthy weight, the pattern may look different in children who already carry extra weight.

The research team stated the burden shouldn’t fall only on families and children, because these foods are often the most accessible, affordable and convenient ones available.

Sources indicate that “Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution,” Dr. Page noted.

It has been revealed that for families in the meantime, Dr. Page said the practical goal is to shift the overall diet toward more minimally processed foods. “Parents should not feel that they have to eliminate every packaged food.”.

Her examples were water instead of soda and fruit instead of fruit juice or fruit snacks. The aim is more vegetables, beans, nuts, eggs and other foods closer to their original form.

One way to test whether the diet is driving the brain response is to change the diet.

Industry observers note that “A future intervention study could test whether replacing ultra-processed foods with mostly minimally processed foods changes how children’s brains respond to food cues and helps prevent excess body-fat gain,” Dr. Page said.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild team will keep following these children through puberty and into young adulthood.

Dr. Page stated the next step is to see how their diets relate to changes in the developing brain. The team will also look at their risk for obesity over time.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

Carbon sinking into Antarctica’s deep ocean holds a surprise

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses Antarctica’s continental shelf, offering new insight into the ocean’s carbon cycle.
  • A recent study suggests that dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses the Antarctic continental shelf and sinks toward the deep ocean.
  • Despite abundant marine life and shifting water masses, researchers found little change in its amount or chemical composition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses Antarctica’s continental shelf, offering new insight into the ocean’s carbon cycle.

A recent study suggests that dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses the Antarctic continental shelf and sinks toward the deep ocean.

Despite abundant marine life and shifting water masses, researchers found little change in its amount or chemical composition.

The study drew on water samples from two expeditions aboard the Polarstern, an icebreaker operated by the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research (AWI).

It has been revealed that ocean currents move water around the globe in a vast circulation system. The Antarctic continental shelf plays an essential part.

Industry observers note that deep water arrives from the north and rises onto the shelf. Extreme cold and sea ice formation make it denser.

This heavy water then sinks into the deep ocean. It helps form Antarctic bottom water, the coldest, densest, and one of the most voluminous water masses in the world’s oceans.

As the water crosses the shelf, it passes abundant marine life. Researchers wanted to know if these processes change the carbon before the water sinks.

The answer matters since rising temperatures and declining sea ice could change how the Southern Ocean stores and transports carbon.

Recent findings suggest that the southern Weddell Sea shelf is a key place for Antarctic bottom water formation. It is remote and hard to reach. Studying it depends on specialized research vessels like the Polarstern.

In a recent development, dissolved organic matter plays a crucial role in the global carbon cycle. It is released during the production and breakdown of marine life.

Recent findings suggest that this matter holds tens of thousands of different compounds. Some are rapidly eaten by microbes, while others persist for a long time.

Industry observers note that it is the largest reservoir of organic carbon in the ocean. Understanding how it changes and moves is key to predicting the ocean’s response to climate change.

It has been revealed that the team analyzed water samples from two Polarstern expeditions to the southern Weddell Sea (2016 and 2021). To find out whether the carbon changed, the team used several complementary methods.

Industry observers note that the Institute for Chemistry and Biology of the Marine Environment (ICBM) at the University of Oldenburg has a distinctive collection of advanced analytical instruments. These allow detailed study of the molecular make-up and structure of complex organic matter mixtures.

State-of-the-art analytics at AWI’s MICADAS (Mini Carbon Dating System) facility helped the team determine the age of the carbon.

The shelf sees intense seasonal blooms of phytoplankton, so scientists expected freshly produced organic matter that microbes can readily break down to leave a clear molecular imprint on the sinking water.

Instead, they found almost no detectable change in the amount or composition of dissolved organic matter carried into the deep ocean.

The key to this paradox is time. Dense waters stay on the Weddell Sea continental shelf for an unusually long period, between six and twelve years.

During this time, the water also circulates beneath the large Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf.

The researchers suggest that this extended stay gives microbes time to break down newly produced organic matter, converting its carbon into dissolved inorganic carbon before the water leaves the shelf.

“Our study reveals that the molecular properties of dissolved organic matter are conserved during deep-water formation in the southern Weddell Sea,” noted lead author Gonzalo Gomez-Saez from AWI.

“Our findings highlight dissolved organic matter as a stable component of the regional Southern Ocean carbon cycle.”.

It has been revealed that “Dissolved organic matter is a huge and complex store of carbon in the ocean. By examining its molecules in detail, we can investigate how it changes as water moves through the Antarctic continental shelf,” added senior author Thorsten Dittmar from ICBM.

The findings suggest that this large carbon store changes little during water movement and transformation on the southern Weddell Sea shelf.

“Global warming is now reaching the Antarctic shelf seas. If the large reservoir of dissolved organic matter is scarcely affected by processes on the shelf, this suggests that this carbon reservoir could remain largely unaffected by climate change in this region,” stated study co-author Moritz Holtappels from AWI.

But not all ocean carbon behaves the same way.

Dissolved organic carbon remained largely stable in this study, while other forms of carbon may respond differently to environmental change.

That includes organic particles sinking to the seabed and dissolved inorganic carbon in seawater. These may react more to changes in temperature, sea ice cover, and marine life.

Researchers will keep studying how different forms of carbon respond to environmental change.

One effort is Antarctica InSync, an international initiative bringing scientists together to study the rapidly changing Antarctic environment.

Oceanographer and co-author Alexander Haumann will help lead a Polarstern expedition in 2028.

The team will investigate how carbon moves through the Southern Ocean during the Antarctic winter.

These observations will help scientists understand how climate change may affect the ocean’s ability to transport and store carbon.

Intense biological activity does not necessarily leave a lasting imprint on the dissolved organic matter carried into the deep ocean.

In the southern Weddell Sea, the water’s long journey across the shelf may help explain why.

Microbes get years, not weeks, to finish the job.

That stability is good news in one sense. This carbon reservoir may hold up as the region warms.

In a recent development, but it is not a blanket reassurance. Other carbon pools could shift.

It has been revealed that the team’s next steps will probe those differences. For now, the southern Weddell Sea offers a rare case of carbon holding steady in a changing world.

The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single nuclear explosion in space would wipe out 98 per cent of satellites within a week, sending vital technology around the world into disarray from which it would take years to recover, warn experts.

In a recent development, zachary Petersen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and his colleagues modelled the effect of a 1 megaton explosion 500 kilometres above the South Atlantic. They found that an initial spike of X-rays from the blast was damaging, but it wasn’t the most disruptive part: electrons released by radioactive fission would become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, exposing satellites to a kind of artificial radiation belt, over and over again.

Industry observers note that this level of exposure would take out 98 per cent of satellites within one week. And while many spacecraft use specialised computer chips that are more resistant to radiation, the researchers found that even when they altered their simulations to assume that satellites were three times more resilient to radiation damage, the effects were still disastrous, with 97 per cent still failing within two weeks.

UK military taps up astronomers to spot snooping foreign satellites.

Worryingly, such explosions aren’t without precedent. The US detonated a 1.4 megaton nuclear bomb at an altitude of 400 km in 1962. Satellites were disrupted by the blast, but Earth was orbited by only a relatively small number of devices at the time – humans have now rolled out around 25,000 objects into space, many of which still orbit the planet. Global navigation systems like GPS, internet connections and weather forecasts rely on these satellites and the data they provide.

A nuclear explosion in space would probably have long-lasting repercussions, not only because satellites would need to be replaced, but because there would be an estimated 20 collisions within two years as broken satellites drifted aimlessly. Those collisions present a risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical scenario in which debris hits other satellites, creating more debris and a chain reaction of destruction that would make orbit lethal to future launches for decades, or even longer.

The Outer Space Treaty now bans the launch of nuclear weapons into space, and all major spacefaring nations are party to it. But tensions remain. In 2024 a vote was raised at the UN to reaffirm commitment to the rule, which Russia vetoed. Earlier that year, the US had warned that Russia plans to launch a space weapon with possible nuclear capabilities.

Petersen and his colleagues didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but Craig Underwood at the University of Surrey, UK, indicates the consequences of losing so many of our satellites would be catastrophic for society because we are so dependent on space technology.

“The recent low-Earth orbit mega constellations [like Starlink] would be particularly affected,” states Underwood. “During the Cold War, much thought was given to protecting critical space systems and our societies were much less dependent on electronic technology. I suspect that since the 1990s, less attention has been paid to the prospect of having to survive a nuclear conflict. Our civil defence infrastructure has been dismantled, and society is much more vulnerable.”.

In a recent development, “While individual satellites can, in principle, be replaced relatively quickly, recovery would not be straightforward. New satellites would have to be debuted into an environment still affected by elevated radiation levels and increased debris, potentially limiting their operational lifetime and effectiveness. As a result, restoring orbital infrastructure could take years,” says Chantal Cappelletti at the University of Nottingham, UK. “The result would not be an immediate collapse of modern society, but rather a prolonged degradation of many services that we now take for granted. Recovery would likely require years of rebuilding orbital infrastructure while managing elevated radiation and debris hazards.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans.
  • Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties.
  • Sources indicate that “Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans. Across Egypt, the cemeteries of Bubastis in the eastern Nile Delta, the Bubasteion in northern Saqqara, and Speos Artemidos near Beni Hassan, along with others in Giza and the Dakhla Oasis, were meant for animals, especially cats. Cats were seen as the earthly embodiment of the feline goddess Bastet. Yet although they were often mummified as votive offerings, their treatment did not always match their status.

Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties. Some animal mummies were used as ship ballast for the journey home after an expedition, while others were powdered for questionable medicine, burned for fuel, or ground into fertilizer. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, however, some animal mummies were unwrapped (without a party) so that their skeletal remains could inform studies of Egyptian fauna. Many of these skulls remain in museum collections in Egypt and abroad. Zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences and his research team studied one such collection: 131 exceptionally well-preserved skulls of small cats from Beni Hassan, now housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Their goal was to find out how the cats lived before they died.

Sources indicate that “Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. In addition to carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis to determine diet, “characteristics such as dental abnormalities, infectious or metabolic disorders and trauma were recorded.”.

Most of the skulls turned out to be from domestic cats (Felis catus), with several jungle cats (Felis chaus) among them. Many of the animals apparently suffered from conditions such as gum disease and infections, and some skulls had puncture marks and fractures that could indicate fights between cats. How the cats met their end, however, was more disturbing. Evidence suggests that cats were deliberately killed so they could be turned into offerings to Bastet. Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma. Sharp-force trauma is thought to have possibly killed the humans who were sacrificed to join First Dynasty pharaohs in the afterlife. Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.

Industry observers note that when Van Neer and his team took a closer look at one skull, they found marks consistent with blows from a sharp metal weapon. Wounds on some of the other skulls were thought to have been made by strikes from a heavy wooden implement. The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today. Isotope analysis showed that the jungle cats’ diet clearly differed from that of the domestic cats, further suggesting that this species was unlikely to have been bred in captivity.

Sources indicate that even among the wild-caught jungle cats, six of the seven skulls came from animals with conditions similar to those of their domestic relatives. This was probably a sign that all of the cats, the overwhelming majority of which were adults, were kept in conditions that caused illness and injury before death. Radiocarbon dating revealed when they died.

Cats are generally thought to have first been domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago, although some recent genetic studies suggest it happened later, in Egypt or elsewhere in North Africa. In Egypt, the earliest clear evidence of domestic cats dates to the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 B.C.E.). However, demand for mummified cat offerings was greatest much later, in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods. Older feline mummies do exist, and one of the nine dated skulls goes back to the Third Intermediate Period. The other eight, however, date to between 380 and 40 B.C.E., from the end of the Late Period into the Ptolemaic era.

Industry observers note that as for how the cats were killed, blunt- or sharp-force trauma appears to have been the main cause of death. Some cats were strangled, but a blow to the head was apparently the more common method. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers mentioned. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”.
